abstract: We present the "Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network" (MS-TDNN) as an extension of the TDNN to robust word recognition. Unlike most other hybrid methods. the MS-TDNN embeds an alignment search procedure into the con(cid:173) nectionist architecture. and allows for word level supervision. The resulting system has the ability to manage the sequential order of subword units. while optimizing for the recognizer performance. In this paper we present extensive new evaluations of this approach over speaker-dependent and speaker-indepen(cid:173) dent connected alphabet.

Unlike most other hybrid methods. the MS-TDNN embeds an alignment search procedure into the con(cid:173) nectionist architecture. and allows for word level supervision. paragraphs: This paper extends the time-delay neural network into a Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network for word recognition. A central issue is how to manage the sequence of smaller speech units that makes up a word. Recognizing those components must be coordinated with their order and their alignment to the incoming speech.

The architecture embeds an alignment search inside the neural system and allows supervision at the word level. This connects the handling of subword sequences directly to the recognition objective. Training can therefore operate on the desired word outcome while the architecture manages the internal alignment needed to relate that outcome to the speech signal.

The paper presents extensive evaluations on connected alphabet speech in both speaker-dependent and speaker-independent settings. These settings examine the approach with different relationships between training speakers and recognition use. The central contribution is the integration of alignment and neural recognition within one architecture, making sequential organization part of the system being optimized for recognizer performance.
summary.tldr: The MS-TDNN embeds alignment search within a neural speech recognizer, enabling word-level supervision while managing subword order.

title: Multi-State Time Delay Networks for Continuous Speech Recognition

abstract: A method is described for generating plan-like. reflexive. obstacle avoidance behaviour in a mobile robot. The experiments reported here use a simulated vehicle with a primitive range sensor. Avoidance behaviour is encoded as a set of continuous functions of the perceptual input space. These functions are stored using CMACs and trained by a variant of Barto and Sutton's adaptive critic algorithm. As the vehicle explores its surroundings it adapts its responses to sensory stimuli so as to minimise the negative reinforcement arising from collisions. Strategies for local navigation are therefore acquired in an explicitly goal-driven fashion. The resulting trajectories form elegant collision(cid:173) free paths through the environment

paragraphs: The paper investigates how a mobile robot can learn obstacle avoidance through experience. Its experiments use a simulated vehicle equipped with a simple range sensor. The aim is to produce immediate responses to sensory input that nevertheless form organized, plan-like paths through the environment.

Avoidance behavior is represented by continuous functions over the space of perceptual inputs. These functions are stored using CMAC representations and trained with a variant of the adaptive critic algorithm. As the vehicle explores, collisions supply negative reinforcement, and the learned responses change to reduce that negative feedback.

The reported trajectories are collision-free paths through the simulated environment. Their significance is that coherent local navigation emerges from sensory responses trained toward an explicit objective: avoiding collisions. The work connects reflexive control with reinforcement learning by showing how feedback from exploration can shape a set of immediate response functions into behavior that looks organized over an extended path.
summary.tldr: A simulated vehicle learns collision-free local navigation by adapting continuous sensory responses to collision penalties.

title: Obstacle Avoidance through Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper discusses the parameterization of speech by an analog cochlear model. The tradeoff between time and frequency resolution is viewed as the fundamental difference between conventional spectrographic analysis and cochlear signal processing for broadband, rapid-changing signals. The model's response exhibits a wavelet-like analysis in the scale domain that preserves good temporal resolution; the frequency of each spectral compo(cid:173) nent in a broadband signal can be accurately determined from the inter(cid:173) peak intervals in the instantaneous firing rates of auditory fibers. Such properties of the cochlear model are demonstrated with natural speech and synthetic complex signals.

Such properties of the cochlear model are demonstrated with natural speech and synthetic complex signals.

paragraphs: This paper explores how an analog model of the cochlea can represent speech. Its starting point is the tension between identifying frequencies precisely and locating rapid changes in time. That tension is particularly important for broadband signals, which contain multiple frequency components and can change too quickly for a single fixed analysis resolution to capture everything clearly.

The model produces a response resembling wavelet analysis across scales while retaining good temporal resolution. It also carries frequency information in the timing of its auditory-fiber responses. Specifically, the intervals between peaks in instantaneous firing rates allow the frequencies of individual components in a broadband signal to be determined accurately.

The authors demonstrate these properties using natural speech and synthetic complex signals. The significance is that frequency information need not be read only from a conventional spectral display: response timing also provides useful structure. The cochlear model combines analysis across scales with a temporal code, offering a way to describe rapidly changing speech while preserving information about its constituent frequencies.
summary.tldr: An analog cochlear model combines wavelet-like analysis with response timing to preserve rapid changes and identify frequencies in speech.

title: Analog Cochlear Model for Multiresolution Speech Analysis

abstract: Networks with local inhibition are shown to have enhanced compu(cid:173) tational performance with respect to the classical Hopfield-like net(cid:173) works. In particular the critical capacity of the network is increased as well as its capability to store correlated patterns. Chaotic dy(cid:173) namic behaviour (exponentially long transients) of the devices in(cid:173) dicates the overloading of the associative memory. An implementa(cid:173) tion based on a programmable logic device is here presented. A 16 neurons circuit is implemented whit a XILINK 4020 device. The peculiarity of this solution is the possibility to change parts of the project (weights, transfer function or the whole architecture) with a simple software download of the configuration into the XILINK chip.

paragraphs: The paper studies associative neural networks with local inhibition, where inhibitory interactions shape how activity develops. It reports improved computational performance relative to classical Hopfield-like networks. Two specific benefits are increased critical storage capacity and a greater ability to store correlated patterns, which share structure rather than being entirely distinct.

The network's dynamics also provide information about memory overload. When too much is stored, the devices exhibit chaotic behavior with exponentially long transients. A transient is the period before the system settles into its eventual behavior, so prolonged unsettled activity becomes an indicator that the associative memory has exceeded its useful loading regime.

The authors connect this analysis to a programmable hardware implementation containing 16 neurons. A major feature is reconfigurability: weights, transfer functions, or even the architecture can be changed by downloading a new configuration to the chip. The work therefore combines a claim about improved memory behavior with a concrete implementation that supports modifying the network design through software.
summary.tldr: Local inhibition improves associative-memory capacity and correlated-pattern storage, with the design demonstrated in a reconfigurable 16-neuron circuit.

title: Attractor Neural Networks with Local Inhibition: from Statistical Physics to a Digitial Programmable Integrated Circuit

abstract: Functional complexity of a software module can be measured in terms of static complexity metrics of the program text. Classify(cid:173) ing software modules, based on their static complexity measures, into different fault-prone categories is a difficult problem in soft(cid:173) ware engineering. This research investigates the applicability of neural network classifiers for identifying fault-prone software mod(cid:173) ules using a data set from a commercial software system. A pre(cid:173) liminary empirical comparison is performed between a minimum distance based Gaussian classifier, a perceptron classifier and a multilayer layer feed-forward network classifier constructed using a modified Cascade-Correlation algorithm. The modified version of the Cascade-Correlation algorithm constrains the growth of the network size by incorporating a cross-validation check during the output layer training phase. Our preliminary results suggest that a multilayer feed-forward network can be used as a tool for iden(cid:173) tifying fault-prone software modules early during the development cycle. Other issues such as representation of software metrics and selection of a proper training samples are also discussed.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether neural networks can identify software modules likely to contain faults using static complexity measurements from program text. These measurements describe aspects of a module's functional complexity. The classification problem is to translate them into fault-proneness categories, potentially providing useful information early in software development.

Using data from a commercial software system, the authors make a preliminary comparison among a minimum-distance Gaussian classifier, a perceptron, and a multilayer feedforward network. The multilayer network is built with a modified Cascade-Correlation algorithm. Its modification introduces a cross-validation check during output-layer training to constrain growth in network size.

The preliminary results suggest that a multilayer network can help identify fault-prone modules early in the development cycle. The abstract supports this applicability claim without identifying a decisive winner among all compared methods. The paper also discusses how software metrics should be represented and how training examples should be selected. These choices connect the classifier's design to the practical problem of turning code measurements into useful predictions.
summary.tldr: A commercial-software case study suggests that multilayer networks can use static code metrics to identify fault-prone modules early.

title: Identifying Fault-Prone Software Modules Using Feed-Forward Networks: A Case Study

abstract: We use mean-field theory methods from Statistical Mechanics to derive the "softmax" nonlinearity from the discontinuous winner(cid:173) take-all (WTA) mapping. We give two simple ways of implementing "soft max" as a multiterminal network element. One of these has a number of important network-theoretic properties. It is a recipro(cid:173) cal, passive, incrementally passive, nonlinear, resistive multitermi(cid:173) nal element with a content function having the form of information(cid:173) theoretic entropy. These properties should enable one to use this element in nonlinear RC networks with such other reciprocal el(cid:173) ements as resistive fuses and constraint boxes to implement very high speed analog optimization algorithms using a minimum of hardware.

paragraphs: The paper derives softmax from a discontinuous winner-take-all mapping using mean-field methods from statistical mechanics. Winner-take-all selects a winning input through an abrupt decision. The derivation connects that competition mechanism with the softmax nonlinearity, providing a theoretical route between the two forms of network behavior.

The authors also describe two simple implementations of softmax as a network element with multiple terminals. One implementation has several useful circuit properties: it is reciprocal, passive, incrementally passive, nonlinear, and resistive. Its content function has the mathematical form of information-theoretic entropy. These properties connect the element's nonlinear computation with quantities and relationships useful in network analysis.

The proposed application is analog optimization using nonlinear resistor-capacitor networks. The authors suggest combining the softmax element with other reciprocal components, including resistive fuses and constraint boxes, to obtain very fast optimization with little hardware. This is presented as an opportunity enabled by the element's properties. The contribution combines a statistical-mechanical derivation with circuit implementations suited to that proposed use.
summary.tldr: The paper derives softmax from winner-take-all competition and proposes analog implementations with properties useful for optimization circuits.

title: The "Softmax" Nonlinearity: Derivation Using Statistical Mechanics and Useful Properties as a Multiterminal Analog Circuit Element

abstract: A fundamental open problem in computer vision-determining pose and correspondence between two sets of points in space(cid:173) is solved with a novel, robust and easily implementable algorithm. The technique works on noisy point sets that may be of unequal sizes and may differ by non-rigid transformations. A 2D varia(cid:173) tion calculates the pose between point sets related by an affine transformation-translation, rotation, scale and shear. A 3D to 3D variation calculates translation and rotation. An objective describ(cid:173) ing the problem is derived from Mean field theory. The objective is minimized with clocked (EM-like) dynamics. Experiments with both handwritten and synthetic data provide empirical evidence for the method.

The technique works on noisy point sets that may be of unequal sizes and may differ by non-rigid transformations. A 2D varia(cid:173) tion calculates the pose between point sets related by an affine transformation-translation, rotation, scale and shear. A 3D to 3D variation calculates translation and rotation. An objective describ(cid:173) ing the problem is derived from Mean field theory. The objective is minimized with clocked (EM-like) dynamics. paragraphs: The paper addresses two linked questions in matching point sets: which points correspond, and how the sets are positioned relative to one another. These questions arise together because the apparent match between points depends on alignment. The authors propose an algorithm that handles noisy sets, unequal numbers of points, and differences that can include nonrigid transformations.

Two variants cover different alignment models. The two-dimensional version estimates an affine transformation, including translation, rotation, scale, and shear. The three-dimensional version estimates translation and rotation between two three-dimensional point sets. These distinctions specify the transformations recovered by each version of the method.

The authors derive an objective from mean field theory and minimize it using clocked dynamics resembling expectation-maximization. This provides a shared optimization formulation for pose and correspondence. Experiments on handwritten and synthetic data offer empirical support for the approach. The contribution is a robust, readily implementable matching procedure designed to cope with point sets that do not arrive as clean, equally sized copies.
summary.tldr: A mean-field-based optimization method jointly estimates point correspondences and alignment for noisy two- and three-dimensional data.

title: New Algorithms for 2D and 3D Point Matching: Pose Estimation and Correspondence

abstract: An extended version of the dual constraint model of motor end(cid:173) plate morphogenesis is presented that includes activity dependent and independent competition. It is supported by a wide range of recent neurophysiological evidence that indicates a strong relation(cid:173) ship between synaptic efficacy and survival. The computational model is justified at the molecular level and its predictions match the developmental and regenerative behaviour of real synapses.
originalAbstract: An extended version of the dual constraint model of motor end(cid:173) plate morphogenesis is presented that includes activity dependent and independent competition. It is supported by a wide range of recent neurophysiological evidence that indicates a strong relation(cid:173) ship between synaptic efficacy and survival. The computational model is justified at the molecular level and its predictions match the developmental and regenerative behaviour of real synapses.

paragraphs: The paper extends a computational model of how motor endplates develop at the junction between nerves and muscles. Its focus is synaptic competition: how the connections involved in this organization persist or are lost. The proposed extension includes competition that depends on activity as well as competition that does not.

The model is motivated by neurophysiological evidence linking synaptic efficacy with synaptic survival. Efficacy concerns how effectively a connection functions, while survival concerns whether it remains present. Bringing both activity-dependent and activity-independent competition into the dual constraint model allows these influences to be considered within the same account of synaptic organization.

The authors provide a molecular justification for the computational model and report that its predictions match the behavior of real synapses during development and regeneration. Agreement in both settings matters because the model addresses the formation and reformation of connections. The contribution links functional effectiveness, competition, and biological mechanisms in an explanation of which synapses survive.
summary.tldr: An extended synaptic competition model combines activity-dependent and independent mechanisms to explain developmental and regenerative behavior.

title: The Role of Activity in Synaptic Competition at the Neuromuscular Junction

abstract: In this article, we propose a new reinforcement learning (RL) method based on an actor-critic architecture. The actor and the critic are approximated by Normalized Gaussian Networks (NGnet), which are networks of local linear regression units. The NGnet is trained by the on-line EM algorithm proposed in our pre(cid:173) vious paper. We apply our RL method to the task of swinging-up and stabilizing a single pendulum and the task of balancing a dou(cid:173) ble pendulum near the upright position. The experimental results show that our RL method can be applied to optimal control prob(cid:173) lems having continuous state/action spaces and that the method achieves good control with a small number of trial-and-errors.
originalAbstract: In this article, we propose a new reinforcement learning (RL) method based on an actor-critic architecture. The actor and the critic are approximated by Normalized Gaussian Networks (NGnet), which are networks of local linear regression units. The NGnet is trained by the on-line EM algorithm proposed in our pre(cid:173) vious paper. We apply our RL method to the task of swinging-up and stabilizing a single pendulum and the task of balancing a dou(cid:173) ble pendulum near the upright position. The experimental results show that our RL method can be applied to optimal control prob(cid:173) lems having continuous state/action spaces and that the method achieves good control with a small number of trial-and-errors.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a reinforcement learning method using an actor–critic architecture. The actor supplies the action-selection component, while the critic provides an evaluation component. Both are represented by Normalized Gaussian Networks, which combine local linear regression units. This gives the two parts of the learning system a shared type of function approximation.

The networks are trained with an online expectation-maximization algorithm developed in the authors' earlier work. The combination brings that network-training procedure into reinforcement learning for control problems with continuous states and actions. The local regression units provide the representation through which the actor and critic learn their respective functions.

The authors test the method on swinging up and stabilizing a single pendulum and on balancing a double pendulum near its upright position. The experimental results show good control with a small number of trial-and-error attempts. These findings support the method's applicability to continuous optimal-control problems through the demonstrated pendulum tasks, without establishing that every such problem will require similarly few trials.
summary.tldr: An actor–critic method trained through online EM achieves good continuous pendulum control with relatively few trial-and-error attempts.

title: Reinforcement Learning Based on On-Line EM Algorithm

abstract: Visual search is the task of finding a target in an image against a background of distractors. Unique features of targets enable them to pop out against the background, while targets defined by lacks of features or conjunctions of features are more difficult to spot. It is known that the ease of target detection can change when the roles of figure and ground are switched. The mechanisms underlying the ease of pop out and asymmetry in visual search have been elusive. This paper shows that a model of segmentation in VI based on intracortical interactions can explain many of the qualitative aspects of visual search.
originalAbstract: Visual search is the task of finding a target in an image against a background of distractors. Unique features of targets enable them to pop out against the background, while targets defined by lacks of features or conjunctions of features are more difficult to spot. It is known that the ease of target detection can change when the roles of figure and ground are switched. The mechanisms underlying the ease of pop out and asymmetry in visual search have been elusive. This paper shows that a model of segmentation in VI based on intracortical interactions can explain many of the qualitative aspects of visual search.

paragraphs: Visual search involves locating a target among distracting items. A target with a distinctive feature can stand out immediately, while one identified by an absent feature or a combination of features can be harder to find. The paper addresses the mechanisms behind these differences in the ease of detecting a target.

A second puzzle is that exchanging the target and the background can change search difficulty. The same pair of visual patterns can therefore produce different search experiences depending on which pattern forms the background. Explaining this asymmetry requires accounting for the relationship between a target and its surroundings, alongside the properties of the target itself.

The paper shows that a model of segmentation in primary visual cortex, V1, based on interactions within the cortex can explain many qualitative aspects of visual search. Its contribution is to connect the separation of visual regions with both pop-out and search asymmetry. The stated result concerns qualitative patterns of behavior, supporting this cortical interaction model as an explanation for several observed search phenomena.
summary.tldr: A V1 segmentation model based on intracortical interactions explains many qualitative patterns of visual pop-out and search asymmetry.

title: A V1 Model of Pop Out and Asymmetty in Visual Search

abstract: We investigate a general characteristic of the trade-off in learning problems between goodness-of-fit and model complexity. Specifically we characterize a general class of learning problems where the goodness-of-fit function can be shown to be convex within firstorder as a function of model complexity. This general property of "diminishing returns" is illustrated on a number of real data sets and learning problems, including finite mixture modeling and multivariate linear regression.
originalAbstract: We investigate a general characteristic of the trade-off in learning problems between goodness-of-fit and model complexity. Specifically we characterize a general class of learning problems where the goodness-of-fit function can be shown to be convex within firstorder as a function of model complexity. This general property of "diminishing returns" is illustrated on a number of real data sets and learning problems, including finite mixture modeling and multivariate linear regression.

paragraphs: The paper investigates the relationship between model complexity and goodness of fit in learning problems. Its focus is the pattern of improvement as a model becomes more complex. The authors study when this relationship has a diminishing-returns character, so that adding complexity brings progressively smaller gains in fit.

The theoretical contribution is to characterize a general class of learning problems for which the goodness-of-fit function has a first-order convexity property as a function of complexity. This gives a mathematical description of the trade-off within that class. The claim concerns problems satisfying the characterization, rather than every possible learning task or model family.

The paper illustrates the property using several real datasets and learning problems, including finite mixture modeling and multivariate linear regression. These examples show the same broad question arising in different settings: how much additional fit accompanies additional complexity? The contribution is a shared account of that relationship, helping explain why increasingly elaborate models can deliver diminishing improvements in the fit being measured.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes a class of learning problems with diminishing returns in goodness of fit as model complexity increases.

title: Model Complexity, Goodness of Fit and Diminishing Returns

abstract: We propose analysis of information in speech using three sources - language (phone), speaker and channeL Information in speech is measured as mutual information between the source and the set of features extracted from speech signaL We assume that distribu(cid:173) tion of features can be modeled using Gaussian distribution. The mutual information is computed using the results of analysis of variability in speech. We observe similarity in the results of phone variability and phone information, and show that the results of the proposed analysis have more meaningful interpretations than the analysis of variability.

The mutual information is computed using the results of analysis of variability in speech. paragraphs: The paper analyzes what speech features reveal about three sources of variation: the phone being spoken, the speaker, and the channel. These sources describe different aspects of the same signal. The aim is to express their contributions in terms of information, giving the analysis a direct interpretation in relation to each source.

The authors measure mutual information between a source and the features extracted from speech. In plain terms, this concerns how much observing the features tells us about that source. Their calculation uses results from an analysis of speech variability and assumes that the feature distribution can be modeled as Gaussian.

For phones, the authors observe similar patterns in the variability analysis and the information analysis. They nevertheless report that the information-based results support more meaningful interpretations. The contribution is therefore a way to turn variability findings into statements about information carried by speech features, under the stated distributional assumption, while retaining a connection to the earlier variability view.
summary.tldr: Under a Gaussian feature assumption, the paper converts speech variability analysis into information measures for phones, speakers, and channels.

title: Analysis of Information in Speech Based on MANOVA

abstract: A distance-based conditional model on the ranking poset is presented for use in classiﬁcation and ranking. The model is an extension of the Mallows model, and generalizes the classiﬁer combination methods used by several ensemble learning algorithms, including error correcting output codes, discrete AdaBoost, logistic regression and cranking. The algebraic structure of the ranking poset leads to a simple Bayesian inter- pretation of the conditional model and its special cases. In addition to a unifying view, the framework suggests a probabilistic interpretation for error correcting output codes and an extension beyond the binary coding scheme.
originalAbstract: A distance-based conditional model on the ranking poset is presented for use in classiﬁcation and ranking. The model is an extension of the Mallows model, and generalizes the classiﬁer combination methods used by several ensemble learning algorithms, including error correcting output codes, discrete AdaBoost, logistic regression and cranking. The algebraic structure of the ranking poset leads to a simple Bayesian inter- pretation of the conditional model and its special cases. In addition to a unifying view, the framework suggests a probabilistic interpretation for error correcting output codes and an extension beyond the binary coding scheme.

paragraphs: Classification and ranking both involve expressing preferences among possible outputs. This paper presents a distance-based conditional model on a ranking poset, an ordered mathematical structure for rankings. The model extends the Mallows model and provides a framework for studying classification and ranking within the same probabilistic construction.

A central contribution is showing how the framework generalizes combination methods used in several learning algorithms. These include error-correcting output codes, discrete AdaBoost, logistic regression, and cranking. Bringing these methods into one model makes their relationships explicit rather than treating each combination rule as a separate construction.

The algebraic structure also gives the conditional model and its special cases a simple Bayesian interpretation. In particular, the framework suggests a probabilistic reading of error-correcting output codes and a way to extend them beyond binary coding. The stated contribution is thus both explanatory and constructive: it unifies existing methods and indicates a broader family of output representations for classification.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model over rankings unifies several classifier combination methods and suggests output codes beyond binary schemes.

title: Conditional Models on the Ranking Poset
Local Phase Coherence and the Perception of Blur

abstract: It has been demonstrated that basic aspects of human visual motion perception are qualitatively consistent with a Bayesian estimation framework, where the prior probability distribution on velocity favors slow speeds. Here, we present a refined probabilistic model that can account for the typical trial-to-trial variabilities observed in psychophysical speed perception experiments. We also show that data from such experiments can be used to constrain both the likelihood and prior functions of the model. Specifically, we measured matching speeds and thresholds in a two-alternative forced choice speed discrimination task. Parametric fits to the data reveal that the likelihood function is well approximated by a LogNormal distribution with a characteristic contrast-dependent variance, and that the prior distribution on velocity exhibits significantly heavier tails than a Gaussian, and approximately follows a power-law function.
originalAbstract: It has been demonstrated that basic aspects of human visual motion perception are qualitatively consistent with a Bayesian estimation framework, where the prior probability distribution on velocity favors slow speeds. Here, we present a refined probabilistic model that can account for the typical trial-to-trial variabilities observed in psychophysical speed perception experiments. We also show that data from such experiments can be used to constrain both the likelihood and prior functions of the model. Specifically, we measured matching speeds and thresholds in a two-alternative forced choice speed discrimination task. Parametric fits to the data reveal that the likelihood function is well approximated by a LogNormal distribution with a characteristic contrast-dependent variance, and that the prior distribution on velocity exhibits significantly heavier tails than a Gaussian, and approximately follows a power-law function.

paragraphs: The paper refines a Bayesian account of how people perceive visual speed. Earlier work had shown qualitative agreement with a model whose prior favors slow motion. The authors extend that account to explain the variability in judgments across repeated trials, bringing the model closer to the measurements collected in speed-perception experiments.

They measure matching speeds and discrimination thresholds in a task where participants choose between two alternatives. These measurements constrain both the likelihood, which describes the sensory evidence in the model, and the prior, which expresses expectations about velocity. Using both kinds of measurements helps connect the model's internal probability functions to observable judgments.

Parametric fits suggest that a LogNormal distribution approximates the likelihood well, with variance depending on contrast. The fitted velocity prior has substantially heavier tails than a Gaussian and approximately follows a power law. These findings give a more specific account of sensory uncertainty and speed expectations while preserving their status as conclusions drawn from model fits to experimental data.
summary.tldr: Speed-discrimination measurements constrain a Bayesian model's sensory likelihood and prior, suggesting contrast-dependent uncertainty and a heavy-tailed velocity prior.

title: Constraining a Bayesian Model of Human Visual Speed Perception

abstract: This paper presents a new ﬁlter for online data association problems in high-dimensional spaces. The key innovation is a representation of the data association posterior in information form, in which the “proxim- ity” of objects and tracks are expressed by numerical links. Updating these links requires linear time, compared to exponential time required for computing the exact posterior probabilities. The paper derives the algorithm formally and provides comparative results using data obtained by a real-world camera array and by a large-scale sensor network simu- lation.

Updating these links requires linear time, compared to exponential time required for computing the exact posterior probabilities. The paper derives the algorithm formally and provides comparative results using data obtained by a real-world camera array and by a large-scale sensor network simu- lation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a filter for online data association in high-dimensional settings. Data association concerns deciding how objects and tracks correspond as observations arrive. Maintaining a posterior over possible associations can be computationally demanding, especially when exact probabilities must account for many competing possibilities.

The central idea is to express the association posterior in information form. In this representation, numerical links encode the proximity between objects and tracks. Updating those links takes linear time, compared with the exponential time required to compute exact posterior probabilities. The computational contribution is therefore tied to the representation and its update operation.

The authors formally derive the algorithm and provide comparative results using data from a real camera array and a large sensor-network simulation. These settings examine its use in both physical observations and a simulated large system. The stated efficiency difference makes the filter relevant to online processing, where associations must be updated repeatedly. It describes an efficient filtering representation without equating its linear-time updates with full exact posterior computation.
summary.tldr: An information-form association filter updates numerical object-track links in linear time, avoiding the exponential cost of exact posterior computation.

title: The Information-Form Data Association Filter

abstract: The observed physiological dynamics of an infant receiving intensive care are affected by many possible factors, including interventions to the baby, the operation of the monitoring equipment and the state of health. The Factorial Switching Kalman Filter can be used to infer the presence of such factors from a sequence of observations, and to estimate the true values where these observations have been corrupted. We apply this model to clinical time series data and show it to be effective in identifying a number of artifactual and physiological patterns.

paragraphs: Physiological measurements from an infant in intensive care can change for several reasons. They may reflect the infant's health, an intervention, or the behavior of monitoring equipment. The paper addresses the problem of interpreting these overlapping influences from a sequence of observations, where a recorded change does not by itself identify its cause.

The authors use a Factorial Switching Kalman Filter to infer the presence of such factors. The model also estimates the underlying values when observations have been corrupted. These two functions address related needs: identifying influences on a monitored signal and recovering an estimate of the physiological quantity when the measurement is unreliable.

Applied to clinical time series, the model is reported to identify several physiological patterns and artifacts effectively. This supports its use for distinguishing meaningful changes from some forms of measurement disturbance in the studied data. The contribution centers on interpreting the dynamics of monitoring signals, bringing factor detection and estimation of corrupted observations into the same modeling approach.
summary.tldr: A Factorial Switching Kalman Filter identifies physiological and artifactual patterns in neonatal monitoring data and estimates values corrupted by measurement disturbances.

title: Factorial Switching Kalman Filters for Condition Monitoring in Neonatal Intensive Care

abstract: Image Congealing (IC) is a non-parametric method for the joint alignment of a col- lection of images affected by systematic and unwanted deformations. The method attempts to undo the deformations by minimizing a measure of complexity of the image ensemble, such as the averaged per-pixel entropy. This enables alignment without an explicit model of the aligned dataset as required by other methods (e.g. transformed component analysis). While IC is simple and general, it may intro- duce degenerate solutions when the transformations allow minimizing the com- plexity of the data by collapsing them to a constant. Such solutions need to be explicitly removed by regularization. In this paper we propose an alternative formulation which solves this regulariza- tion issue on a more principled ground. We make the simple observation that alignment should simplify the data while preserving the useful information car- ried by them. Therefore we trade off ﬁdelity and complexity of the aligned en- semble rather than minimizing the complexity alone. This eliminates the need for an explicit regularization of the transformations, and has a number of other useful properties such as noise suppression. We show the modeling and computa- tional beneﬁts of the approach to the some of the problems on which IC has been demonstrated.

paragraphs: Joint image alignment tries to undo unwanted deformations across a collection so that shared patterns line up. Image Congealing approaches this by making the aligned collection simpler, for example by reducing the variability at each pixel. Its attraction is that it does not require an explicit model describing what the aligned images should look like.

Simplicity alone, however, can reward an unhelpful result: transformations may collapse the images into something constant. Conventional Image Congealing must explicitly constrain transformations to exclude such solutions. This paper instead balances the complexity of the aligned collection against fidelity to the information in the original data. Alignment should remove unwanted variation while retaining useful content.

The resulting formulation addresses the collapse problem through the objective itself, eliminating the need for explicit transformation regularization. The authors also identify noise suppression as a useful property and demonstrate modeling and computational benefits on some problems previously addressed with Image Congealing. The contribution is a more principled criterion for deciding which simplifications count as successful alignment.
summary.tldr: Balancing information preservation against simplicity makes joint image alignment less vulnerable to collapsed solutions.

title: A Complexity-Distortion Approach to Joint Pattern Alignment

abstract: We consider the estimation problem in Gaussian graphical models with arbitrary structure. We analyze the Embedded Trees algorithm, which solves a sequence of problems on tractable subgraphs thereby leading to the solution of the estimation problem on an intractable graph. Our analysis is based on the recently developed walk-sum interpretation of Gaussian estimation. We show that non-stationary iterations of the Embedded Trees algorithm using any sequence of subgraphs converge in walk-summable models. Based on walk-sum calculations, we develop adaptive methods that optimize the choice of subgraphs used at each iteration with a view to achieving maximum reduction in error. These adaptive procedures provide a significant speedup in convergence over stationary iterative methods, and also appear to converge in a larger class of models.

We show that non-stationary iterations of the Embedded Trees algorithm using any sequence of subgraphs converge in walk-summable models. Based on walk-sum calculations, we develop adaptive methods that optimize the choice of subgraphs used at each iteration with a view to achieving maximum reduction in error. paragraphs: Estimation in a Gaussian graphical model can be difficult when the graph has a complicated structure. The Embedded Trees algorithm addresses this by repeatedly solving easier problems on tractable subgraphs. This paper examines how those successive solutions can lead to the solution for the full graph, including when the selected subgraph changes between iterations.

The analysis uses a walk-sum interpretation of Gaussian estimation, which expresses the calculation through contributions associated with walks through the graph. For models satisfying the walk-summability condition, the authors prove convergence of non-stationary Embedded Trees iterations using any sequence of subgraphs. This gives a theoretical basis for varying the subgraphs during computation.

The authors then use walk-sum calculations to adaptively choose subgraphs, aiming for the greatest reduction in error at each iteration. These procedures substantially accelerate convergence compared with stationary iterative methods. They also appear to converge for a broader class of models. That broader behavior is reported as an observation, whereas the convergence guarantee specifically applies to walk-summable models.
summary.tldr: Walk-sum analysis supports adaptive subgraph selection that speeds Gaussian estimation, with convergence guaranteed for walk-summable models.

title: Adaptive Embedded Subgraph Algorithms using Walk-Sum Analysis

abstract: Many machine learning algorithms can be formulated in the framework of statistical independence such as the Hilbert Schmidt Independence Criterion. In this paper, we extend this criterion to deal with with structured and interdependent observations. This is achieved by modeling the structures using undirected graphical models and comparing the Hilbert space embeddings of distributions. We apply this new criterion to independent component analysis and sequence clustering.
originalAbstract: Many machine learning algorithms can be formulated in the framework of statistical independence such as the Hilbert Schmidt Independence Criterion. In this paper, we extend this criterion to deal with with structured and interdependent observations. This is achieved by modeling the structures using undirected graphical models and comparing the Hilbert space embeddings of distributions. We apply this new criterion to independent component analysis and sequence clustering.

paragraphs: The paper extends a kernel-based criterion for statistical independence to observations that have structure and depend on one another. Its starting point is the Hilbert Schmidt Independence Criterion, a framework relevant to many machine learning algorithms. The problem is how to carry this independence-based approach into settings where observations cannot simply be treated as independent.

The authors represent the structure of the observations using undirected graphical models. They then compare Hilbert-space embeddings of distributions to construct the extended criterion. This brings the modeled relationships among observations into the distributional comparison used to assess independence, connecting graphical structure with a kernel-based representation of probability distributions.

The criterion is applied to independent component analysis and sequence clustering. These applications illustrate two uses for an independence measure that accommodates structured observations. The contribution described is a methodological extension and its application to these learning problems. Its significance is that dependence among observations becomes part of the formulation, expanding the setting in which an independence-based learning criterion can be used.
summary.tldr: An extension of the Hilbert Schmidt Independence Criterion uses graphical models to accommodate structured, interdependent observations.

title: Kernel Measures of Independence for non-iid Data

abstract: Robust low-level image features have been proven to be effective representations for a variety of visual recognition tasks such as object recognition and scene classification; but pixels, or even local image patches, carry little semantic meanings. For high level visual tasks, such low-level image representations are potentially not enough. In this paper, we propose a high-level image representation, called the Object Bank, where an image is represented as a scale invariant response map of a large number of pre-trained generic object detectors, blind to the testing dataset or visual task. Leveraging on the Object Bank representation, superior performances on high level visual recognition tasks can be achieved with simple off-the-shelf classifiers such as logistic regression and linear SVM. Sparsity algorithms make our representation more efficient and scalable for large scene datasets, and reveal semantically meaningful feature patterns.

paragraphs: Pixels and local image patches can support effective visual recognition, but they contain little explicit semantic meaning. For tasks such as scene classification, a representation organized around objects may provide more useful information. This paper introduces Object Bank, a way to describe an image through the responses of a large collection of pretrained generic object detectors.

The representation takes the form of a scale-invariant response map. The detectors are pretrained without knowledge of the testing dataset or target visual task, so the resulting representation draws on generic object information. This changes the features supplied to a classifier: the learning system receives object-detector responses as its description of an image.

The authors report superior performance on high-level recognition tasks using ordinary classifiers, including logistic regression and linear support vector machines. Sparsity algorithms improve efficiency and scalability for large scene datasets while revealing meaningful semantic feature patterns. The findings show how investing in the image representation can make relatively simple classifiers effective on tasks requiring higher-level visual information.
summary.tldr: Object Bank represents images with generic object-detector responses, enabling strong high-level recognition with simple classifiers.

title: Object Bank: A High-Level Image Representation for Scene Classification & Semantic Feature Sparsification

abstract: Log-linear models are widely used probability models for statistical pattern recognition. Typically, log-linear models are trained according to a convex criterion. In recent years, the interest in log-linear models has greatly increased. The optimization of log-linear model parameters is costly and therefore an important topic, in particular for large-scale applications. Different optimization algorithms have been evaluated empirically in many papers. In this work, we analyze the optimization problem analytically and show that the training of log-linear models can be highly ill-conditioned. We verify our findings on two handwriting tasks. By making use of our convergence analysis, we obtain good results on a large-scale continuous handwriting recognition task with a simple and generic approach.

paragraphs: Log-linear probability models are widely used in pattern recognition, but fitting their parameters can be computationally expensive. This paper investigates why training can be difficult even when its objective is convex. Rather than relying only on empirical comparisons of optimization algorithms, the authors analyze the optimization problem itself to understand the behavior of training.

Their central finding is that log-linear training can be highly ill-conditioned. In plain language, the optimization problem can have an uneven geometry that makes progress difficult for a training procedure. Convexity therefore does not by itself settle the practical question of how efficiently parameters can be learned. The analysis identifies conditioning as an important issue for large-scale applications.

The authors verify their analytical findings on two handwriting tasks. They then use the convergence analysis to guide a simple, generic approach that obtains good results on a large-scale continuous handwriting recognition task. The contribution connects a theoretical explanation of training difficulty with a practical application, without claiming that every log-linear training problem has equally poor conditioning.
summary.tldr: An analysis of log-linear training reveals potentially severe ill-conditioning and guides a simple approach with good handwriting recognition results.

title: A Convergence Analysis of Log-Linear Training

abstract: In the vast majority of recent work on sparse estimation algorithms, performance has been evaluated using ideal or quasi-ideal dictionaries (e.g., random Gaussian or Fourier) characterized by unit $\ell_2$ norm, incoherent columns or features. But in reality, these types of dictionaries represent only a subset of the dictionaries that are actually used in practice (largely restricted to idealized compressive sensing applications). In contrast, herein sparse estimation is considered in the context of structured dictionaries possibly exhibiting high coherence between arbitrary groups of columns and/or rows. Sparse penalized regression models are analyzed with the purpose of finding, to the extent possible, regimes of dictionary invariant performance. In particular, a Type II Bayesian estimator with a dictionary-dependent sparsity penalty is shown to have a number of desirable invariance properties leading to provable advantages over more conventional penalties such as the $\ell_1$ norm, especially in areas where existing theoretical recovery guarantees no longer hold. This can translate into improved performance in applications such as model selection with correlated features, source localization, and compressive sensing with constrained measurement directions.

paragraphs: Sparse estimation seeks a representation using relatively few dictionary components. Much theoretical work evaluates it with idealized dictionaries whose columns are normalized and weakly correlated. This paper instead considers structured dictionaries that may contain strongly correlated groups of columns or rows, bringing the analysis closer to settings where those ideal conditions fail.

The authors analyze sparsity-penalized regression to identify regimes where performance is invariant to dictionary structure, as far as possible. Their central example is a Type II Bayesian estimator whose sparsity penalty depends on the dictionary itself. That dependence lets the penalty account for structural properties that a conventional fixed penalty may not capture.

The estimator has several provable invariance properties that yield advantages over penalties such as the l1 norm, especially where existing recovery guarantees no longer apply. The authors explain that these advantages can translate into better performance for correlated-feature selection, source localization, and compressive sensing with constrained measurement directions. The claim is about particular advantageous regimes and potential application benefits, rather than unrestricted independence from the dictionary.
summary.tldr: A dictionary-dependent Bayesian sparsity penalty offers provable invariance advantages in structured settings where conventional recovery guarantees may fail.

title: Sparse Estimation with Structured Dictionaries

abstract: Category-level object detection has a crucial need for informative object representations. This demand has led to feature descriptors of ever increasing dimensionality like co-occurrence statistics and self-similarity. In this paper we propose a new object representation based on curvature self-similarity that goes beyond the currently popular approximation of objects using straight lines. However, like all descriptors using second order statistics, ours also exhibits a high dimensionality. Although improving discriminability, the high dimensionality becomes a critical issue due to lack of generalization ability and curse of dimensionality. Given only a limited amount of training data, even sophisticated learning algorithms such as the popular kernel methods are not able to suppress noisy or superfluous dimensions of such high-dimensional data. Consequently, there is a natural need for feature selection when using present-day informative features and, particularly, curvature self-similarity. We therefore suggest an embedded feature selection method for SVMs that reduces complexity and improves generalization capability of object models. By successfully integrating the proposed curvature self-similarity representation together with the embedded feature selection in a widely used state-of-the-art object detection framework we show the general pertinence of the approach.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an object representation based on curvature self-similarity, extending representations that approximate objects with straight lines. Its goal is to provide informative features for category-level detection. Comparing curvature structure produces a rich descriptor, but its second-order statistics also create a high-dimensional representation.

The authors integrate both the curvature descriptor and the feature-selection method into an established object detection framework, demonstrating the approach's relevance. The contribution combines a more informative representation with a learning mechanism suited to its dimensionality. The result emphasizes that adding descriptive detail and selecting useful dimensions are connected parts of building an effective object model under limited training data.
summary.tldr: Curvature self-similarity features are paired with embedded SVM feature selection to reduce complexity and improve object-model generalization.

title: Visual Recognition using Embedded Feature Selection for Curvature Self-Similarity

abstract: Given their pervasive use, social media, such as Twitter, have become a leading source of breaking news. A key task in the automated identification of such news is the detection of novel documents from a voluminous stream of text documents in a scalable manner. Motivated by this challenge, we introduce the problem of online L1-dictionary learning where unlike traditional dictionary learning, which uses squared loss, the L1-penalty is used for measuring the reconstruction error. We present an efficient online algorithm for this problem based on alternating directions method of multipliers, and establish a sublinear regret bound for this algorithm. Empirical results on news-stream and Twitter data, shows that this online L1-dictionary learning algorithm for novel document detection gives more than an order of magnitude speedup over the previously known batch algorithm, without any significant loss in quality of results. Our algorithm for online L1-dictionary learning could be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Detecting a genuinely new document in a rapid news stream requires a representation that can update without repeatedly processing the whole archive. This paper develops online dictionary learning for that setting. Unlike conventional formulations with squared reconstruction error, it measures reconstruction through an ℓ₁ penalty.

The authors derive an efficient online algorithm using the alternating direction method of multipliers and prove a sublinear regret bound. The learned dictionary adapts as documents arrive, supporting novelty assessment in a changing stream. This turns a batch representation-learning problem into a sequential procedure with a formal performance guarantee.

On news and Twitter data, the method is more than an order of magnitude faster than the previous batch algorithm without significant loss of detection quality. The contribution is both an application to emerging information and a reusable online optimization method. It shows that a representation can remain useful for novelty detection while being updated at streaming scale.
summary.tldr: Online ℓ₁ dictionary learning detects novel documents with a sublinear-regret algorithm and much faster updates than the compared batch method.

title: Online L1-Dictionary Learning with Application to Novel Document Detection

abstract: Population neural recordings with long-range temporal structure are often best understood in terms of a shared underlying low-dimensional dynamical process. Advances in recording technology provide access to an ever larger fraction of the population, but the standard computational approaches available to identify the collective dynamics scale poorly with the size of the dataset. Here we describe a new, scalable approach to discovering the low-dimensional dynamics that underlie simultaneously recorded spike trains from a neural population. Our method is based on recurrent linear models (RLMs), and relates closely to timeseries models based on recurrent neural networks. We formulate RLMs for neural data by generalising the Kalman-filter-based likelihood calculation for latent linear dynamical systems (LDS) models to incorporate a generalised-linear observation process. We show that RLMs describe motor-cortical population data better than either directly-coupled generalised-linear models or latent linear dynamical system models with generalised-linear observations. We also introduce the cascaded linear model (CLM) to capture low-dimensional instantaneous correlations in neural populations. The CLM describes the cortical recordings better than either Ising or Gaussian models and, like the RLM, can be fit exactly and quickly. The CLM can also be seen as a generalization of a low-rank Gaussian model, in this case factor analysis. The computational tractability of the RLM and CLM allow both to scale to very high-dimensional neural data.

paragraphs: Large neural recordings often contain shared, low-dimensional dynamics extending over time. Discovering those dynamics becomes computationally difficult as more neurons are recorded simultaneously. This paper introduces recurrent linear models to identify such collective processes from spike trains while supporting much larger datasets.

It also relates closely to recurrent neural-network time-series models. On motor-cortical population data, recurrent linear models describe the recordings better than the directly coupled generalized-linear models and latent dynamical models with generalized-linear observations used for comparison.

This model generalizes a low-rank Gaussian approach, factor analysis, and describes the cortical recordings better than the compared Ising and Gaussian models. Both proposed model classes can be fitted exactly and quickly. Their tractability is central to the contribution: the paper connects descriptions of collective neural structure with methods that can scale to very high-dimensional recordings.
summary.tldr: Recurrent and cascaded linear models efficiently capture temporal dynamics and instantaneous correlations in large neural recordings.

title: Recurrent linear models of simultaneously-recorded neural populations

abstract: Traditional convolutional neural networks (CNN) are stationary and feedforward. They neither change their parameters during evaluation nor use feedback from higher to lower layers. Real brains, however, do. So does our Deep Attention Selective Network (dasNet) architecture. DasNet's feedback structure can dynamically alter its convolutional filter sensitivities during classification. It harnesses the power of sequential processing to improve classification performance, by allowing the network to iteratively focus its internal attention on some of its convolutional filters. Feedback is trained through direct policy search in a huge million-dimensional parameter space, through scalable natural evolution strategies (SNES). On the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, dasNet outperforms the previous state-of-the-art model on unaugmented datasets.

paragraphs: Traditional convolutional networks process an image through a fixed sequence of layers without feedback from higher layers to lower ones. This paper introduces dasNet, a network whose feedback connections can alter the sensitivities of convolutional filters during classification. Its internal processing can therefore adapt as it examines an input.

The central mechanism is sequential attention within the network. Across successive processing steps, feedback allows dasNet to focus selectively on some of its filters. This makes classification an iterative process in which internal emphasis can change, rather than relying entirely on the responses produced by one fixed forward evaluation.

The feedback behavior is trained using direct policy search with scalable natural evolution strategies, operating in a parameter space with about a million dimensions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 without dataset augmentation, dasNet surpasses the previous state-of-the-art model reported in the abstract. These results support the usefulness of learned feedback and repeated internal attention in the evaluated classification setting; the architectural contribution is the ability to adjust filter sensitivity during evaluation.
summary.tldr: DasNet learns feedback that adjusts convolutional filter sensitivities during iterative classification, improving results on unaugmented CIFAR datasets.

title: Deep Networks with Internal Selective Attention through Feedback Connections

abstract: We provide statistical and computational analysis of sparse Principal Component Analysis (PCA) in high dimensions. The sparse PCA problem is highly nonconvex in nature. Consequently, though its global solution attains the optimal statistical rate of convergence, such solution is computationally intractable to obtain. Meanwhile, although its convex relaxations are tractable to compute, they yield estimators with suboptimal statistical rates of convergence. On the other hand, existing nonconvex optimization procedures, such as greedy methods, lack statistical guarantees. In this paper, we propose a two-stage sparse PCA procedure that attains the optimal principal subspace estimator in polynomial time. The main stage employs a novel algorithm named sparse orthogonal iteration pursuit, which iteratively solves the underlying nonconvex problem. However, our analysis shows that this algorithm only has desired computational and statistical guarantees within a restricted region, namely the basin of attraction. To obtain the desired initial estimator that falls into this region, we solve a convex formulation of sparse PCA with early stopping. Under an integrated analytic framework, we simultaneously characterize the computational and statistical performance of this two-stage procedure. Computationally, our procedure converges at the rate of $1/\sqrt{t}$ within the initialization stage, and at a geometric rate within the main stage. Statistically, the final principal subspace estimator achieves the minimax-optimal statistical rate of convergence with respect to the sparsity level $s^*$, dimension $d$ and sample size $n$. Our procedure motivates a general paradigm of tackling nonconvex statistical learning problems with provable statistical guarantees.

Our procedure motivates a general paradigm of tackling nonconvex statistical learning problems with provable statistical guarantees.

paragraphs: Sparse PCA presents a tension between statistical accuracy and computational tractability. Its global solution has an optimal statistical rate but is computationally intractable to obtain, while tractable convex relaxations can have weaker statistical rates. This paper combines a convex initialization with a nonconvex refinement to obtain an optimal principal-subspace estimator in polynomial time.

The refinement algorithm, sparse orthogonal iteration pursuit, has the desired guarantees only inside a restricted basin of attraction. The first stage therefore solves a convex formulation with early stopping to produce an initial estimate within that region. Initialization has a specific role: placing the estimate where the more accurate nonconvex procedure is theoretically reliable.

The analysis tracks computation and statistical error together. The initialization stage converges at a rate of 1/√t, while the main stage converges geometrically. The final estimator achieves a minimax-optimal statistical rate in sparsity, dimension, and sample size. The result supports a two-stage strategy whose success depends on reaching the required basin, rather than implying that arbitrary initializations make the nonconvex problem easy.
summary.tldr: Convex initialization followed by nonconvex sparse orthogonal iteration achieves minimax-optimal sparse PCA estimation in polynomial time under the analyzed conditions.

title: Tighten after Relax: Minimax-Optimal Sparse PCA in Polynomial Time

abstract: We propose a multimodal retrieval procedure based on latent feature models. The procedure consists of a nonparametric Bayesian framework for learning underlying semantically meaningful abstract features in a multimodal dataset, a probabilistic retrieval model that allows cross-modal queries and an extension model for relevance feedback. Experiments on two multimodal datasets, PASCAL-Sentence and SUN-Attribute, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed retrieval procedure in comparison to the state-of-the-art algorithms for learning binary codes.

paragraphs: This paper addresses retrieval in datasets containing multiple kinds of information. Its central goal is to learn abstract features that carry semantic meaning across those modalities, then use those features to support search. A cross-modal query asks the system to retrieve information across modality boundaries, making the relationship between different representations central to the task.

The proposed procedure has three connected parts. A nonparametric Bayesian latent feature framework learns the underlying representation. A probabilistic retrieval model then uses that representation to support cross-modal queries. An additional model incorporates relevance feedback, extending the procedure beyond its initial retrieval stage. Together, these components connect representation learning, retrieval, and feedback within a probabilistic framework.

The authors evaluate the procedure on PASCAL-Sentence and SUN-Attribute. The experiments demonstrate its effectiveness compared with state-of-the-art algorithms for learning binary codes. The stated contribution is a complete retrieval procedure built around semantically meaningful latent features, with empirical support on two multimodal datasets for using that representation in cross-modal search.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian latent feature framework combines multimodal representation learning, cross-modal retrieval, and relevance feedback.

title: A Probabilistic Framework for Multimodal Retrieval using Integrative Indian Buffet Process

abstract: This paper studies theoretically and empirically a method of turning machine-learning algorithms into probabilistic predictors that automatically enjoys a property of validity (perfect calibration) and is computationally efficient. The price to pay for perfect calibration is that these probabilistic predictors produce imprecise (in practice, almost precise for large data sets) probabilities. When these imprecise probabilities are merged into precise probabilities, the resulting predictors, while losing the theoretical property of perfect calibration, are consistently more accurate than the existing methods in empirical studies.
originalAbstract: This paper studies theoretically and empirically a method of turning machine-learning algorithms into probabilistic predictors that automatically enjoys a property of validity (perfect calibration) and is computationally efficient. When these imprecise probabilities are merged into precise probabilities, the resulting predictors, while losing the theoretical property of perfect calibration, are consistently more accurate than the existing methods in empirical studies.

paragraphs: A probabilistic predictor attaches probabilities to possible outcomes, making the reliability of those probabilities part of the learning problem. This paper studies a computationally efficient way to turn machine-learning algorithms into probabilistic predictors with a theoretical validity property described as perfect calibration. The method is examined both theoretically and empirically.

The guarantee comes with a tradeoff: the predictor returns imprecise probabilities rather than a single precise probability. In practice, the authors find that this imprecision becomes very small for large datasets. This means the guaranteed form can become almost precise empirically while still retaining the distinction between an imprecise output and one exact probability.

The paper also considers merging the imprecise outputs into precise probabilities. That step loses the theoretical perfect-calibration property, but the resulting predictors consistently outperform existing methods in the reported empirical accuracy studies. The two versions therefore offer different supported benefits: one retains a formal validity guarantee, while the merged version provides precise outputs with favorable observed accuracy.
summary.tldr: An efficient predictor conversion guarantees perfect calibration with imprecise probabilities; merging them yields strong empirical accuracy but loses that guarantee.

title: Large-scale probabilistic predictors with and without guarantees of validity

abstract: In this work, we are interested in generalizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) from low-dimensional regular grids, where image, video and speech are represented, to high-dimensional irregular domains, such as social networks, brain connectomes or words’ embedding, represented by graphs. We present a formulation of CNNs in the context of spectral graph theory, which provides the necessary mathematical background and efficient numerical schemes to design fast localized convolutional filters on graphs. Importantly, the proposed technique offers the same linear computational complexity and constant learning complexity as classical CNNs, while being universal to any graph structure. Experiments on MNIST and 20NEWS demonstrate the ability of this novel deep learning system to learn local, stationary, and compositional features on graphs.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks commonly operate on regular grids, such as the pixels of an image. Many other datasets have irregular relationships better represented by graphs, including social networks and brain connections. This paper develops a way to bring convolutional learning to those graph domains while preserving efficient local filtering.

The formulation uses spectral graph theory to define the filters and the numerical procedures that apply them. The proposed technique works with any graph structure and has the same stated linear computational complexity and constant learning complexity as classical convolutional networks. The significance is that irregular connectivity can be incorporated without giving up the complexity properties emphasized by the authors.

Experiments on MNIST and 20NEWS demonstrate learning of local, stationary, and compositional graph features. These properties concern patterns associated with neighborhoods, reused across locations, and combined into richer representations. The findings support the paper's central claim that the useful feature-building behavior of convolutional networks can extend beyond regular grids to data organized by graph relationships.
summary.tldr: A spectral formulation extends convolutional networks to arbitrary graphs using efficient localized filters and demonstrates graph-based feature learning.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks on Graphs with Fast Localized Spectral Filtering

abstract: We develop a nonparametric and online learning algorithm that estimates the triggering functions of a multivariate Hawkes process (MHP). The approach we take approximates the triggering function $f_{i,j}(t)$ by functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), and maximizes a time-discretized version of the log-likelihood, with Tikhonov regularization. Theoretically, our algorithm achieves an $\calO(\log T)$ regret bound. Numerical results show that our algorithm offers a competing performance to that of the nonparametric batch learning algorithm, with a run time comparable to the parametric online learning algorithm.

paragraphs: Multivariate Hawkes processes model event sequences through triggering functions that describe how events affect subsequent activity. This paper develops an online method for estimating those functions without imposing a fixed parametric form. Its aim is to combine the flexibility of nonparametric estimation with the computational advantages of learning as data arrive.

The method approximates each triggering function within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, providing a function-based representation for the interactions. It optimizes a time-discretized log-likelihood with Tikhonov regularization. Together, these choices define both how the functions are represented and the regularized objective used to estimate them.

The authors prove a regret bound that grows logarithmically with T, giving a theoretical guarantee on the algorithm’s accumulated online learning performance. Numerical results show estimation performance competitive with a nonparametric batch algorithm and runtime comparable to a parametric online algorithm. The contribution is this combination of flexibility, online efficiency, and a regret guarantee, with the empirical comparisons supporting its practical usefulness.
summary.tldr: Kernel-based online estimation learns flexible Hawkes triggering functions with logarithmic regret and competitive empirical efficiency.

title: Online Learning for Multivariate Hawkes Processes

abstract: We present a formulation of deep learning that aims at producing a large margin classifier. The notion of \emc{margin}, minimum distance to a decision boundary, has served as the foundation of several theoretically profound and empirically successful results for both classification and regression tasks. However, most large margin algorithms are applicable only to shallow models with a preset feature representation; and conventional margin methods for neural networks only enforce margin at the output layer. Such methods are therefore not well suited for deep networks. In this work, we propose a novel loss function to impose a margin on any chosen set of layers of a deep network (including input and hidden layers). Our formulation allows choosing any $l_p$ norm ($p \geq 1$) on the metric measuring the margin. We demonstrate that the decision boundary obtained by our loss has nice properties compared to standard classification loss functions. Specifically, we show improved empirical results on the MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets on multiple tasks: generalization from small training sets, corrupted labels, and robustness against adversarial perturbations. The resulting loss is general and complementary to existing data augmentation (such as random/adversarial input transform) and regularization techniques such as weight decay, dropout, and batch norm. \footnote{Code for the large margin loss function is released at \url{https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/large_margin}}
