paragraphs: A classification margin measures the minimum distance to a decision boundary. Large-margin methods aim to place examples farther from that boundary, but many established methods assume fixed features or enforce margins only at a neural network's output. This paper develops a loss that brings the margin objective into selected parts of a deep network.

The proposed loss can impose a margin at input, hidden, or output layers, including any chosen set of layers. It also allows the distance measure to use any l_p norm with p at least one. This makes margin enforcement compatible with learned internal representations and lets the formulation express different ways of measuring distance.

Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet show improved results for learning from small training sets, training with corrupted labels, and resisting adversarial perturbations. These are empirical findings about the resulting decision boundaries and models. The loss is also described as complementary to data augmentation and existing regularization techniques, so its role can fit alongside other training practices.
summary.tldr: A loss that enforces margins at selected network layers improves several empirical measures of generalization and robustness.

title: Large Margin Deep Networks for Classification

abstract: Recent progress in deep generative models has been fueled by two paradigms -- autoregressive and adversarial models. We propose a combination of both approaches with the goal of learning generative models of text. Our method first produces a high-level sentence outline and then generates words sequentially, conditioning on both the outline and the previous outputs. We generate outlines with an adversarial model trained to approximate the distribution of sentences in a latent space induced by general-purpose sentence encoders. This provides strong, informative conditioning for the autoregressive stage. Our quantitative evaluations suggests that conditioning information from generated outlines is able to guide the autoregressive model to produce realistic samples, comparable to maximum-likelihood trained language models, even at high temperatures with multinomial sampling. Qualitative results also demonstrate that this generative procedure yields natural-looking sentences and interpolations.

paragraphs: The paper combines adversarial and autoregressive modeling for text generation. Its procedure first generates a high-level sentence outline and then produces words one at a time. Each word depends on both that outline and the preceding outputs, giving the sequential generator a source of sentence-level conditioning throughout generation.

The outlines are representations in a latent space defined by general-purpose sentence encoders. An adversarial model learns to approximate the distribution of sentences in that space. This separates the task of producing informative sentence-level guidance from the task of turning that guidance into a sequence of words, while connecting the two through conditioning.

Quantitative evaluations suggest that generated outlines guide the autoregressive model toward realistic text comparable to maximum-likelihood-trained language models, even with high-temperature multinomial sampling. Qualitative results also show natural-looking sentences and interpolations. These findings support the usefulness of learned latent outlines as guidance for word-by-word generation, with the quantitative comparison presented as evidence from the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Adversarially generated latent sentence outlines guide an autoregressive model toward realistic text, including under high-temperature sampling in evaluations.

title: Towards Text Generation with Adversarially Learned Neural Outlines

abstract: Unsupervised image-to-image translation is a class of computer vision problems which aims at modeling conditional distribution of images in the target domain, given a set of unpaired images in the source and target domains. An image in the source domain might have multiple representations in the target domain. Therefore, ambiguity in modeling of the conditional distribution arises, specially when the images in the source and target domains come from different modalities. Current approaches mostly rely on simplifying assumptions to map both domains into a shared-latent space. Consequently, they are only able to model the domain-invariant information between the two modalities. These approaches cannot model domain-specific information which has no representation in the target domain. In this work, we propose an unsupervised image-to-image translation framework which maximizes a domain-specific variational information bound and learns the target domain-invariant representation of the two domain. The proposed framework makes it possible to map a single source image into multiple images in the target domain, utilizing several target domain-specific codes sampled randomly from the prior distribution, or extracted from reference images.

paragraphs: Unsupervised image translation learns from source and target image collections without matched examples. A single source image may correspond to several valid target images, particularly when the domains use different modalities. The task therefore involves modeling a range of possible outputs and the information that distinguishes those possibilities.

The paper argues that approaches relying on a shared latent space capture information common to both domains but cannot adequately represent domain-specific information. Its framework maximizes a domain-specific variational information bound while learning a representation of information shared across the domains. This makes domain-specific variation an explicit part of the translation process.

To translate one source image in multiple ways, the framework uses different target-domain codes. These can be sampled from a prior distribution or extracted from reference images. The stated result is the ability to generate multiple target images from the same source, with the target-specific code providing variation alongside the shared representation.
summary.tldr: Separating shared image information from domain-specific codes enables multiple target-domain translations from one unpaired source image.

title: Unsupervised Image-to-Image Translation Using Domain-Specific Variational Information Bound

abstract: We consider the problem of efficient credit assignment in reinforcement learning. In order to efficiently and meaningfully utilize new data, we propose to explicitly assign credit to past decisions based on the likelihood of them having led to the observed outcome. This approach uses new information in hindsight, rather than employing foresight. Somewhat surprisingly, we show that value functions can be rewritten through this lens, yielding a new family of algorithms. We study the properties of these algorithms, and empirically show that they successfully address important credit assignment challenges, through a set of illustrative tasks.

In order to efficiently and meaningfully utilize new data, we propose to explicitly assign credit to past decisions based on the likelihood of them having led to the observed outcome. This approach uses new information in hindsight, rather than employing foresight. Somewhat surprisingly, we show that value functions can be rewritten through this lens, yielding a new family of algorithms. We study the properties of these algorithms, and empirically show that they successfully address important credit assignment challenges, through a set of illustrative tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning requires deciding which earlier actions deserve credit for an eventual outcome. This paper proposes using the outcome itself as new information when making that judgment. The guiding question is how likely a past decision was to have led to what was subsequently observed, giving the learner an explicit hindsight-based perspective.

This changes how information from an experience is used. Rather than assigning credit only through expectations formed before the outcome, the method looks back after the outcome is known. The authors show that value functions can be rewritten in terms of this perspective, connecting the idea to a central object already used in reinforcement learning.

That reformulation produces a family of algorithms whose properties the authors study. Experiments on illustrative tasks show that these algorithms address important credit-assignment challenges. The reported evidence supports hindsight as a useful way to extract learning signals from observed outcomes, while the value-function reformulation explains how the idea can become a concrete learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Hindsight credit assignment uses observed outcomes to reassess which past decisions should receive credit.

title: Hindsight Credit Assignment

abstract: We present a new deep multi-state Dynamic Recurrent Neural Network (DRNN) architecture for Brain Machine Interface (BMI) applications. Our DRNN is used to predict Cartesian representation of a computer cursor movement kinematics from open-loop neural data recorded from the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) of a human subject in a BMI system. We design the algorithm to achieve a reasonable trade-off between performance and robustness, and we constrain memory usage in favor of future hardware implementation. We feed the predictions of the network back to the input to improve prediction performance and robustness. We apply a scheduled sampling approach to the model in order to solve a statistical distribution mismatch between the ground truth and predictions. Additionally, we configure a small DRNN to operate with a short history of input, reducing the required buffering of input data and number of memory accesses. This configuration lowers the expected power consumption in a neural network accelerator. Operating on wavelet-based neural features, we show that the average performance of DRNN surpasses other state-of-the-art methods in the literature on both single- and multi-day data recorded over 43 days. Results show that multi-state DRNN has the potential to model the nonlinear relationships between the neural data and kinematics for robust BMIs.

paragraphs: This paper develops a deep multi-state Dynamic Recurrent Neural Network for predicting computer cursor movement from neural recordings. The design balances prediction performance, robustness, and memory demands for possible future hardware implementation.

summary.tldr: A compact recurrent network predicts cursor movement from neural features while balancing accuracy, robustness, and anticipated hardware efficiency.

title: Deep Multi-State Dynamic Recurrent Neural Networks Operating on Wavelet Based Neural Features for Robust Brain Machine Interfaces

abstract: Time series forecasting is an important problem across many domains, including predictions of solar plant energy output, electricity consumption, and traffic jam situation. In this paper, we propose to tackle such forecasting problem with Transformer. Although impressed by its performance in our preliminary study, we found its two major weaknesses: (1) locality-agnostics: the point-wise dot- product self-attention in canonical Transformer architecture is insensitive to local context, which can make the model prone to anomalies in time series; (2) memory bottleneck: space complexity of canonical Transformer grows quadratically with sequence length L, making directly modeling long time series infeasible. In order to solve these two issues, we first propose convolutional self-attention by producing queries and keys with causal convolution so that local context can be better incorporated into attention mechanism. Then, we propose LogSparse Transformer with only O(L(log L)^2) memory cost, improving forecasting accuracy for time series with fine granularity and strong long-term dependencies under constrained memory budget. Our experiments on both synthetic data and real- world datasets show that it compares favorably to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: The paper adapts Transformers for time-series forecasting by addressing two weaknesses identified in the standard architecture. Pointwise attention can overlook local context, making forecasts vulnerable to anomalous observations. Meanwhile, attention memory grows quadratically with sequence length, restricting how much history a model can directly process when memory is limited.

To incorporate nearby observations into attention, the authors generate queries and keys using causal convolutions. Attention comparisons can then reflect local patterns instead of relying only on individual time points. They also introduce LogSparse Transformer, whose memory requirement grows as O(L(log L)^2) for sequence length L. This substantially changes how memory requirements increase as longer histories are considered.

The two changes address complementary forecasting needs: recognizing local context and retaining access to long-term information. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets compare favorably with the state of the art. The abstract specifically reports improved forecasting for finely sampled series with strong long-term dependencies under constrained memory, connecting the architectural changes to a setting where both weaknesses matter.
summary.tldr: Convolutional attention and a sparse Transformer design improve local-context modeling and reduce memory requirements for long time-series forecasting.

title: Enhancing the Locality and Breaking the Memory Bottleneck of Transformer on Time Series Forecasting

abstract: In many machine learning applications, it is necessary to meaningfully aggregate, through alignment, different but related datasets. Optimal transport (OT)-based approaches pose alignment as a divergence minimization problem: the aim is to transform a source dataset to match a target dataset using the Wasserstein distance as a divergence measure. We introduce a hierarchical formulation of OT which leverages clustered structure in data to improve alignment in noisy, ambiguous, or multimodal settings. To solve this numerically, we propose a distributed ADMM algorithm that also exploits the Sinkhorn distance, thus it has an efficient computational complexity that scales quadratically with the size of the largest cluster. When the transformation between two datasets is unitary, we provide performance guarantees that describe when and how well aligned cluster correspondences can be recovered with our formulation, as well as provide worst-case dataset geometry for such a strategy. We apply this method to synthetic datasets that model data as mixtures of low-rank Gaussians and study the impact that different geometric properties of the data have on alignment. Next, we applied our approach to a neural decoding application where the goal is to predict movement directions and instantaneous velocities from populations of neurons in the macaque primary motor cortex. Our results demonstrate that when clustered structure exists in datasets, and is consistent across trials or time points, a hierarchical alignment strategy that leverages such structure can provide significant improvements in cross-domain alignment.

paragraphs: Aligning related datasets means finding a transformation that makes their contents meaningfully correspond. Optimal transport approaches express this through distribution matching. This paper introduces a hierarchical formulation that uses clusters within the data to improve alignment when the distributions are noisy, ambiguous, or contain several distinct modes.

The numerical method combines distributed ADMM with the Sinkhorn distance, with computational complexity scaling quadratically in the size of the largest cluster. The paper also gives performance guarantees for recovering cluster correspondences when the transformation between datasets is unitary. The results show that exploiting clusters can substantially improve cross-domain alignment when those clusters exist and remain consistent across trials or time points. That consistency is central to the stated benefit: the hierarchy supplies useful correspondence information when the datasets share its structure.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical optimal transport improves alignment by exploiting consistent cluster structure, with conditional recovery guarantees and evidence from synthetic and neural datasets.

title: Hierarchical Optimal Transport for Multimodal Distribution Alignment

abstract: The study of quantum generative models is well-motivated, not only because of its importance in quantum machine learning and quantum chemistry but also because of the perspective of its implementation on near-term quantum machines. Inspired by previous studies on the adversarial training of classical and quantum generative models, we propose the first design of quantum Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks (WGANs), which has been shown to improve the robustness and the scalability of the adversarial training of quantum generative models even on noisy quantum hardware. Specifically, we propose a definition of the Wasserstein semimetric between quantum data, which inherits a few key theoretical merits of its classical counterpart. We also demonstrate how to turn the quantum Wasserstein semimetric into a concrete design of quantum WGANs that can be efficiently implemented on quantum machines. Our numerical study, via classical simulation of quantum systems, shows the more robust and scalable numerical performance of our quantum WGANs over other quantum GAN proposals. As a surprising application, our quantum WGAN has been used to generate a 3-qubit quantum circuit of ~50 gates that well approximates a 3-qubit 1-d Hamiltonian simulation circuit that requires over 10k gates using standard techniques.

We also demonstrate how to turn the quantum Wasserstein semimetric into a concrete design of quantum WGANs that can be efficiently implemented on quantum machines. As a surprising application, our quantum WGAN has been used to generate a 3-qubit quantum circuit of ~50 gates that well approximates a 3-qubit 1-d Hamiltonian simulation circuit that requires over 10k gates using standard techniques.

paragraphs: The paper develops a quantum version of Wasserstein generative adversarial networks to improve adversarial training of quantum generative models. Its starting point is a proposed Wasserstein semimetric for quantum data. This measure inherits several theoretical benefits of its classical counterpart and provides the basis for the training design.

The authors explain how to turn the semimetric into quantum WGANs that can be implemented efficiently on quantum machines. Numerical studies using classical simulations of quantum systems show more robust and scalable performance than other quantum GAN proposals. The work also describes robustness in the presence of noisy quantum hardware as part of the approach's motivation and claimed benefits.

One application generates a roughly 50-gate, three-qubit circuit that closely approximates a three-qubit, one-dimensional Hamiltonian simulation circuit requiring more than 10,000 gates with standard techniques. This is a specific approximation result illustrating the method's potential for compact circuit generation. The reported numerical comparisons come from classical simulation of quantum systems.
summary.tldr: A quantum Wasserstein training framework improves simulated quantum GAN performance and demonstrates a compact approximation of a much larger quantum circuit.

title: Quantum Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Detecting where and when brain regions activate in a cognitive task or in a given clinical condition is the promise of non-invasive techniques like magnetoencephalography (MEG) or electroencephalography (EEG). This problem, referred to as source localization, or source imaging, poses however a high-dimensional statistical inference challenge. While sparsity promoting regularizations have been proposed to address the regression problem, it remains unclear how to ensure statistical control of false detections in this setting. Moreover, MEG/EEG source imaging requires to work with spatio-temporal data and autocorrelated noise. To deal with this, we adapt the desparsified Lasso estimator ---an estimator tailored for high dimensional linear model that asymptotically follows a Gaussian distribution under sparsity and moderate feature correlation assumptions--- to temporal data corrupted with autocorrelated noise. We call it the desparsified multi-task Lasso (d-MTLasso). We combine d-MTLasso with spatially constrained clustering to reduce data dimension and with ensembling to mitigate the arbitrary choice of clustering; the resulting estimator is called ensemble of clustered desparsified multi-task Lasso (ecd-MTLasso). With respect to the current procedures, the two advantages of ecd-MTLasso are that i)it offers statistical guarantees and ii)it allows to trade spatial specificity for sensitivity, leading to a powerful adaptive method. Extensive simulations on realistic head geometries, as well as empirical results on various MEG datasets, demonstrate the high recovery performance of ecd-MTLasso and its primary practical benefit: offer a statistically principled way to threshold MEG/EEG source maps.

The task is a high-dimensional inference problem, and sparse regression alone leaves uncertainty about controlling false detections. Temporal dependence in both the data and noise adds another difficulty when deciding which apparent activations are statistically supported.

Simulations using realistic head geometries and evaluations on multiple MEG datasets demonstrate strong recovery performance. Its main practical contribution is a statistically principled way to threshold source maps, connecting the displayed activation regions to an inference procedure while allowing spatial resolution and detection sensitivity to be balanced.
summary.tldr: An ensemble of clustered desparsified estimators enables statistically principled MEG/EEG source-map thresholding with a specificity–sensitivity tradeoff.

title: Statistical control for spatio-temporal MEG/EEG source imaging with desparsified mutli-task Lasso

abstract: Randomized classifiers have been shown to provide a promising approach for achieving certified robustness against adversarial attacks in deep learning. However, most existing methods only leverage Gaussian smoothing noise and only work for $\ell_2$ perturbation. We propose a general framework of adversarial certification with non-Gaussian noise and for more general types of attacks, from a unified \functional optimization perspective. Our new framework allows us to identify a key trade-off between accuracy and robustness via designing smoothing distributions, helping to design new families of non-Gaussian smoothing distributions that work more efficiently for different $\ell_p$ settings, including $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$ and $\ell_\infty$ attacks. Our proposed methods achieve better certification results than previous works and provide a new perspective on randomized smoothing certification.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing uses added noise to support guarantees about a classifier's resistance to adversarial changes. Much existing work relies on Gaussian noise and focuses on perturbations measured with the l2 norm. This paper develops a broader framework for certification that accommodates non-Gaussian noise and more general attack types.

The framework treats certification as a functional optimization problem. This perspective lets the authors analyze how the choice of smoothing distribution affects the balance between accuracy and robustness. They use that analysis to design families of non-Gaussian distributions suited to different perturbation measures, including l1, l2, and l-infinity attacks.

The proposed methods achieve better certification results than previous work in the reported comparisons. Their significance is both methodological and practical: noise selection becomes an explicit design decision tied to the attack setting, and the same framework can address several settings. The accuracy–robustness trade-off remains part of the design, so changing the smoothing distribution is a choice about which properties to prioritize.
summary.tldr: A functional optimization framework designs non-Gaussian smoothing distributions for stronger certification across several adversarial perturbation measures.

title: Black-Box Certification with Randomized Smoothing: A Functional Optimization Based Framework

abstract: Continually solving new, unsolved tasks is the key to learning diverse behaviors. Through reinforcement learning (RL), we have made massive strides towards solving tasks that have a single goal. However, in the multi-task domain, where an agent needs to reach multiple goals, the choice of training goals can largely affect sample efficiency. When biological agents learn, there is often an organized and meaningful order to which learning happens. Inspired by this, we propose setting up an automatic curriculum for goals that the agent needs to solve. Our key insight is that if we can sample goals at the frontier of the set of goals that an agent is able to reach, it will provide a significantly stronger learning signal compared to randomly sampled goals. To operationalize this idea, we introduce a goal proposal module that prioritizes goals that maximize the epistemic uncertainty of the Q-function of the policy. This simple technique samples goals that are neither too hard nor too easy for the agent to solve, hence enabling continual improvement. We evaluate our method across 13 multi-goal robotic tasks and 5 navigation tasks, and demonstrate performance gains over current state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: In reinforcement learning with many goals, choosing what to practice can strongly affect how efficiently an agent learns. Randomly selecting goals may spend effort on tasks the agent already handles or tasks it cannot yet solve. This paper proposes automatically organizing training around the frontier of the agent’s current abilities, where new successes can extend its range of behaviors.

The method adds a goal proposal module that prioritizes uncertainty in the policy’s Q-function, which estimates the value of actions. Specifically, it targets epistemic uncertainty: uncertainty associated with what the learner does not yet know. Value disagreement supplies a way to select goals intended to be neither too easy nor too difficult, turning the agent’s developing knowledge into a training curriculum.

The authors evaluate the approach on 13 robotic tasks with multiple goals and five navigation tasks, reporting gains over current state-of-the-art methods. The results support the usefulness of choosing practice goals adaptively in those settings. The contribution is a simple mechanism for directing experience toward goals that provide a stronger learning signal.
summary.tldr: An automatic curriculum prioritizes goals with uncertain action values, improving learning across tested robotic and navigation tasks.

title: Automatic Curriculum Learning through Value Disagreement

abstract: Boosting is a widely used learning technique in machine learning for solving classification problems. In boosting, one predicts the label of an example using an ensemble of weak classifiers. While boosting has shown tremendous success on many classification problems involving tabular data, it performs poorly on complex classification tasks involving low-level features such as image classification tasks. This drawback stems from the fact that boosting builds an additive model of weak classifiers, each of which has very little predictive power. Often, the resulting additive models are not powerful enough to approximate the complex decision boundaries of real-world classification problems. In this work, we present a general framework for boosting where, similar to traditional boosting, we aim to boost the performance of a weak learner and transform it into a strong learner. However, unlike traditional boosting, our framework allows for more complex forms of aggregation of weak learners. In this work, we specifically focus on one form of aggregation - \emph{function composition}. We show that many popular greedy algorithms for learning deep neural networks (DNNs) can be derived from our framework using function compositions for aggregation. Moreover, we identify the drawbacks of these greedy algorithms and propose new algorithms that fix these issues. Using thorough empirical evaluation, we show that our learning algorithms have superior performance over traditional additive boosting algorithms, as well as existing greedy learning techniques for DNNs. An important feature of our algorithms is that they come with strong theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Traditional boosting builds a strong classifier by adding together weak classifiers. Although effective on many tabular problems, this additive construction can lack the expressive power needed for complex decisions based on low-level inputs such as images. The paper asks how boosting can retain its weak-to-strong learning goal while allowing richer combinations.

The proposed framework broadens the aggregation mechanism and focuses on function composition, where one learned function feeds into another. Under this view, several popular greedy methods for learning deep neural networks can be derived as instances of generalized boosting. The framework therefore provides a connection between boosting and the sequential construction of more complex learned functions.

The authors identify drawbacks in those existing greedy algorithms and introduce alternatives intended to fix them. Their empirical evaluation reports superior performance over both traditional additive boosting and existing greedy neural-network learning methods. The new algorithms also carry strong theoretical guarantees. Together, these results support studying the form of aggregation itself as a central ingredient in turning weak learners into more capable predictors.
summary.tldr: Generalized boosting allows function composition, connecting boosting to greedy deep-network learning and yielding algorithms with theoretical and empirical support.

title: Generalized Boosting

abstract: We analyze the extent to which existing methods rely on accurate training data for a specific class of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, known as Safe and Seldonian RL. We introduce a new measure of security to quantify the susceptibility to perturbations in training data by creating an attacker model that represents a worst-case analysis, and show that a couple of Seldonian RL methods are extremely sensitive to even a few data corruptions. We then introduce a new algorithm that is more robust against data corruptions, and demonstrate its usage in practice on some RL problems, including a grid-world and a diabetes treatment simulation.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how much Safe and Seldonian reinforcement-learning methods depend on accurate training data. Its focus is the effect of corrupted data on algorithms intended to support safe decision-making. This connects the reliability of a learned policy to the integrity of the information used to train it.

The authors introduce a security measure based on an attacker model representing worst-case perturbations of the training data. They use that measure to examine susceptibility to corruption and find that a couple of Seldonian methods are extremely sensitive even when only a few data points are corrupted. This is a targeted finding about the studied methods, rather than a statement that every safe-learning algorithm behaves identically.

The paper then proposes an algorithm with greater robustness to data corruption. Demonstrations include a grid-world problem and a diabetes treatment simulation. These applications illustrate how the method can be used within reinforcement-learning problems while keeping the evidence at the level of the studied settings. The contribution combines an explicit way to assess training-data security with an algorithm designed to improve it.
summary.tldr: A worst-case security analysis exposes corruption sensitivity in selected Seldonian RL methods and motivates a more robust algorithm.

title: Security Analysis of Safe and Seldonian Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

abstract: In this paper, we show that under over-parametrization several standard stochastic optimization algorithms escape saddle-points and converge to local-minimizers much faster. One of the fundamental aspects of over-parametrized models is that they are capable of interpolating the training data. We show that, under interpolation-like assumptions satisfied by the stochastic gradients in an over-parametrization setting, the first-order oracle complexity of Perturbed Stochastic Gradient Descent (PSGD) algorithm to reach an $\epsilon$-local-minimizer, matches the corresponding deterministic rate of $O(1/\epsilon^{2})$. We next analyze Stochastic Cubic-Regularized Newton (SCRN) algorithm under interpolation-like conditions, and show that the oracle complexity to reach an $\epsilon$-local-minimizer under interpolation-like conditions, is $O(1/\epsilon^{2.5})$. While this obtained complexity is better than the corresponding complexity of either PSGD, or SCRN without interpolation-like assumptions, it does not match the rate of $O(1/\epsilon^{1.5})$ corresponding to deterministic Cubic-Regularized Newton method. It seems further Hessian-based interpolation-like assumptions are necessary to bridge this gap. We also discuss the corresponding improved complexities in the zeroth-order settings.

paragraphs: Overparameterized models can fit their training data exactly, a property called interpolation. This paper studies how related assumptions on stochastic gradients affect optimization near saddle points. Under these interpolation-like conditions, several standard stochastic methods can escape saddle points and reach approximate local minimizers faster than their usual complexity guarantees suggest.

For Perturbed Stochastic Gradient Descent, the first-order oracle complexity of reaching an epsilon-local-minimizer is O(1/epsilon²). This matches the corresponding deterministic rate. The result connects a particular property of the stochastic gradients to a strong optimization guarantee, rather than asserting that every overparameterized model automatically enjoys the same behavior.

For Stochastic Cubic-Regularized Newton, the authors obtain complexity O(1/epsilon²·⁵). This improves on the corresponding guarantees without interpolation-like assumptions, but still falls short of the deterministic cubic-regularized Newton rate of O(1/epsilon¹·⁵). The authors suggest that additional interpolation-like assumptions involving Hessians may be needed to close that gap. They also discuss improved complexities for zeroth-order settings, extending the investigation beyond algorithms supplied with gradients.
summary.tldr: Interpolation-like gradient conditions improve saddle-point escape guarantees, allowing perturbed stochastic gradient descent to match its deterministic complexity rate.

title: Escaping Saddle-Point Faster under Interpolation-like Conditions

abstract: Inspired by the robustness and efficiency of sparse representation in sparse coding based image restoration models, we investigate the sparsity of neurons in deep networks. Our method structurally enforces sparsity constraints upon hidden neurons. The sparsity constraints are favorable for gradient-based learning algorithms and attachable to convolution layers in various networks. Sparsity in neurons enables computation saving by only operating on non-zero components without hurting accuracy. Meanwhile, our method can magnify representation dimensionality and model capacity with negligible additional computation cost. Experiments show that sparse representation is crucial in deep neural networks for multiple image restoration tasks, including image super-resolution, image denoising, and image compression artifacts removal.

paragraphs: This paper brings ideas from sparse coding into deep networks for image restoration. Its focus is sparsity in hidden neurons: arranging the representation so that only some components are nonzero. The authors introduce structural sparsity constraints that work with gradient-based learning and can be attached to convolution layers in different networks.

The computational benefit comes from operating only on nonzero components. The paper reports that this can save computation without reducing accuracy. It also allows the representation to have more dimensions and greater model capacity with negligible additional computational cost. The distinction between available capacity and active computation is central to the proposed approach.

Experiments cover image super-resolution, denoising, and removal of compression artifacts. Across these restoration tasks, the authors find sparse neural representations to be important to performance. Their contribution is a way to incorporate sparsity into trainable network components while connecting it directly to computational savings. The results support the method as a means of expanding useful representations without paying the full computational cost of operating on every component.
summary.tldr: Structured sparsity in hidden neurons reduces image-restoration computation and expands representation capacity with negligible added cost.

title: Neural Sparse Representation for Image Restoration

abstract: We initiate the study of fair classifiers that are robust to perturbations in the training distribution. Despite recent progress, the literature on fairness has largely ignored the design of fair and robust classifiers. In this work, we develop classifiers that are fair not only with respect to the training distribution but also for a class of distributions that are weighted perturbations of the training samples. We formulate a min-max objective function whose goal is to minimize a distributionally robust training loss, and at the same time, find a classifier that is fair with respect to a class of distributions. We first reduce this problem to finding a fair classifier that is robust with respect to the class of distributions. Based on an online learning algorithm, we develop an iterative algorithm that provably converges to such a fair and robust solution. Experiments on standard machine learning fairness datasets suggest that, compared to the state-of-the-art fair classifiers, our classifier retains fairness guarantees and test accuracy for a large class of perturbations on the test set. Furthermore, our experiments show that there is an inherent trade-off between fairness robustness and accuracy of such classifiers.

paragraphs: A classifier can satisfy a fairness criterion on its training distribution yet lose that property when the distribution changes. This paper studies fairness across a specified family of changes formed by reweighting training samples. Its target is a classifier that remains fair throughout that family while also controlling prediction loss.

The authors formulate a min-max objective combining distributionally robust loss minimization with fairness across the distribution class. They reduce the problem to finding a fair classifier robust to those distributions and develop an iterative method based on online learning. The algorithm is proved to converge to such a fair and robust solution.

Experiments on standard fairness datasets suggest that the method preserves fairness guarantees and test accuracy across a broad set of test-set perturbations compared with existing fair classifiers. The experiments also reveal a trade-off between fairness robustness and accuracy. The contribution extends fairness beyond a single empirical distribution, with protection tied specifically to the perturbation class considered rather than to arbitrary changes in deployment data.
summary.tldr: The paper develops classifiers with fairness guarantees across sample-reweighting perturbations and studies the associated trade-off with accuracy.

title: Ensuring Fairness Beyond the Training Data

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of signal estimation from noisy non-linear measurements when the unknown $n$-dimensional signal is in the range of an $L$-Lipschitz continuous generative model with bounded $k$-dimensional inputs. We make the assumption of sub-Gaussian measurements, which is satisfied by a wide range of measurement models, such as linear, logistic, 1-bit, and other quantized models. In addition, we consider the impact of adversarial corruptions on these measurements. Our analysis is based on a generalized Lasso approach (Plan and Vershynin, 2016). We first provide a non-uniform recovery guarantee, which states that under i.i.d.~Gaussian measurements, roughly $O\left(\frac{k}{\epsilon^2}\log L\right)$ samples suffice for recovery with an $\ell_2$-error of $\epsilon$, and that this scheme is robust to adversarial noise. Then, we apply this result to neural network generative models, and discuss various extensions to other models and non-i.i.d.~measurements. Moreover, we show that our result can be extended to the uniform recovery guarantee under the assumption of a so-called local embedding property, which is satisfied by the 1-bit and censored Tobit models.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of a high-dimensional signal from noisy nonlinear measurements when the signal lies in the range of a generative model. The model maps bounded k-dimensional inputs into n-dimensional signals and is L-Lipschitz continuous. This structure supplies a low-dimensional description of the signals eligible for recovery.

Using a generalized Lasso approach, the authors analyze sub-Gaussian measurement models and allow adversarial corruption. Under independent, identically distributed Gaussian measurements, they establish a non-uniform guarantee requiring roughly order (k/ε²) log L samples for Euclidean error ε. The recovery scheme is also robust to adversarial noise. The bound ties the sample requirement to the generator's input dimension and regularity.

The authors apply the result to neural-network generators and discuss extensions to other models and measurements that are not independent and identically distributed. A uniform recovery guarantee is also available under an additional local embedding property, which they show holds for 1-bit and censored Tobit models. The stronger guarantee therefore retains a specific additional assumption.
summary.tldr: Generalized Lasso recovers signals described by Lipschitz generators from nonlinear measurements, with conditional sample and robustness guarantees.

title: The Generalized Lasso with Nonlinear Observations and Generative Priors

abstract: Transformers have been proven a successful model for a variety of tasks in sequence modeling. However, computing the attention matrix, which is their key component, has quadratic complexity with respect to the sequence length, thus making them prohibitively expensive for large sequences. To address this, we propose clustered attention, which instead of computing the attention for every query, groups queries into clusters and computes attention just for the centroids. To further improve this approximation, we use the computed clusters to identify the keys with the highest attention per query and compute the exact key/query dot products. This results in a model with linear complexity with respect to the sequence length for a fixed number of clusters. We evaluate our approach on two automatic speech recognition datasets and show that our model consistently outperforms vanilla transformers for a given computational budget. Finally, we demonstrate that our model can approximate arbitrarily complex attention distributions with a minimal number of clusters by approximating a pretrained BERT model on GLUE and SQuAD benchmarks with only 25 clusters and no loss in performance.

paragraphs: Standard transformer attention becomes expensive on long sequences because its computation grows quadratically with sequence length. This paper reduces that cost by sharing attention calculations among groups of queries. The goal is to retain useful attention behavior while spending less computation on separate query-by-key comparisons.

Clustered attention groups queries and computes attention for each cluster’s centroid. It then improves this approximation by using the clusters to identify keys receiving high attention for each query and calculating those query–key dot products exactly. With the number of clusters fixed, the resulting computation grows linearly with sequence length.

On two speech-recognition datasets, the method consistently outperforms standard transformers at a given computational budget. The authors also approximate a pretrained BERT model on GLUE and SQuAD using only 25 clusters, reporting no loss of performance. These results show that shared coarse attention, supplemented with targeted exact calculations, can preserve detailed attention behavior in the evaluated tasks while reducing the cost of handling longer sequences.
summary.tldr: Clustered attention shares computations across queries and selectively refines them, achieving linear sequence-length complexity for a fixed cluster count.

title: Fast Transformers with Clustered Attention

abstract: Block-based visual programming environments play a critical role in introducing computing concepts to K-12 students. One of the key pedagogical challenges in these environments is in designing new practice tasks for a student that match a desired level of difficulty and exercise specific programming concepts. In this paper, we formalize the problem of synthesizing visual programming tasks. In particular, given a reference visual task $\task^{in}$ and its solution code $\code^{in}$, we propose a novel methodology to automatically generate a set $\{(\task^{out}, \code^{out})\}$ of new tasks along with solution codes such that tasks $\task^{in}$ and $\task^{out}$ are conceptually similar but visually dissimilar. Our methodology is based on the realization that the mapping from the space of visual tasks to their solution codes is highly discontinuous; hence, directly mutating reference task $\task^{in}$ to generate new tasks is futile. Our task synthesis algorithm operates by first mutating code $\code^{in}$ to obtain a set of codes $\{\code^{out}\}$. Then, the algorithm performs symbolic execution over a code $\code^{out}$ to obtain a visual task $\task^{out}$; this step uses the Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) procedure to guide the search in the symbolic tree. paragraphs: Creating programming practice requires matching the concepts and difficulty a student should encounter. This paper formalizes automatic task generation for block-based visual programming. Given a reference task and its solution, the goal is to produce new task-and-solution pairs that exercise similar concepts while looking different.

The authors observe that changes in a visual task can correspond to abrupt changes in the code needed to solve it. Their algorithm therefore begins by modifying the reference solution code. It then uses symbolic execution to construct a corresponding visual task, with Monte Carlo Tree Search guiding exploration of the symbolic execution tree.

Starting from code gives the synthesis process a direct connection to the programming structure that the practice should exercise. The authors evaluate the method through extensive experiments and a user study using tasks from Code.org's Classic Maze challenge and CodeHS's introductory Karel course. The reported results demonstrate the effectiveness of generating visually varied practice tasks together with solutions through this code-first procedure.
summary.tldr: The method generates conceptually similar but visually different programming exercises by modifying solution code and constructing tasks through guided symbolic execution.

title: Synthesizing Tasks for Block-based Programming

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a cornerstone of machine learning. When the number $N$ of data items is large, SGD relies on constructing an unbiased estimator of the gradient of the empirical risk using a small subset of the original dataset, called a minibatch. Default minibatch construction involves uniformly sampling a subset of the desired size, but alternatives have been explored for variance reduction. In particular, experimental evidence suggests drawing minibatches from determinantal point processes (DPPs), tractable distributions over minibatches that favour diversity among selected items. However, like in recent work on DPPs for coresets, providing a systematic and principled understanding of how and why DPPs help has been difficult. In this work, we contribute an orthogonal polynomial-based determinantal point process paradigm for performing minibatch sampling in SGD. Our approach leverages the specific data distribution at hand, which endows it with greater sensitivity and power over existing data-agnostic methods. We substantiate our method via a detailed theoretical analysis of its convergence properties, interweaving between the discrete data set and the underlying continuous domain. In particular, we show how specific DPPs and a string of controlled approximations can lead to gradient estimators with a variance that decays faster with the batchsize than under uniform sampling. Coupled with existing finite-time guarantees for SGD on convex objectives, this entails that, for a large enough batchsize and a fixed budget of item-level gradients to evaluate, DPP minibatches lead to a smaller bound on the mean square approximation error than uniform minibatches. Moreover, our estimators are amenable to a recent algorithm that directly samples linear statistics of DPPs (i.e., the gradient estimator) without sampling the underlying DPP (i.e., the minibatch), thereby reducing computational overhead. We provide detailed synthetic as well as real data experiments to substantiate our theoretical claims.

title: Determinantal point processes based on orthogonal polynomials for sampling minibatches in SGD

abstract: To perform well on unseen and potentially out-of-distribution samples, it is desirable for machine learning models to have a predictable response with respect to transformations affecting the factors of variation of the input. Here, we study the relative importance of several types of inductive biases towards such predictable behavior: the choice of data, their augmentations, and model architectures. Invariance is commonly achieved through hand-engineered data augmentation, but do standard data augmentations address transformations that explain variations in real data? While prior work has focused on synthetic data, we attempt here to characterize the factors of variation in a real dataset, ImageNet, and study the invariance of both standard residual networks and the recently proposed vision transformer with respect to changes in these factors. We show standard augmentation relies on a precise combination of translation and scale, with translation recapturing most of the performance improvement---despite the (approximate) translation invariance built in to convolutional architectures, such as residual networks. In fact, we found that scale and translation invariance was similar across residual networks and vision transformer models despite their markedly different architectural inductive biases. We show the training data itself is the main source of invariance, and that data augmentation only further increases the learned invariances. Notably, the invariances learned during training align with the ImageNet factors of variation we found. Finally, we find that the main factors of variation in ImageNet mostly relate to appearance and are specific to each class.

paragraphs: A useful image model should respond predictably when visual properties change. This paper investigates where such invariance comes from: the training images, transformations added through augmentation, or the model architecture. It studies factors of variation in ImageNet and examines residual networks and vision transformers under changes in those factors.

The authors find that standard augmentation depends on a particular combination of translation and scale, with translation accounting for most of the performance improvement. That benefit remains despite the approximate translation invariance built into convolutional architectures. Residual networks and vision transformers also show similar scale and translation invariance, even though their architectural biases differ substantially.

Those learned behaviors align with the factors of variation identified in ImageNet. The authors further find that the dataset's dominant variations mostly concern appearance and differ by class. These findings emphasize examining actual data variation when explaining a model's invariance.
summary.tldr: An ImageNet study finds that training-data variation is the main source of learned invariance, with augmentation strengthening it across different architectures.

title: Grounding inductive biases in natural images: invariance stems from variations in data

abstract: Dealing with severe class imbalance poses a major challenge for many real-world applications, especially when the accurate classification and generalization of minority classes are of primary interest.In computer vision and NLP, learning from datasets with long-tail behavior is a recurring theme, especially for naturally occurring labels. Existing solutions mostly appeal to sampling or weighting adjustments to alleviate the extreme imbalance, or impose inductive bias to prioritize generalizable associations. Here we take a novel perspective to promote sample efficiency and model generalization based on the invariance principles of causality. Our contribution posits a meta-distributional scenario, where the causal generating mechanism for label-conditional features is invariant across different labels. Such causal assumption enables efficient knowledge transfer from the dominant classes to their under-represented counterparts, even if their feature distributions show apparent disparities. This allows us to leverage a causal data augmentation procedure to enlarge the representation of minority classes. Our development is orthogonal to the existing imbalanced data learning techniques thus can be seamlessly integrated. The proposed approach is validated on an extensive set of synthetic and real-world tasks against state-of-the-art solutions.

paragraphs: Severe class imbalance leaves minority classes with little data from which to learn reliable predictions. This paper proposes transferring knowledge from dominant classes to underrepresented ones through a causal view of feature generation. The aim is to improve sample efficiency and generalization even when the observed feature distributions of different classes look substantially different.

The approach assumes a meta-distributional setting in which the causal mechanism generating label-conditional features remains invariant across labels. Under this assumption, shared generating structure enables transfer despite those apparent distributional differences. The authors use that structure for causal data augmentation, enlarging the representation of minority classes through information learned from more abundant classes.

The method is designed to be compatible with existing imbalance-learning techniques, so it can be combined with approaches such as sampling or weighting adjustments. Evaluation covers synthetic and real-world tasks against leading solutions. The central contribution is the proposed route from an explicit invariance assumption to minority-class augmentation, with the transfer rationale depending on that shared causal mechanism.
summary.tldr: A shared causal feature-generation assumption enables knowledge transfer and augmentation from majority to minority classes.

title: Supercharging Imbalanced Data Learning With Energy-based Contrastive Representation Transfer

abstract: Recent years have witnessed a surge of approaches to use neural networks to help tackle combinatorial optimization problems, including graph optimization problems. However, theoretical understanding of such approaches remains limited. In this paper, we consider the geometric setting, where graphs are induced by points in a fixed dimensional Euclidean space. We show that several graph optimization problems can be approximated by an algorithm that is polynomial in graph size n via a framework we propose, call the Baker-paradigm. More importantly, a key advantage of the Baker-paradigm is that it decomposes the input problem into (at most linear number of) small sub-problems of fixed sizes (independent of the size of the input). For the family of such fixed-size sub-problems, we can now design neural networks with universal approximation guarantees to solve them. This leads to a mixed algorithmic-ML framework, which we call NN-Baker that has the capacity to approximately solve a family of graph optimization problems (e.g, maximum independent set and minimum vertex cover) in time linear to input graph size, and only polynomial to approximation parameter. We instantiate our NN-Baker by a CNN version and GNN version, and demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach via a range of experiments.

paragraphs: Neural networks are increasingly used for graph optimization, but their theoretical capabilities can be difficult to characterize. NN-Baker studies graphs arising from points in a fixed-dimensional Euclidean space. Its central strategy is to combine an algorithmic decomposition with neural networks that handle the resulting small optimization problems.

The proposed Baker-paradigm breaks an input into at most a linear number of subproblems whose sizes are independent of the input graph's size. This fixed-size structure permits neural networks with universal approximation guarantees for the subproblem family. The decomposition therefore provides a specific role for learning inside an algorithm with an analyzable structure.

The authors implement both convolutional and graph neural network versions and report experimental effectiveness and efficiency. The guarantees are tied to the geometric setting and the framework's approximation construction.
summary.tldr: NN-Baker decomposes geometric graph optimization into fixed-size subproblems that neural networks can approximately solve within an analyzable framework.

title: NN-Baker: A Neural-network Infused Algorithmic Framework for Optimization Problems on Geometric Intersection Graphs

abstract: Human language learners are exposed to a trickle of informative, context-sensitive language, but a flood of raw sensory data. Through both social language use and internal processes of rehearsal and practice, language learners are able to build high-level, semantic representations that explain their perceptions. Here, we take inspiration from such processes of "inner speech" in humans (Vygotsky, 1934) to better understand the role of intra-agent speech in embodied behavior. First, we formally pose intra-agent speech as a semi-supervised problem and develop two algorithms that enable visually grounded captioning with little labeled language data. We then experimentally compute scaling curves over different amounts of labeled data and compare the data efficiency against a supervised learning baseline. Finally, we incorporate intra-agent speech into an embodied, mobile manipulator agent operating in a 3D virtual world, and show that with as few as 150 additional image captions, intra-agent speech endows the agent with the ability to manipulate and answer questions about a new object without any related task-directed experience (zero-shot). Taken together, our experiments suggest that modelling intra-agent speech is effective in enabling embodied agents to learn new tasks efficiently and without direct interaction experience.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether an embodied agent can benefit from a process inspired by human inner speech. The motivating imbalance is familiar: a learner can observe abundant sensory information while receiving relatively little language tied to those observations. The authors ask how language-related internal processing can help turn that experience into useful semantic representations.

They formulate intra-agent speech as a semi-supervised learning problem and develop two algorithms for visually grounded captioning with limited labeled language data. Experiments vary the amount of labeled data to measure scaling behavior and compare data efficiency with a supervised baseline. This connects the proposed mechanism to a concrete learning task before placing it inside an acting agent.

In a three-dimensional virtual world, a mobile manipulator equipped with intra-agent speech learns to manipulate and answer questions about a new object using as few as 150 additional image captions. It receives no related task-directed experience. The reported zero-shot capability therefore concerns transfer to those tasks after caption-based learning, and suggests a route to more data-efficient embodied learning.
summary.tldr: Caption-based intra-agent speech enables a virtual embodied agent to acquire new object-related tasks without related task-directed experience.

title: Intra-agent speech permits zero-shot task acquisition

abstract: Despite the enormous success of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) in modeling graph-structured data, most of the current GCNs are shallow due to the notoriously challenging problems of over-smoothening and information squashing along with conventional difficulty caused by vanishing gradients and over-fitting. Previous works have been primarily focused on the study of over-smoothening and over-squashing phenomena in training deep GCNs. Surprisingly, in comparison with CNNs/RNNs, very limited attention has been given to understanding how healthy gradient flow can benefit the trainability of deep GCNs. In this paper, firstly, we provide a new perspective of gradient flow to understand the substandard performance of deep GCNs and hypothesize that by facilitating healthy gradient flow, we can significantly improve their trainability, as well as achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) level performance from vanilla-GCNs. Next, we argue that blindly adopting the Glorot initialization for GCNs is not optimal, and derive a topology-aware isometric initialization scheme for vanilla-GCNs based on the principles of isometry. Additionally, contrary to ad-hoc addition of skip-connections, we propose to use gradient-guided dynamic rewiring of vanilla-GCNs with skip connections. Our dynamic rewiring method uses the gradient flow within each layer during training to introduce on-demand skip-connections adaptively. We provide extensive empirical evidence across multiple datasets that our methods improve gradient flow in deep vanilla-GCNs and significantly boost their performance to comfortably compete and outperform many fancy state-of-the-art methods. Codes are available at: https://github.com/VITA-Group/GradientGCN.

paragraphs: Deep graph convolutional networks can be difficult to train for several reasons, including overly similar node representations, compressed information, vanishing gradients, and overfitting. This paper focuses on gradient flow, which the authors argue has received less attention than other explanations. They hypothesize that improving it can make ordinary deep GCNs substantially more trainable.

The authors introduce two interventions. First, they derive a topology-aware initialization based on isometry principles, arguing that simply applying Glorot initialization is not optimal for GCNs. Second, they dynamically add skip connections using gradient information from each layer during training. These connections are introduced adaptively when the observed gradient flow indicates a need.

Experiments across multiple datasets show improved gradient flow and substantially better performance for deep vanilla GCNs. The resulting models compete with and outperform many sophisticated state-of-the-art methods in the evaluations. The findings support gradient flow as a productive target for improving deep graph networks, showing that initialization and adaptive connectivity can unlock stronger performance from an otherwise basic architecture.
summary.tldr: Topology-aware initialization and gradient-guided skip connections substantially improve the training and performance of deep vanilla GCNs.

title: Old can be Gold: Better Gradient Flow can Make Vanilla-GCNs Great Again

abstract: The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) has emerged as a powerful tool to provide memorization, optimization and generalization guarantees in deep neural networks. A line of work has studied the NTK spectrum for two-layer and deep networks with at least a layer with $\Omega(N)$ neurons, $N$ being the number of training samples. Furthermore, there is increasing evidence suggesting that deep networks with sub-linear layer widths are powerful memorizers and optimizers, as long as the number of parameters exceeds the number of samples. Thus, a natural open question is whether the NTK is well conditioned in such a challenging sub-linear setup. In this paper, we answer this question in the affirmative. Our key technical contribution is a lower bound on the smallest NTK eigenvalue for deep networks with the minimum possible over-parameterization: up to logarithmic factors, the number of parameters is $\Omega(N)$ and, hence, the number of neurons is as little as $\Omega(\sqrt{N})$. To showcase the applicability of our NTK bounds, we provide two results concerning memorization capacity and optimization guarantees for gradient descent training.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel, or NTK, is a mathematical tool for studying neural-network training. Earlier spectral analyses considered networks with at least one layer containing a number of neurons proportional to the number of training examples. This paper asks whether useful NTK conditioning can also hold when layer widths grow more slowly than the dataset.

The main technical result is a lower bound on the smallest NTK eigenvalue for deep networks in a minimally over-parameterized regime. Up to logarithmic factors, the parameter count scales as Ω(N), while the number of neurons can be as small as Ω(√N), where N is the number of training samples. The result answers the conditioning question affirmatively in the setup studied.

The authors apply this spectral bound to obtain results on memorization capacity and gradient-descent optimization. This matters because theoretical explanations of successful training need not always depend on layers as wide as the dataset. The contribution extends NTK-based guarantees into a narrower-network regime while retaining enough total parameters relative to the number of samples.
summary.tldr: New NTK spectral bounds support memorization and optimization guarantees for deep networks with sublinear widths and near-linear parameter counts.

title: Memorization and Optimization in Deep Neural Networks with Minimum Over-parameterization

abstract: Graph (structure) augmentation aims to perturb the graph structure through heuristic or probabilistic rules, enabling the nodes to capture richer contextual information and thus improving generalization performance. While there have been a few graph structure augmentation methods proposed recently, none of them are aware of a potential negative augmentation problem, which may be caused by overly severe distribution shifts between the original and augmented graphs. In this paper, we take an important graph property, namely graph homophily, to analyze the distribution shifts between the two graphs and thus measure the severity of an augmentation algorithm suffering from negative augmentation. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel Knowledge Distillation for Graph Augmentation (KDGA) framework, which helps to reduce the potential negative effects of distribution shifts, i.e., negative augmentation problem. Specifically, KDGA extracts the knowledge of any GNN teacher model trained on the augmented graphs and injects it into a partially parameter-shared student model that is tested on the original graph. As a simple but efficient framework, KDGA is applicable to a variety of existing graph augmentation methods and can significantly improve the performance of various GNN architectures. For three popular graph augmentation methods, namely GAUG, MH-Aug, and GraphAug, the experimental results show that the learned student models outperform their vanilla implementations by an average accuracy of 4.6% (GAUG), 4.2% (MH-Aug), and 4.6% (GraphAug) on eight graph datasets.

paragraphs: Graph augmentation changes a graph’s structure to expose nodes to richer contextual information during learning. However, a sufficiently large shift between the augmented and original graphs can hurt performance. This paper studies that negative augmentation problem using graph homophily as a property for analyzing the distribution shift.

The proposed Knowledge Distillation for Graph Augmentation framework separates learning on augmented graphs from testing on the original graph. A teacher GNN learns from augmented graphs and transfers its knowledge into a student that partially shares parameters with it. The student is then evaluated on the original graph, helping reduce the potential harm caused by structural augmentation.

The framework applies to a variety of augmentation methods and GNN architectures. Across eight graph datasets, students improve over the vanilla implementations of GAUG, MH-Aug, and GraphAug by reported average accuracy gains of 4.6%, 4.2%, and 4.6%, respectively. These results support using distillation to retain useful knowledge from augmentation while reducing the negative effects of the resulting distribution shift.
summary.tldr: KDGA transfers knowledge from augmented-graph teachers to students tested on original graphs, reducing harmful augmentation effects.

title: Knowledge Distillation Improves Graph Structure Augmentation for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Optical computing has become emerging technology in next-generation efficient artificial intelligence (AI) due to its ultra-high speed and efficiency. Electromagnetic field simulation is critical to the design, optimization, and validation of photonic devices and circuits.However, costly numerical simulation significantly hinders the scalability and turn-around time in the photonic circuit design loop. Recently, physics-informed neural networks were proposed to predict the optical field solution of a single instance of a partial differential equation (PDE) with predefined parameters. Their complicated PDE formulation and lack of efficient parametrization mechanism limit their flexibility and generalization in practical simulation scenarios. In this work, for the first time, a physics-agnostic neural operator-based framework, dubbed NeurOLight, is proposed to learn a family of frequency-domain Maxwell PDEs for ultra-fast parametric photonic device simulation. Specifically, we discretize different devices into a unified domain, represent parametric PDEs with a compact wave prior, and encode the incident light via masked source modeling. We design our model to have parameter-efficient cross-shaped NeurOLight blocks and adopt superposition-based augmentation for data-efficient learning. With those synergistic approaches, NeurOLight demonstrates 2-orders-of-magnitude faster simulation speed than numerical solvers and outperforms prior NN-based models by ~54% lower prediction error using ~44% fewer parameters.
originalAbstract: Optical computing has become emerging technology in next-generation efficient artificial intelligence (AI) due to its ultra-high speed and efficiency. Electromagnetic field simulation is critical to the design, optimization, and validation of photonic devices and circuits.However, costly numerical simulation significantly hinders the scalability and turn-around time in the photonic circuit design loop. Recently, physics-informed neural networks were proposed to predict the optical field solution of a single instance of a partial differential equation (PDE) with predefined parameters. Their complicated PDE formulation and lack of efficient parametrization mechanism limit their flexibility and generalization in practical simulation scenarios. In this work, for the first time, a physics-agnostic neural operator-based framework, dubbed NeurOLight, is proposed to learn a family of frequency-domain Maxwell PDEs for ultra-fast parametric photonic device simulation. Specifically, we discretize different devices into a unified domain, represent parametric PDEs with a compact wave prior, and encode the incident light via masked source modeling. We design our model to have parameter-efficient cross-shaped NeurOLight blocks and adopt superposition-based augmentation for data-efficient learning. With those synergistic approaches, NeurOLight demonstrates 2-orders-of-magnitude faster simulation speed than numerical solvers and outperforms prior NN-based models by ~54% lower prediction error using ~44% fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Designing photonic devices requires electromagnetic field simulations, but numerical solvers can make repeated design and validation expensive. The paper addresses learning across a family of simulation problems. It contrasts this goal with neural approaches that predict the solution of one partial differential equation instance with predefined parameters.

NeurOLight learns a family of frequency-domain Maxwell equations through a neural operator framework. It represents different devices on a common discretized domain, uses a compact wave prior to express parameterized equations, and encodes incoming light through masked source modeling. Cross-shaped network blocks reduce parameter requirements, while augmentation based on superposition improves data efficiency.

The authors report simulation speeds roughly two orders of magnitude faster than numerical solvers. Against prior neural models, they report approximately 54% lower prediction error with approximately 44% fewer parameters. These findings indicate that a shared representation of devices, parameters, and light sources can support fast parametric simulation while improving prediction quality and model compactness in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: NeurOLight learns families of photonic simulations and reports much faster execution with lower error and fewer parameters than prior neural models.

title: NeurOLight: A Physics-Agnostic Neural Operator Enabling Parametric Photonic Device Simulation

abstract: By learning a sequence of tasks continually, an agent in continual learning (CL) can improve the learning performance of both a new task and `old' tasks by leveraging the forward knowledge transfer and the backward knowledge transfer, respectively. However, most existing CL methods focus on addressing catastrophic forgetting in neural networks by minimizing the modification of the learnt model for old tasks. This inevitably limits the backward knowledge transfer from the new task to the old tasks, because judicious model updates could possibly improve the learning performance of the old tasks as well. To tackle this problem, we first theoretically analyze the conditions under which updating the learnt model of old tasks could be beneficial for CL and also lead to backward knowledge transfer, based on the gradient projection onto the input subspaces of old tasks. Building on the theoretical analysis, we next develop a ContinUal learning method with Backward knowlEdge tRansfer (CUBER), for a fixed capacity neural network without data replay. In particular, CUBER first characterizes the task correlation to identify the positively correlated old tasks in a layer-wise manner, and then selectively modifies the learnt model of the old tasks when learning the new task. Experimental studies show that CUBER can even achieve positive backward knowledge transfer on several existing CL benchmarks for the first time without data replay, where the related baselines still suffer from catastrophic forgetting (negative backward knowledge transfer). The superior performance of CUBER on the backward knowledge transfer also leads to higher accuracy accordingly.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to learn successive tasks while retaining earlier abilities. Many methods protect old tasks by restricting changes to what the network has already learned. This paper examines a further possibility: carefully chosen changes during a new task could actually improve performance on earlier tasks.

The authors analyze conditions for this backward knowledge transfer using projections of gradients onto the input subspaces associated with old tasks. They then develop CUBER, which identifies positively related earlier tasks separately at different network layers. During new learning, it selectively changes the model associated with those tasks. The network has fixed capacity, and the method does not replay data from previous tasks.

On several continual learning benchmarks, CUBER achieves positive backward transfer, while the compared baselines still lose performance on earlier tasks. Better backward transfer also accompanies higher accuracy. The result supports selective adaptation as a way to improve past learning, with the theoretical analysis explaining conditions under which such updates can be beneficial.
summary.tldr: CUBER selectively updates knowledge from related earlier tasks, achieving positive backward transfer on several benchmarks without replaying old data.

title: Beyond Not-Forgetting: Continual Learning with Backward Knowledge Transfer

abstract: We propose a new "Poisson flow" generative model~(PFGM) that maps a uniform distribution on a high-dimensional hemisphere into any data distribution. We interpret the data points as electrical charges on the $z=0$ hyperplane in a space augmented with an additional dimension $z$, generating a high-dimensional electric field (the gradient of the solution to Poisson equation). We prove that if these charges flow upward along electric field lines, their initial distribution in the $z=0$ plane transforms into a distribution on the hemisphere of radius $r$ that becomes uniform in the $r \to\infty$ limit. To learn the bijective transformation, we estimate the normalized field in the augmented space. For sampling, we devise a backward ODE that is anchored by the physically meaningful additional dimension: the samples hit the (unaugmented) data manifold when the $z$ reaches zero. Experimentally, PFGM achieves current state-of-the-art performance among the normalizing flow models on CIFAR-10, with an Inception score of $9.68$ and a FID score of $2.35$. It also performs on par with the state-of-the-art SDE approaches while offering $10\times $ to $20 \times$ acceleration on image generation tasks. Additionally, PFGM appears more tolerant of estimation errors on a weaker network architecture and robust to the step size in the Euler method. The code is available at https://github.com/Newbeeer/poisson_flow .
