paragraphs: Poisson Flow Generative Models builds a generative transformation using an electrostatic interpretation of data. Each data point acts like an electrical charge on a plane, and an added coordinate creates a larger space in which these charges define an electric field. The model learns the normalized direction of that field.

The authors prove that moving charges upward along field lines produces a distribution that approaches uniformity on a hemisphere as its radius tends to infinity. Generation reverses this process through an ordinary differential equation. The added coordinate supplies a meaningful stopping point: when it reaches zero, the generated sample arrives on the original data manifold.

On CIFAR-10, the paper reports an Inception score of 9.68 and FID of 2.35, described as leading results among normalizing flows. It also reports performance comparable to leading stochastic-differential-equation approaches with 10–20 times faster image generation. Experiments further suggest tolerance to field-estimation errors with a weaker network and robustness to Euler step size; these are empirical observations.
summary.tldr: Poisson Flow Generative Models learns an electric-field-inspired transformation that generates images by reversing a flow from a hemisphere toward the data.

title: Poisson Flow Generative Models

abstract: Contrastive learning, which learns to contrast positive with negative pairs of samples, has been popular for self-supervised visual representation learning. Although great effort has been made to design proper positive pairs through data augmentation, few works attempt to generate optimal positives for each instance. Inspired by semantic consistency and computational advantage in latent space of pretrained generative models, this paper proposes to learn instance-specific latent transformations to generate Contrastive Optimal Positives (COP-Gen) for self-supervised contrastive learning. Specifically, we formulate COP-Gen as an instance-specific latent space navigator which minimizes the mutual information between the generated positive pair subject to the semantic consistency constraint. Theoretically, the learned latent transformation creates optimal positives for contrastive learning, which removes as much nuisance information as possible while preserving the semantics. Empirically, using generated positives by COP-Gen consistently outperforms other latent transformation methods and even real-image-based methods in self-supervised contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds visual representations by distinguishing positive pairs from negative pairs. Choosing positives is therefore central: paired examples should share their meaning without encouraging dependence on irrelevant details. This paper proposes generating positives separately for each instance through transformations inside the latent space of a pretrained generative model.

The method, COP-Gen, learns an instance-specific navigator through that latent space. Its objective minimizes mutual information between the generated positive pair while imposing a semantic-consistency constraint. The intended balance is to remove as much shared nuisance information as possible while retaining what makes the two examples semantically related. The constraint is essential because reducing shared information alone would not preserve a meaningful positive pair.

The theoretical analysis identifies the learned transformations as producing optimal positives under this formulation. Empirically, COP-Gen positives consistently outperform the compared latent-transformation methods and even methods based on real images in self-supervised contrastive learning. The work shows how positive-pair generation can itself become a learned objective, with semantic preservation directing which variation is useful.
summary.tldr: COP-Gen learns instance-specific latent transformations that remove shared nuisance information while preserving semantics for contrastive positive pairs.

title: Optimal Positive Generation via Latent Transformation for Contrastive Learning

abstract: The main challenge of multiagent reinforcement learning is the difficulty of learning useful policies in the presence of other simultaneously learning agents whose changing behaviors jointly affect the environment's transition and reward dynamics. An effective approach that has recently emerged for addressing this non-stationarity is for each agent to anticipate the learning of other agents and influence the evolution of future policies towards desirable behavior for its own benefit. Unfortunately, previous approaches for achieving this suffer from myopic evaluation, considering only a finite number of policy updates. As such, these methods can only influence transient future policies rather than achieving the promise of scalable equilibrium selection approaches that influence the behavior at convergence. In this paper, we propose a principled framework for considering the limiting policies of other agents as time approaches infinity. Specifically, we develop a new optimization objective that maximizes each agent's average reward by directly accounting for the impact of its behavior on the limiting set of policies that other agents will converge to. Our paper characterizes desirable solution concepts within this problem setting and provides practical approaches for optimizing over possible outcomes. As a result of our farsighted objective, we demonstrate better long-term performance than state-of-the-art baselines across a suite of diverse multiagent benchmark domains.

paragraphs: When several reinforcement learning agents learn simultaneously, each agent faces an environment that changes as the others update their behavior. One response is to anticipate those updates and act in ways that influence other agents' future policies. This paper argues that looking ahead through only a finite number of updates can favor temporary outcomes rather than desirable long-term behavior.

The authors introduce an objective that considers the limiting policies of other agents as time approaches infinity. Each agent seeks to maximize its average reward while accounting directly for how its own behavior affects the set of policies the others converge to. This makes influence over eventual outcomes part of the optimization target.

The paper characterizes desirable solution concepts for this setting and develops practical ways to optimize over possible outcomes. Across a diverse collection of multiagent benchmarks, the resulting approach achieves better long-term performance than leading baselines. The contribution is a framework for reasoning about influence at convergence, supported by experiments showing advantages from that longer perspective in the evaluated domains.
summary.tldr: A multiagent learning objective accounts for other agents' limiting policies and improves long-term performance on evaluated benchmarks.

title: Influencing Long-Term Behavior in Multiagent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning typically relies heavily on a well-designed reward signal, which gets more challenging in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Alternatively, unsupervised reinforcement learning (URL) has delivered on its promise in the recent past to learn useful skills and explore the environment without external supervised signals. These approaches mainly aimed for the single agent to reach distinguishable states, insufficient for multi-agent systems due to that each agent interacts with not only the environment, but also the other agents. We propose Synergy Pattern Diversifying Oriented Unsupervised Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (SPD) to learn generic coordination policies for agents with no extrinsic reward. Specifically, we devise the Synergy Pattern Graph (SPG), a graph depicting the relationships of agents at each time step. Furthermore, we propose an episode-wise divergence measurement to approximate the discrepancy of synergy patterns. To overcome the challenge of sparse return, we decompose the discrepancy of synergy patterns to per-time-step pseudo-reward. Empirically, we show the capacity of SPD to acquire meaningful coordination policies, such as maintaining specific formations in Multi-Agent Particle Environment and pass-and-shoot in Google Research Football. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the same instructive pretrained policy's parameters can serve as a good initialization for a series of downstream tasks' policies, achieving higher data efficiency and outperforming state-of-the-art approaches in Google Research Football.

paragraphs: Learning cooperative behavior usually depends on carefully designed rewards, which become harder to specify when several agents must coordinate. Unsupervised reinforcement learning offers an alternative, but encouraging a single agent to reach distinct states does not fully capture relationships among agents. SPD instead aims to learn varied coordination policies without extrinsic rewards.

The method represents relationships among agents at each time step using a Synergy Pattern Graph. It then measures how coordination patterns differ across episodes. Because an episode-level signal can be sparse, SPD decomposes this discrepancy into pseudo-rewards at individual time steps, providing more frequent learning signals for developing diverse forms of cooperation.

Experiments show meaningful behaviors, including maintaining formations in Multi-Agent Particle Environment and passing and shooting in Google Research Football. The authors also reuse the same pretrained policy parameters to initialize policies for multiple downstream tasks. In the reported football experiments, this improves data efficiency and outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, supporting coordination-focused pretraining as a useful starting point.
summary.tldr: SPD learns diverse multi-agent coordination without extrinsic rewards and provides useful policy initializations for downstream cooperative tasks.

title: SPD: Synergy Pattern Diversifying Oriented Unsupervised Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Internet ad auctions have evolved from a few lines of text to richer informational layouts that include images, sitelinks, videos, etc. Ads in these new formats occupy varying amounts of space, and an advertiser can provide multiple formats, only one of which can be shown.The seller is now faced with a multi-parameter mechanism design problem.Computing an efficient allocation is computationally intractable, and therefore the standard Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) auction, while truthful and welfare-optimal, is impractical. In this paper, we tackle a fundamental problem in the design of modern ad auctions. We adopt a ``Myersonian'' approach and study allocation rules that are monotone both in the bid and set of rich ads. We show that such rules can be paired with a payment function to give a truthful auction. Our main technical challenge is designing a monotone rule that yields a good approximation to the optimal welfare. Monotonicity doesn't hold for standard algorithms, e.g. the incremental bang-per-buck order, that give good approximations to ``knapsack-like'' problems such as ours. In fact, we show that no deterministic monotone rule can approximate the optimal welfare within a factor better than $2$ (while there is a non-monotone FPTAS). Our main result is a new, simple, greedy and monotone allocation rule that guarantees a $3$ approximation. In ad auctions in practice, monotone allocation rules are often paired with the so-called \emph{Generalized Second Price (GSP)} payment rule, which charges the minimum threshold price below which the allocation changes. We prove that, even though our monotone allocation rule paired with GSP is not truthful, its Price of Anarchy (PoA) is bounded. Under standard no-overbidding assumptions, we prove bounds on the a pure and Bayes-Nash PoA. Finally, we experimentally test our algorithms on real-world data.

summary.tldr: A simple monotone greedy rule gives a factor-three welfare approximation for rich-ad auctions, with separate guarantees for truthful and GSP payment settings.

title: Simple Mechanisms for Welfare Maximization in Rich Advertising Auctions

abstract: We present Falconn++, a novel locality-sensitive filtering (LSF) approach for approximate nearest neighbor search on angular distance. Falconn++ can filter out potential far away points in any hash bucket before querying, which results in higher quality candidates compared to other hashing-based solutions. Theoretically, Falconn++ asymptotically achieves lower query time complexity than Falconn, an optimal locality-sensitive hashing scheme on angular distance. Empirically, Falconn++ achieves a higher recall-speed tradeoff than Falconn on many real-world data sets. Falconn++ is also competitive with HNSW, an efficient representative of graph-based solutions on high search recall regimes.

Falconn++ can filter out potential far away points in any hash bucket before querying, which results in higher quality candidates compared to other hashing-based solutions. Theoretically, Falconn++ asymptotically achieves lower query time complexity than Falconn, an optimal locality-sensitive hashing scheme on angular distance. paragraphs: Approximate nearest neighbor search seeks nearby data points while trading some retrieval accuracy for faster search. Falconn++ addresses this problem for angular distance. Its starting point is that a hash bucket may contain points that are poor candidates, even though the bucket itself is relevant to the search.

The method uses locality-sensitive filtering to remove potentially distant points from hash buckets before querying. This produces higher-quality candidate sets than other hashing-based solutions described in the paper. The theoretical analysis establishes a lower asymptotic query-time complexity than Falconn, a locality-sensitive hashing scheme that is optimal within its setting. Filtering therefore offers a way to improve search beyond the comparison hashing approach.

Experiments on many real-world datasets show a better recall-speed tradeoff than Falconn: the relationship between retrieval success and search speed improves. Falconn++ is also competitive with HNSW, a graph-based search method, when high search recall is required. These findings support its practical relevance alongside the theoretical improvement, particularly for searches where recovering a high proportion of neighbors matters.
summary.tldr: Falconn++ filters likely distant points from hash buckets, improving theoretical query complexity and empirical recall-speed tradeoffs over Falconn.

title: Falconn++: A Locality-sensitive Filtering Approach for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search

abstract: Despite the prevalence of recent success in learning from static graphs, learning from time-evolving graphs remains an open challenge. In this work, we design new, more stringent evaluation procedures for link prediction specific to dynamic graphs, which reflect real-world considerations, to better compare the strengths and weaknesses of methods. First, we create two visualization techniques to understand the reoccurring patterns of edges over time and show that many edges reoccur at later time steps. Based on this observation, we propose a pure memorization-based baseline called EdgeBank. EdgeBank achieves surprisingly strong performance across multiple settings which highlights that the negative edges used in the current evaluation are easy. To sample more challenging negative edges, we introduce two novel negative sampling strategies that improve robustness and better match real-world applications. Lastly, we introduce six new dynamic graph datasets from a diverse set of domains missing from current benchmarks, providing new challenges and opportunities for future research. Our code repository is accessible at https://github.com/fpour/DGB.git.

paragraphs: Dynamic link prediction concerns connections in graphs that evolve over time. This paper examines whether existing evaluations adequately test that ability. The authors introduce two visualization techniques for inspecting recurring edges and find that many connections appear again at later times, making historical repetition an important feature of the evaluation setting.

Motivated by that observation, they propose EdgeBank, a baseline based purely on memorizing edges. Its surprisingly strong performance across several settings reveals that the negative edges used in current evaluations are easy to distinguish. A method can therefore perform well in those settings using remembered connectivity, which changes how more elaborate methods' apparent strengths should be assessed.

The authors introduce two negative-sampling strategies to create more challenging comparisons and better reflect real applications. They also add six dynamic graph datasets from domains absent in existing benchmarks. Together, the visualizations, baseline, sampling procedures, and datasets provide tools for evaluating which aspects of temporal connectivity a method handles successfully.
summary.tldr: A strong memorization baseline exposes easy dynamic-link evaluations, motivating harder negative sampling and six additional datasets.

title: Towards Better Evaluation for Dynamic Link Prediction

abstract: Understanding emerging behaviors of reinforcement learning (RL) agents may be difficult since such agents are often trained in complex environments using highly complex decision making procedures. This has given rise to a variety of approaches to explainability in RL that aim to reconcile discrepancies that may arise between the behavior of an agent and the behavior that is anticipated by an observer. Most recent approaches have relied either on domain knowledge, that may not always be available, on an analysis of the agent’s policy, or on an analysis of specific elements of the underlying environment, typically modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Our key claim is that even if the underlying model is not fully known (e.g., the transition probabilities have not been accurately learned) or is not maintained by the agent (i.e., when using model-free methods), the model can nevertheless be exploited to automatically generate explanations. For this purpose, we suggest using formal MDP abstractions and transforms, previously used in the literature for expediting the search for optimal policies, to automatically produce explanations. Since such transforms are typically based on a symbolic representation of the environment, they can provide meaningful explanations for gaps between the anticipated and actual agent behavior. We formally define the explainability problem, suggest a class of transforms that can be used for explaining emergent behaviors, and suggest methods that enable efficient search for an explanation. We demonstrate the approach on a set of standard benchmarks.

paragraphs: An observer may expect a reinforcement-learning agent to behave one way and then see it act differently. This paper treats explanation as a way to reconcile that discrepancy. Complex environments and decision procedures make the task difficult, while existing approaches often depend on domain expertise, policy analysis, or selected parts of the environment model.

The authors propose using transformations and abstractions of the environment's Markov decision process to generate explanations automatically. Such operations have previously helped search for optimal policies. Here, their typically symbolic representation provides a basis for expressing meaningful changes that explain the gap between anticipated and observed behavior.

A central claim is that the environment model can still help when it is only partially known or when the agent uses a model-free method and does not maintain one. The paper formally defines the explanation problem, introduces a class of suitable transformations, and develops methods for efficient explanation search. Demonstrations on standard benchmarks show the approach in use, connecting model-based reasoning to explanations of agents that need not themselves be model-based.
summary.tldr: Transforming environment models can automatically explain unexpected reinforcement-learning behavior, even when an agent lacks a complete model.

title: Explainable Reinforcement Learning via Model Transforms

abstract: An off-the-shelf model as a commercial service could be stolen by model stealing attacks, posing great threats to the rights of the model owner. Model fingerprinting aims to verify whether a suspect model is stolen from the victim model, which gains more and more attention nowadays. Previous methods always leverage the transferable adversarial examples as the model fingerprint, which is sensitive to adversarial defense or transfer learning scenarios. To address this issue, we consider the pairwise relationship between samples instead and propose a novel yet simple model stealing detection method based on SAmple Correlation (SAC). Specifically, we present SAC-w that selects wrongly classified normal samples as model inputs and calculates the mean correlation among their model outputs. To reduce the training time, we further develop SAC-m that selects CutMix Augmented samples as model inputs, without the need for training the surrogate models or generating adversarial examples. Extensive results validate that SAC successfully defends against various model stealing attacks, even including adversarial training or transfer learning, and detects the stolen models with the best performance in terms of AUC across different datasets and model architectures. The codes are available at https://github.com/guanjiyang/SAC.

paragraphs: Model fingerprinting asks whether a suspicious model was derived from an owner's model. This paper targets weaknesses in fingerprints based on transferable adversarial examples, which can be sensitive to adversarial defenses or transfer learning. Its alternative examines relationships between model outputs across multiple input samples.

The proposed Sample Correlation method, SAC, has two versions. SAC-w uses ordinary samples that a model classifies incorrectly and calculates the average correlation among their outputs. SAC-m uses CutMix-augmented samples to reduce preparation time. That version avoids both training surrogate models and generating adversarial examples, making the fingerprinting procedure simpler to prepare.

Across the evaluated datasets and architectures, SAC detects stolen models under several attack settings, including adversarial training and transfer learning. The authors report the best detection performance in terms of AUC among the compared methods. The central finding is that correlations across responses can provide useful evidence of model derivation even in settings that challenge adversarial-example fingerprints. This is evidence for detecting theft in the tested settings, rather than preventing a model from being copied.
summary.tldr: SAC fingerprints models through correlations between sample outputs, detecting stolen models across several tested attack settings.

title: Are You Stealing My Model? Sample Correlation for Fingerprinting Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Membership inference attacks are designed to determine, using black box access to trained models, whether a particular example was used in training or not. Membership inference can be formalized as a hypothesis testing problem. The most effective existing attacks estimate the distribution of some test statistic (usually the model's confidence on the true label) on points that were (and were not) used in training by training many \emph{shadow models}---i.e. models of the same architecture as the model being attacked, trained on a random subsample of data. While effective, these attacks are extremely computationally expensive, especially when the model under attack is large. \footnotetext[0]{Martin and Shuai are the lead authors, and other authors are ordered alphabetically. \{maberlop,shuat\}@amazon.com}We introduce a new class of attacks based on performing quantile regression on the distribution of confidence scores induced by the model under attack on points that are not used in training. We show that our method is competitive with state-of-the-art shadow model attacks, while requiring substantially less compute because our attack requires training only a single model. Moreover, unlike shadow model attacks, our proposed attack does not require any knowledge of the architecture of the model under attack and is therefore truly ``black-box". We show the efficacy of this approach in an extensive series of experiments on various datasets and model architectures. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/amazon-science/quantile-mia}{github.com/amazon-science/quantile-mia.}

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular example appeared in a model's training data using access to the trained model's outputs. Strong existing attacks often train many shadow models to estimate how confidence differs between training members and nonmembers. This can be expensive, especially when the target model is large, and typically requires knowing its architecture.

The proposed attack uses quantile regression on confidence scores that the target model produces for examples outside its training set. Framing membership as hypothesis testing makes this nonmember confidence distribution useful for assessing candidate examples. Only one attack model must be trained, avoiding the repeated target-like training required by shadow-model approaches.

Across experiments with various datasets and model architectures, the method is competitive with state-of-the-art shadow-model attacks while requiring substantially less computation. It also needs no knowledge of the target architecture, making its access requirements more fully black-box. The findings show that strong membership-inference assessments can remain feasible even when reproducing and repeatedly training the target architecture would be impractical.
summary.tldr: Quantile regression enables competitive black-box membership inference with one trained attack model and substantially less computation than shadow-model attacks.

title: Scalable Membership Inference Attacks via Quantile Regression

abstract: This paper proposes a novel strategy for estimating the heterogeneous treatment effect called the Fused and Accurate Shrinkage Tree ($\mathrm{FAST}$). Our approach utilizes both trial and observational data to improve the accuracy and robustness of the estimator. Inspired by the concept of shrinkage estimation in statistics, we develop an optimal weighting scheme and a corresponding estimator that balances the unbiased estimator based on the trial data with the potentially biased estimator based on the observational data. Specifically, combined with tree-based techniques, we introduce a new split criterion that utilizes both trial data and observational data to more accurately estimate the treatment effect. Furthermore, we confirm the consistency of our proposed tree-based estimator and demonstrate the effectiveness of our criterion in reducing prediction error through theoretical analysis. The advantageous finite sample performance of the $\mathrm{FAST}$ and its ensemble version over existing methods is demonstrated via simulations and real data analysis.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can differ across people or groups, so estimating one average effect may leave important variation unresolved. FAST is a tree-based method for estimating these heterogeneous effects using both trial and observational data. The challenge is to benefit from both sources while accounting for their different statistical properties.

The method draws on shrinkage estimation to combine an unbiased trial-based estimator with an observational estimator that may be biased. The authors develop an optimal weighting scheme to balance the two. They also introduce a tree-splitting criterion that uses both datasets, so the combination influences how the tree divides the population as well as how treatment effects are estimated.

The theoretical analysis establishes consistency of the proposed tree estimator and supports the split criterion's ability to reduce prediction error. Simulations and real-data analysis show favorable finite-sample performance for FAST and its ensemble version compared with existing methods. The findings support carefully weighted integration of the two sources, with potential observational bias explicitly represented in the estimation strategy.
summary.tldr: FAST combines trial and observational estimates through shrinkage weighting and tree splits to improve heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation.

title: FAST: a Fused and Accurate Shrinkage Tree for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects Estimation

abstract: Deep learning-based reaction predictors have undergone significant architectural evolution. However, their reliance on reactions from the US Patent Office results in a lack of interpretable predictions and limited generalizability to other chemistry domains, such as radical and atmospheric chemistry. To address these challenges, we introduce a new reaction predictor system, RMechRP, that leverages contrastive learning in conjunction with mechanistic pathways, the most interpretable representation of chemical reactions. Specifically designed for radical reactions, RMechRP provides different levels of interpretation of chemical reactions. We develop and train multiple deep-learning models using RMechDB, a public database of radical reactions, to establish the first benchmark for predicting radical reactions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of RMechRP in providing accurate and interpretable predictions of radical reactions, and its potential for various applications in atmospheric chemistry.

paragraphs: Predicting a chemical reaction is more useful when the prediction also explains how the reaction proceeds. The paper argues that existing deep learning predictors, which rely heavily on patent reactions, offer limited interpretability and do not generalize sufficiently to domains such as radical and atmospheric chemistry. It focuses specifically on radical reactions.

The proposed system, RMechRP, combines contrastive learning with mechanistic pathways. These pathways describe reactions through their underlying chemical steps, giving the prediction a form that supports interpretation. The system provides different levels of interpretation, making explanatory structure part of the prediction task rather than treating the reaction solely as an input-to-output mapping.

The authors develop and train multiple deep learning models using RMechDB, a public radical-reaction database, to establish a benchmark for this domain. They report accurate, interpretable radical-reaction predictions. The stated relevance to atmospheric chemistry is a potential application: the contribution supplies a prediction system and benchmark for investigating such uses, rather than establishing success across atmospheric chemistry as a whole.
summary.tldr: RMechRP combines contrastive learning and mechanistic pathways to make radical-reaction predictions accurate and interpretable.

title: AI for Interpretable Chemistry: Predicting Radical Mechanistic Pathways via Contrastive Learning

abstract: Modern recommender systems perform large-scale retrieval by embedding queries and item candidates in the same unified space, followed by approximate nearest neighbor search to select top candidates given a query embedding. In this paper, we propose a novel generative retrieval approach, where the retrieval model autoregressively decodes the identifiers of the target candidates. To that end, we create semantically meaningful tuple of codewords to serve as a Semantic ID for each item. Given Semantic IDs for items in a user session, a Transformer-based sequence-to-sequence model is trained to predict the Semantic ID of the next item that the user will interact with. We show that recommender systems trained with the proposed paradigm significantly outperform the current SOTA models on various datasets. In addition, we show that incorporating Semantic IDs into the sequence-to-sequence model enhances its ability to generalize, as evidenced by the improved retrieval performance observed for items with no prior interaction history.

paragraphs: Large recommender systems commonly retrieve items by embedding a query and candidate items into a shared space, then searching for nearby candidates. This paper proposes a different retrieval mechanism: a model generates the identifier of the item it predicts the user will interact with next. Retrieval thus becomes a sequence-generation task.

The method assigns each item a Semantic ID composed of a tuple of meaningful codewords. A Transformer sequence-to-sequence model receives the Semantic IDs of items in a user’s session and learns to predict the next item’s ID one part at a time. The identifiers supply semantic structure to the prediction task, rather than functioning only as arbitrary item labels.

Experiments report significant improvements over current state-of-the-art models across several datasets. The authors also find improved retrieval for items without previous interaction history when Semantic IDs are incorporated into the model. That result supports the claim that meaningful identifiers improve generalization, alongside the broader finding that generating identifiers can be an effective recommendation retrieval strategy.
summary.tldr: A recommender generates meaningful item identifiers directly, improving reported retrieval performance and generalization to items without interaction history.

title: Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval

abstract: In many machine learning applications on signals and biomedical data, especially electroencephalogram (EEG), one major challenge is the variability of the data across subjects, sessions, and hardware devices. In this work, we propose a new method called Convolutional Monge Mapping Normalization ($\texttt{CMMN}$), which consists in filtering the signals in order to adapt their power spectrum density (PSD) to a Wasserstein barycenter estimated on training data. $\texttt{CMMN}$ relies on novel closed-form solutions for optimal transport mappings and barycenters and provides individual test time adaptation to new data without needing to retrain a prediction model. Numerical experiments on sleep EEG data show that $\texttt{CMMN}$ leads to significant and consistent performance gains independent from the neural network architecture when adapting between subjects, sessions, and even datasets collected with different hardware. Notably our performance gain is on par with much more numerically intensive Domain Adaptation (DA) methods and can be used in conjunction with those for even better performances.

paragraphs: EEG recordings can vary across people, recording sessions, and hardware, creating difficulties when a prediction model encounters new data. This paper addresses that variability through signal normalization. Its method, Convolutional Monge Mapping Normalization, or CMMN, changes the incoming signals rather than requiring the prediction model to be retrained.

CMMN filters signals so their power spectral density, which describes how signal power is distributed across frequencies, approaches a shared reference. That reference is a Wasserstein barycenter estimated from the training data. The method relies on new closed-form solutions for optimal transport mappings and barycenters, allowing individual adaptation when new data arrive at test time.

Experiments on sleep EEG show significant, consistent performance improvements across the neural architectures tested. These improvements cover transfers between subjects, sessions, and datasets recorded with different hardware. The reported gains are comparable to those from much more computationally intensive domain adaptation methods. CMMN can also be combined with those methods for further improvement, making the normalization approach complementary to model-level adaptation.
summary.tldr: CMMN aligns EEG frequency profiles to a training-derived reference, improving sleep-data prediction across recording conditions without retraining the predictor.

title: Convolution Monge Mapping Normalization for learning on sleep data

abstract: Two-photon optogenetics has transformed our ability to probe the structure and function of neural circuits. However, achieving precise optogenetic control of neural ensemble activity has remained fundamentally constrained by the problem of off-target stimulation (OTS): the inadvertent activation of nearby non-target neurons due to imperfect confinement of light onto target neurons. Here we propose a novel computational approach to this problem called Bayesian target optimisation. Our approach uses nonparametric Bayesian inference to model neural responses to optogenetic stimulation, and then optimises the laser powers and optical target locations needed to achieve a desired activity pattern with minimal OTS. We validate our approach in simulations and using data from in vitro experiments, showing that Bayesian target optimisation considerably reduces OTS across all conditions we test. Together, these results establish our ability to overcome OTS, enabling optogenetic stimulation with substantially improved precision.

paragraphs: Two-photon optogenetics uses light to influence neural activity, allowing researchers to investigate how neural circuits work. A central obstacle is off-target stimulation: light intended for selected neurons can also activate nearby neurons. That makes it harder to produce a desired pattern of activity and to control precisely which parts of a circuit are stimulated.

The paper introduces Bayesian target optimisation as a computational way to address this problem. It first uses nonparametric Bayesian inference to model how neurons respond to stimulation. It then optimizes both laser power and the locations of optical targets, seeking the desired neural activity while minimizing unintended activation.

The authors evaluate the approach through simulations and data from experiments conducted in vitro. They report considerable reductions in off-target stimulation in every tested condition. These findings support improved precision through jointly choosing stimulation locations and powers using a response model. The demonstrated result is reduced unintended activity across the evaluated conditions, rather than a claim that all possible stimulation settings become perfectly selective.
summary.tldr: Bayesian target optimisation models neural responses and adjusts laser locations and powers to reduce unintended stimulation.

title: Bayesian target optimisation for high-precision holographic optogenetics

abstract: Despite their immense success as a model of macaque visual cortex, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have struggled to predict activity in visual cortex of the mouse, which is thought to be strongly dependent on the animal’s behavioral state. Furthermore, most computational models focus on predicting neural responses to static images presented under head fixation, which are dramatically different from the dynamic, continuous visual stimuli that arise during movement in the real world. Consequently, it is still unknown how natural visual input and different behavioral variables may integrate over time to generate responses in primary visual cortex (V1). To address this, we introduce a multimodal recurrent neural network that integrates gaze-contingent visual input with behavioral and temporal dynamics to explain V1 activity in freely moving mice. We show that the model achieves state-of-the-art predictions of V1 activity during free exploration and demonstrate the importance of each component in an extensive ablation study. Analyzing our model using maximally activating stimuli and saliency maps, we reveal new insights into cortical function, including the prevalence of mixed selectivity for behavioral variables in mouse V1. In summary, our model offers a comprehensive deep-learning framework for exploring the computational principles underlying V1 neurons in freely-moving animals engaged in natural behavior.

paragraphs: Predicting activity in mouse primary visual cortex requires understanding the changing visual input experienced during movement. The animal's behavioral state is also thought to strongly affect these responses. This paper studies freely moving mice, addressing a setting that differs substantially from models built around static images shown to head-fixed animals.

The authors develop a multimodal recurrent neural network that combines visual input aligned with the animal's gaze, behavioral information, and temporal dynamics. Recurrence lets the model integrate information over time, matching the continuous nature of natural exploration. An extensive ablation study examines the importance of each component, testing how much the combined prediction depends on these different sources of information.

The model achieves state-of-the-art predictions of V1 activity during free exploration. Analyses using maximally activating stimuli and saliency maps also reveal insights into the modeled responses, including prevalent mixed selectivity for behavioral variables. This suggests that behavioral influences appear in combinations within V1 activity. The framework provides a way to investigate how vision, behavior, and time jointly relate to neural responses during natural movement.
summary.tldr: A recurrent model combining gaze-aligned vision, behavior, and time improves prediction and analysis of V1 activity in freely moving mice.

title: Multimodal Deep Learning Model Unveils Behavioral Dynamics of V1 Activity in Freely Moving Mice

abstract: Federated learning (FL) suffers from data heterogeneity, where the diverse data distributions across clients make it challenging to train a single global model effectively. Existing personalization approaches aim to address the data heterogeneity issue by creating a personalized model for each client from the global model that fits their local data distribution. However, these personalized models may achieve lower accuracy than the global model in some clients, resulting in limited performance improvement compared to that without personalization. To overcome this limitation, we propose a per-instance personalization FL algorithm Flow. Flow creates dynamic personalized models that are adaptive not only to each client’s data distributions but also to each client’s data instances. The personalized model allows each instance to dynamically determine whether it prefers the local parameters or its global counterpart to make correct predictions, thereby improving clients’accuracy. We provide theoretical analysis on the convergence of Flow and empirically demonstrate the superiority of Flow in improving clients’ accuracy compared to state-of-the-art personalization approaches on both vision and language-based tasks.

paragraphs: Federated learning must accommodate clients whose data follow different distributions. Personalization usually adapts a shared global model to each client's local data, but that adaptation can reduce accuracy for some clients. The paper treats this as a reason to make personalization more selective: the useful balance between shared and local knowledge may differ across individual examples.

Flow creates a dynamic personalized model that adapts at both the client and instance levels. For each input, the model can determine whether local parameters or their global counterparts are preferable for making the prediction. This gives examples within the same client access to different choices of parameters, beyond a single fixed client-level adaptation.

The authors provide a convergence analysis and evaluate Flow on vision and language tasks. Their experiments report better client accuracy than state-of-the-art personalization approaches. The findings support finer-grained personalization as a response to heterogeneous data, while the reported superiority remains an empirical result from the tasks studied rather than a guarantee for every client or input.
summary.tldr: Flow personalizes federated models per input by dynamically choosing between local parameters and their global counterparts.

title: Flow: Per-instance Personalized Federated Learning

abstract: Since developing a new multimodal LLM (MLLM) by pre-training on tremendous image-text pairs from scratch can be exceedingly resource-consuming, connecting an existing LLM with a comparatively lightweight visual prompt generator (VPG) becomes a feasible paradigm. However, further tuning the VPG component of the MLLM still incurs significant computational costs, such as thousands of GPU hours and millions of training data points. An alternative solution is transferring an existing VPG from one MLLM to the target MLLM. In this work, we investigate VPG transferability across LLMs for the first time, aiming to reduce the cost of VPG training. Specifically, we explore VPG transfer across different LLM sizes (e.g., small-to-large) and types. We identify key factors to maximize transfer efficiency, based on which we develop a simple yet highly effective two-stage transfer framework, called VPGTrans. Notably, it enables VPG transfer from BLIP-2 OPT 2.7B to BLIP-2 OPT 6.7B with less than 10% of the GPU hours using only 10.7% of the training data compared to training a VPG for OPT 6.7B from scratch. Furthermore, we provide a series of intriguing findings and discuss potential explanations behind them. Finally, we showcase the practical value of our VPGTrans approach, by customizing two novel MLLMs, including VL-LLaMA and VL-Vicuna, with recently released LLaMA and Vicuna LLMs.

paragraphs: A visual prompt generator connects image information to a language model, offering a relatively lightweight route to a multimodal system. Even so, training that connector can require substantial computation and data. This paper investigates whether an existing visual prompt generator can be transferred to another language model instead of being trained afresh.

The authors study transfers across language-model sizes and types, identify factors affecting efficiency, and use those findings to develop VPGTrans. Its two-stage framework aims to reuse the trained visual component when changing the language-model backbone. The practical question is how much of that earlier training can remain useful after the receiving model changes.

For transfer from BLIP-2 OPT 2.7B to BLIP-2 OPT 6.7B, the method uses less than 10% of the GPU hours and 10.7% of the training data required to train the target generator from scratch. The authors also build VL-LLaMA and VL-Vicuna using the approach. These examples demonstrate the potential for reusing visual-language components across different backbones with substantially lower training costs in the reported transfer.
summary.tldr: VPGTrans transfers visual prompt generators between language models, substantially reducing training computation and data in a demonstrated transfer.

title: VPGTrans: Transfer Visual Prompt Generator across LLMs

abstract: This work studies the design of neural networks that can process the weights or gradients of other neural networks, which we refer to as *neural functional networks* (NFNs). Despite a wide range of potential applications, including learned optimization, processing implicit neural representations, network editing, and policy evaluation, there are few unifying principles for designing effective architectures that process the weights of other networks. We approach the design of neural functionals through the lens of symmetry, in particular by focusing on the permutation symmetries that arise in the weights of deep feedforward networks because hidden layer neurons have no inherent order. We introduce a framework for building *permutation equivariant* neural functionals, whose architectures encode these symmetries as an inductive bias. The key building blocks of this framework are *NF-Layers* (neural functional layers) that we constrain to be permutation equivariant through an appropriate parameter sharing scheme. In our experiments, we find that permutation equivariant neural functionals are effective on a diverse set of tasks that require processing the weights of MLPs and CNNs, such as predicting classifier generalization, producing "winning ticket" sparsity masks for initializations, and classifying or editing implicit neural representations (INRs). In addition, we provide code for our models and experiments at https://github.com/AllanYangZhou/nfn.

paragraphs: This paper designs neural networks that process the weights or gradients of other neural networks. Such neural functional networks could support tasks including learned optimization, network editing, and policy evaluation. The design challenge is that the input is itself a network's parameters, whose structure should inform how they are processed.

The authors focus on a symmetry of deep feedforward networks: hidden neurons have no inherent ordering. Their framework encodes this permutation symmetry into neural functional layers through parameter sharing. Permutation equivariance means that reordering the relevant neurons produces the corresponding reordering in the functional network's output, giving the architecture an explicit structural bias.

Experiments find these architectures effective across several tasks involving MLP and CNN weights. These include predicting classifier generalization, producing winning-ticket sparsity masks for initialized networks, and classifying or editing implicit neural representations. The results support symmetry as a useful organizing principle for processing network parameters across varied applications, while the framework supplies reusable building blocks for doing so.
summary.tldr: Neural functional layers use permutation-aware parameter sharing to process other networks' weights effectively across several tasks.

title: Permutation Equivariant Neural Functionals

abstract: We study Proportional Response Dynamics (PRD) in linear Fisher markets, where participants act asynchronously. We model this scenario as a sequential process in which at each step, an adversary selects a subset of the players to update their bids, subject to liveness constraints. We show that if every bidder individually applies the PRD update rule whenever they are included in the group of bidders selected by the adversary, then, in the generic case, the entire dynamic converges to a competitive equilibrium of the market. Our proof technique reveals additional properties of linear Fisher markets, such as the uniqueness of the market equilibrium for generic parameters and the convergence of associated no swap regret dynamics and best response dynamics under certain conditions.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a market can settle into equilibrium when bidders update at different times. It studies proportional response dynamics in linear Fisher markets. The timing is deliberately demanding: at each step, an adversary chooses which bidders may update, rather than requiring everyone to act together.

The scheduling adversary is subject to liveness constraints, so its freedom is restricted by requirements on continued participation. Whenever selected, each bidder applies the proportional response update rule individually. The authors prove that, in the generic case, the resulting overall process converges to a competitive equilibrium. Thus, coordinated update timing is unnecessary for this convergence result under its stated conditions.

The proof also establishes further properties of these markets. These include uniqueness of equilibrium for generic parameters and convergence of associated no-swap-regret and best-response dynamics under certain conditions. The central contribution is a convergence guarantee that accommodates adversarial asynchronous scheduling, while keeping the generic-case and scheduling qualifications essential to the claim.
summary.tldr: Proportional response updates converge in generic linear Fisher markets despite adversarial asynchronous scheduling subject to liveness constraints.

title: Asynchronous Proportional Response Dynamics: Convergence in Markets with Adversarial Scheduling

abstract: We introduce beta diffusion, a novel generative modeling method that integrates demasking and denoising to generate data within bounded ranges. Using scaled and shifted beta distributions, beta diffusion utilizes multiplicative transitions over time to create both forward and reverse diffusion processes, maintaining beta distributions in both the forward marginals and the reverse conditionals, given the data at any point in time. Unlike traditional diffusion-based generative models relying on additive Gaussian noise and reweighted evidence lower bounds (ELBOs), beta diffusion is multiplicative and optimized with KL-divergence upper bounds (KLUBs) derived from the convexity of the KL divergence. We demonstrate that the proposed KLUBs are more effective for optimizing beta diffusion compared to negative ELBOs, which can also be derived as the KLUBs of the same KL divergence with its two arguments swapped. The loss function of beta diffusion, expressed in terms of Bregman divergence, further supports the efficacy of KLUBs for optimization. Experimental results on both synthetic data and natural images demonstrate the unique capabilities of beta diffusion in generative modeling of range-bounded data and validate the effectiveness of KLUBs in optimizing diffusion models, thereby making them valuable additions to the family of diffusion-based generative models and the optimization techniques used to train them.

paragraphs: Beta diffusion introduces a generative process designed for data whose values lie within bounded ranges. It combines removing masks with removing noise, using scaled and shifted beta distributions. Its transitions are multiplicative, providing a different mathematical construction from diffusion methods that progressively add Gaussian noise.

The construction preserves beta distributions in the forward marginals and in reverse conditional distributions when conditioned on the data. The paper also changes how the model is trained. It derives upper bounds on KL divergence, called KLUBs, from the convexity of that divergence and uses these bounds as optimization objectives.

The authors show that KLUB objectives are more effective for training beta diffusion than negative evidence lower bounds. Their analysis connects the objectives through swapping the arguments of the underlying KL divergence and expresses the loss using Bregman divergence. Experiments on synthetic data and natural images support both the bounded-data modeling approach and the proposed training objectives. The contribution therefore concerns the diffusion process itself and the objective used to learn it.
summary.tldr: Beta diffusion uses multiplicative beta-distributed transitions and KL-divergence upper-bound objectives to generate data within bounded ranges.

title: Beta Diffusion

abstract: While most machine learning models can provide confidence in their predictions, confidence is insufficient to understand a prediction's reliability. For instance, the model may have a low confidence prediction if the input is not well-represented in the training dataset or if the input is inherently ambiguous. In this work, we investigate the relationship between how atypical~(rare) a sample or a class is and the reliability of a model's predictions. We first demonstrate that atypicality is strongly related to miscalibration and accuracy. In particular, we empirically show that predictions for atypical inputs or atypical classes are more overconfident and have lower accuracy. Using these insights, we show incorporating atypicality improves uncertainty quantification and model performance for discriminative neural networks and large language models. In a case study, we show that using atypicality improves the performance of a skin lesion classifier across different skin tone groups without having access to the group attributes. Overall, we propose that models should use not only confidence but also atypicality to improve uncertainty quantification and performance. Our results demonstrate that simple post-hoc atypicality estimators can provide significant value.

paragraphs: A prediction's confidence does not fully explain why it may be unreliable. Low confidence can reflect an inherently ambiguous input or an input poorly represented in training data. This paper investigates an additional signal: atypicality, meaning how rare an input or its class is. The goal is to distinguish reliability patterns that confidence alone does not adequately capture.

The authors empirically find that atypical examples and classes tend to have lower accuracy and more overconfident predictions. They then use atypicality information to improve uncertainty estimates and model performance in discriminative neural networks and large language models. Simple estimators applied after training provide value, making atypicality useful beyond an observation about model behavior.

A skin lesion classification case study reports improvements across skin tone groups without using the group attributes. This illustrates how accounting for atypicality can help across groups even when those group labels are unavailable to the method. The findings support combining confidence with information about rarity, while remaining empirical results rather than a guarantee that every rare input will be misclassified.
summary.tldr: Accounting for how atypical an input or class is improves reliability estimates and performance beyond using confidence alone.

title: Beyond Confidence: Reliable Models Should Also Consider Atypicality

abstract: We consider the problem of online allocation subject to a long-term fairness penalty. Contrary to existing works, however, we do not assume that the decision-maker observes the protected attributes---which is often unrealistic in practice. Instead they can purchase data that help estimate them from sources of different quality; and hence reduce the fairness penalty at some cost. We model this problem as a multi-armed bandit problem where each arm corresponds to the choice of a data source, coupled with the fair online allocation problem. We propose an algorithm that jointly solves both problems and show that it has a regret bounded by $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$. A key difficulty is that the rewards received by selecting a source are correlated by the fairness penalty, which leads to a need for randomization (despite a stochastic setting). Our algorithm takes into account contextual information available before the source selection, and can adapt to many different fairness notions.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential allocation decisions subject to a long-term fairness penalty when protected attributes are not directly observed. Instead, the decision-maker can buy information from sources of different quality to estimate those attributes. Better information may reduce the fairness penalty, but acquiring it introduces a cost.

The authors model data-source selection as a multi-armed bandit problem coupled to the allocation problem. Each arm represents a source, and the algorithm jointly decides how to acquire information and make fair allocations. It can also use contextual information available before selecting a source and accommodate multiple notions of fairness.

The proposed algorithm has regret bounded on the order of the square root of the time horizon. A central difficulty is that source rewards are linked through the fairness penalty, creating a need for randomization even in the stochastic setting studied. The result provides a framework for balancing data expense, information quality, and long-term fairness within one sequential decision process.
summary.tldr: A joint bandit-and-allocation algorithm balances data costs and fairness when protected attributes must be estimated, with square-root-order regret.

title: Trading-off price for data quality to achieve fair online allocation

abstract: Latent space EBMs, also known as energy-based priors, have drawn growing interests in the field of generative modeling due to its flexibility in the formulation and strong modeling power of the latent space. However, the common practice of learning latent space EBMs with non-convergent short-run MCMC for prior and posterior sampling is hindering the model from further progress; the degenerate MCMC sampling quality in practice often leads to degraded generation quality and instability in training, especially with highly multi-modal and/or high-dimensional target distributions. To remedy this sampling issue, in this paper we introduce a simple but effective diffusion-based amortization method for long-run MCMC sampling and develop a novel learning algorithm for the latent space EBM based on it. We provide theoretical evidence that the learned amortization of MCMC is a valid long-run MCMC sampler. Experiments on several image modeling benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared with strong counterparts.

paragraphs: Energy-based priors provide a flexible way to model the hidden variables used by generative models. Learning them requires samples from prior and posterior distributions, commonly obtained through Markov chain Monte Carlo, or MCMC. This paper targets a practical weakness: short sampling runs may not converge, producing poor samples that damage generation quality and destabilise training.

The problem is especially pronounced when a target distribution has many distinct high-probability regions or many dimensions. The authors introduce a diffusion-based method that learns to amortise long-run MCMC sampling, incorporating that method into a new training algorithm for latent-space energy-based models. The aim is to improve the sampling component on which learning depends.

The paper provides theoretical evidence that the learned amortisation is a valid long-run MCMC sampler. Experiments on several image-modelling benchmarks report better performance than strong comparison methods. These findings connect a sampling improvement to better generative modelling, treating the quality of prior and posterior samples as an important part of learning a useful latent distribution.
summary.tldr: Diffusion-based amortisation of long-run MCMC improves sampling for energy-based latent priors, with theoretical support and stronger image-modelling results.

title: Learning Energy-Based Prior Model with Diffusion-Amortized MCMC

abstract: We study the problem of learning causal representations from unknown, latent interventions in a general setting, where the latent distribution is Gaussian but the mixing function is completely general. We prove strong identifiability results given unknown single-node interventions, i.e., without having access to the intervention targets. This generalizes prior works which have focused on weaker classes, such as linear maps or paired counterfactual data. This is also the first instance of identifiability from non-paired interventions for deep neural network embeddings and general causal structures. Our proof relies on carefully uncovering the high-dimensional geometric structure present in the data distribution after a non-linear density transformation, which we capture by analyzing quadratic forms of precision matrices of the latent distributions. Finally, we propose a contrastive algorithm to identify the latent variables in practice and evaluate its performance on various tasks.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning seeks underlying causal variables from observations that may combine them in complicated ways. This paper studies a setting with a Gaussian latent distribution and a completely general mixing function. It asks what can be identified when interventions affect hidden variables but the learner does not know their targets.

The authors prove strong identifiability results using unknown single-node interventions. The observations need not be paired counterfactual examples. This extends earlier results restricted to weaker mixing classes or paired data, and establishes identifiability for deep neural network embeddings and general causal structures under the paper’s setting. The Gaussian latent assumption and single-node intervention structure are central parts of that setting.

The proof examines geometric structure that remains in the observed distribution after nonlinear transformation, using quadratic forms of latent precision matrices. The authors also propose a contrastive algorithm for identifying latent variables and evaluate it on several tasks. The contribution combines a theoretical account of recoverability with a practical learning method aimed at recovering the hidden representation.
summary.tldr: Under Gaussian latent structure, unknown single-node interventions enable causal identifiability despite general nonlinear mixing.

title: Learning Linear Causal Representations from Interventions under General Nonlinear Mixing

abstract: Knowledge-based visual question answering (VQA) requires external knowledge to answer the question about an image. Early methods explicitly retrieve knowledge from external knowledge bases, which often introduce noisy information. Recently large language models like GPT-3 have shown encouraging performance as implicit knowledge source and revealed planning abilities. However, current large language models can not effectively understand image inputs, thus it remains an open problem to extract the image information and input to large language models. Prior works have used image captioning and object descriptions to represent the image. However, they may either drop the essential visual information to answer the question correctly or involve irrelevant objects to the task-of-interest. To address this problem, we propose to let large language models make an initial hypothesis according to their knowledge, then actively collect the visual evidence required to verify the hypothesis. In this way, the model can attend to the essential visual information in a task-oriented manner. We leverage several vision modules from the perspectives of spatial attention (i.e., Where to look) and attribute attention (i.e., What to look), which is similar to human cognition. The experiments show that our proposed method outperforms the baselines on open-ended knowledge-based VQA datasets and presents clear reasoning procedure with better interpretability.

paragraphs: Knowledge-based visual question answering combines evidence from an image with knowledge beyond that image. Passing a general caption or object list to a language model can omit a crucial detail or include distracting information. TOA addresses this by making the question and a proposed answer guide which visual evidence the system collects.

The language model first forms an initial hypothesis using its knowledge. It then actively gathers evidence needed to check that hypothesis through vision modules. These modules support spatial attention, deciding where to look, and attribute attention, deciding what to look for. Image understanding therefore becomes a task-oriented process rather than a fixed description prepared independently of the reasoning.

On open-ended knowledge-based visual question answering datasets, the method outperforms the evaluated baselines. The authors also report a clearer reasoning procedure and improved interpretability. The approach matters because it connects a model’s knowledge-based proposal to explicit visual verification, allowing the visual information supplied to the language model to be selected for the particular question being answered.
summary.tldr: TOA forms an answer hypothesis, then actively selects visual evidence to verify it and improve knowledge-based visual question answering.

title: TOA: Task-oriented Active VQA

abstract: Many recent works in simulation-based inference (SBI) rely on deep generative models to approximate complex, high-dimensional posterior distributions. However, evaluating whether or not these approximations can be trusted remains a challenge. Most approaches evaluate the posterior estimator only in expectation over the observation space. This limits their interpretability and is not sufficient to identify for which observations the approximation can be trusted or should be improved. Building upon the well-known classifier two-sample test (C2ST), we introduce $\ell$-C2ST, a new method that allows for a local evaluation of the posterior estimator at any given observation. It offers theoretically grounded and easy to interpret -- e.g. graphical -- diagnostics, and unlike C2ST, does not require access to samples from the true posterior. In the case of normalizing flow-based posterior estimators, $\ell$-C2ST can be specialized to offer better statistical power, while being computationally more efficient. On standard SBI benchmarks, $\ell$-C2ST provides comparable results to C2ST and outperforms alternative local approaches such as coverage tests based on highest predictive density (HPD). We further highlight the importance of local evaluation and the benefit of interpretability of $\ell$-C2ST on a challenging application from computational neuroscience.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference often uses deep generative models to approximate posterior distributions over unknown parameters. An estimator can perform well on average while being unreliable for a particular observation. This paper addresses that gap by developing diagnostics that evaluate the approximation locally, at the observation a user actually wants to analyze.

The method, called L-C2ST, builds on classifier two-sample testing. It provides theoretically grounded, interpretable diagnostics, including graphical ones, without requiring samples from the true posterior. That distinction matters because access to the exact posterior would undermine much of the need for approximation. For posterior estimators built with normalizing flows, a specialized version improves statistical power and computational efficiency.

On standard simulation-based inference benchmarks, L-C2ST produces results comparable to conventional classifier two-sample testing and outperforms alternative local methods such as highest-predictive-density coverage tests. A computational neuroscience application illustrates why observation-specific evaluation and interpretability matter. The contribution is a way to locate approximation problems that an average assessment across observations may fail to reveal.
summary.tldr: L-C2ST evaluates posterior approximations at individual observations without needing true-posterior samples, providing interpretable local diagnostics.

title: L-C2ST: Local Diagnostics for Posterior Approximations in Simulation-Based Inference

abstract: We study design of black-box model extraction attacks that can *send minimal number of queries from* a *publicly available dataset* to a target ML model through a predictive API with an aim *to create an informative and distributionally equivalent replica* of the target.First, we define *distributionally equivalent* and *Max-Information model extraction* attacks, and reduce them into a variational optimisation problem. The attacker sequentially solves this optimisation problem to select the most informative queries that simultaneously maximise the entropy and reduce the mismatch between the target and the stolen models. This leads to *an active sampling-based query selection algorithm*, Marich, which is *model-oblivious*. Then, we evaluate Marich on different text and image data sets, and different models, including CNNs and BERT. Marich extracts models that achieve $\sim 60-95\%$ of true model's accuracy and uses $\sim 1,000 - 8,500$ queries from the publicly available datasets, which are different from the private training datasets. Models extracted by Marich yield prediction distributions, which are $\sim2-4\times$ closer to the target's distribution in comparison to the existing active sampling-based attacks. The extracted models also lead to 84-96$\%$ accuracy under membership inference attacks. Experimental results validate that Marich is *query-efficient*, and capable of performing task-accurate, high-fidelity, and informative model extraction.

paragraphs: Marich studies how a black-box attacker can copy a model through a prediction API using relatively few queries from public data. The goal includes matching the target's prediction distribution and extracting an informative replica. The public query datasets differ from the private datasets used to train the targets.

The authors formalize distributional equivalence and maximum-information extraction as a variational optimization problem. Marich sequentially selects informative queries through active sampling, seeking both higher entropy and lower mismatch between the target and extracted models. The algorithm is model-oblivious and is evaluated on text and image tasks with models including CNNs and BERT.

The extracted models reach roughly 60–95 percent of target accuracy using about 1,000–8,500 queries. Their prediction distributions are approximately two to four times closer to the targets than those from existing active-sampling attacks. The authors also report membership-inference accuracy of 84–96 percent using extracted models. These empirical findings show that limited public-data queries can expose both predictive behavior and information useful for subsequent privacy attacks in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Marich actively selects public-data queries to extract informative replicas that closely match a target model's predictive behavior.

title: Marich: A Query-efficient Distributionally Equivalent Model Extraction Attack

abstract: Self-Distillation is a special type of knowledge distillation where the student model has the same architecture as the teacher model. Despite using the same architecture and the same training data, self-distillation has been empirically observed to improve performance, especially when applied repeatedly. For such a process, there is a fundamental question of interest: How much gain is possible by applying multiple steps of self-distillation? To investigate this relative gain, we propose using the simple but canonical task of linear regression. Our analysis shows that the excess risk achieved by multi-step self-distillation can significantly improve upon a single step of self-distillation, reducing the excess risk by a factor of $d$, where $d$ is the input dimension. Empirical results on regression tasks from the UCI repository show a reduction in the learnt model's risk (MSE) by up to $47$%.

paragraphs: Self-distillation trains a student model from a teacher with the same architecture. Empirically, repeating this process can improve performance even though the architecture and training data stay the same. The paper asks how large the additional benefit of multiple rounds can be compared with performing self-distillation only once.

To make that question mathematically tractable, the authors analyze linear regression. Their result shows that repeated self-distillation can reduce excess risk by a factor of d relative to a single round, where d is the input dimension. This establishes a potentially substantial benefit in the analyzed setting; it does not assert that every repetition or every dataset produces that reduction.

Experiments on regression tasks from the UCI repository provide an empirical counterpart, reporting reductions in mean squared error of up to 47%. The theoretical and experimental results together support studying repeated distillation as more than a minor extension of one-step distillation. They show that meaningful gains are possible even without increasing model architecture size or changing the underlying training data.
summary.tldr: Repeated self-distillation can substantially outperform one round in linear regression, with UCI experiments reporting mean-squared-error reductions up to 47%.

title: Understanding the Gains from Repeated Self-Distillation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved significant success across various domains. However, training these LLMs typically involves substantial memory and computational costs during both forward and backward propagation. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) considerably reduces the training memory associated with parameters, it does not address the significant computational costs and activation memory. In this paper, we propose Dropping Backward Propagation (DropBP), a novel approach designed to reduce computational costs and activation memory while maintaining accuracy. DropBP randomly drops layers during backward propagation, which is essentially equivalent to training shallow submodules generated by undropped layers and residual connections. Additionally, DropBP calculates the sensitivity of each layer to assign an appropriate drop rate, thereby stabilizing the training process. DropBP is not only applicable to full fine-tuning but can also be orthogonally integrated with all types of PEFT by dropping layers during backward propagation. Specifically, DropBP can reduce training time by 44% with comparable accuracy to the baseline, accelerate convergence to the same perplexity by 1.5$\times$, and enable training with a sequence length 6.2$\times$ larger on a single NVIDIA-A100 GPU. Furthermore, our DropBP enabled a throughput increase of 79% on a NVIDIA A100 GPU and 117% on an Intel Gaudi2 HPU. The code is available at [https://github.com/WooSunghyeon/dropbp](https://github.com/WooSunghyeon/dropbp).
