Relatively little work has focused on learning representations for clustering. In this paper, we propose Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC), a method that simultaneously learns feature representations and cluster assignments using deep neural networks. DEC learns a mapping from the data space to a lower-dimensional feature space in which it iteratively optimizes a clustering objective. Our experimental evaluations on image and text corpora show significant improvement over state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Clustering depends on both how data are represented and how groups are formed from that representation. This paper observes that much research has focused on distance measures and grouping algorithms, with less attention to learning representations specifically for clustering. It introduces Deep Embedded Clustering, or DEC, to address that part of the problem.

DEC uses a deep neural network to map data into a lower-dimensional feature space. Within that space, it iteratively optimizes a clustering objective while learning both the representation and cluster assignments. This couples the features used to compare examples with the grouping task itself, making representation learning an integral part of clustering.

Evaluations on image and text corpora show significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The findings support the value of jointly learning the feature space and the groups, across the two evaluated types of data. The paper's central contribution is the combined learning procedure: it makes the representation responsive to the clustering objective throughout iterative optimization.
summary.tldr: DEC jointly learns a lower-dimensional representation and cluster assignments, improving clustering on evaluated image and text datasets.

title: Unsupervised Deep Embedding for Clustering Analysis

abstract: Recent advances on the scalability and flexibility of variational inference have made it successful at unravelling hidden patterns in complex data. In this work we propose a new variational bound formulation, yielding an estimator that extends beyond the conventional variational bound. It naturally subsumes the importance-weighted and Renyi bounds as special cases, and it is provably sharper than these counterparts. We also present an improved estimator for variational learning, and advocate a novel high signal-to-variance ratio update rule for the variational parameters. We discuss model-selection issues associated with existing evidence-lower-bound-based variational inference procedures, and show how to leverage the flexibility of our new formulation to address them. Empirical evidence is provided to validate our claims.

paragraphs: Variational inference uses a tractable learning formulation to uncover hidden structure in complex data. The quality and form of its evidence bound influence both learning and model comparison. This paper proposes a generalized variational bound formulation that extends the conventional approach.

The formulation includes importance-weighted and Renyi bounds as special cases, and the authors establish a provably sharper estimator than those counterparts. They also introduce an improved estimator for variational learning and a parameter-update rule with a high signal-to-variance ratio. These contributions address both the bound being used and the quality of the learning updates derived from it.

It uses the flexibility of the new formulation to address those issues and supplies empirical evidence for its claims. The work therefore connects improved evidence approximation with two practical goals: learning variational parameters effectively and making better-founded use of variational procedures when selecting among models.
summary.tldr: Generalized evidence bounds provide sharper variational estimation, improved learning updates, and a way to address model-selection issues.

title: Variational Inference and Model Selection with Generalized Evidence Bounds

abstract: The score function estimator is widely used for estimating gradients of stochastic objectives in stochastic computation graphs (SCG), eg., in reinforcement learning and meta-learning. While deriving the first-order gradient estimators by differentiating a surrogate loss (SL) objective is computationally and conceptually simple, using the same approach for higher-order derivatives is more challenging. Firstly, analytically deriving and implementing such estimators is laborious and not compliant with automatic differentiation. Secondly, repeatedly applying SL to construct new objectives for each order derivative involves increasingly cumbersome graph manipulations. Lastly, to match the first-order gradient under differentiation, SL treats part of the cost as a fixed sample, which we show leads to missing and wrong terms for estimators of higher-order derivatives. To address all these shortcomings in a unified way, we introduce DiCE, which provides a single objective that can be differentiated repeatedly, generating correct estimators of derivatives of any order in SCGs. Unlike SL, DiCE relies on automatic differentiation for performing the requisite graph manipulations. We verify the correctness of DiCE both through a proof and numerical evaluation of the DiCE derivative estimates. We also use DiCE to propose and evaluate a novel approach for multi-agent learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/alshedivat/lola.

A surrogate loss makes first-order gradient estimation relatively straightforward, but extending that construction to higher derivatives creates difficulties. The paper shows that treating part of a cost as a fixed sample can produce missing or incorrect terms when further derivatives are taken.

The contribution matters when learning depends on derivatives beyond the first order: it provides a consistent objective whose repeated differentiation preserves the required stochastic terms instead of silently dropping them.
summary.tldr: DiCE provides a single automatically differentiable objective that generates correct stochastic derivative estimators at any order.

title: DiCE: The Infinitely Differentiable Monte Carlo Estimator

abstract: Submodular maximization is a general optimization problem with a wide range of applications in machine learning (e.g., active learning, clustering, and feature selection). In large-scale optimization, the parallel running time of an algorithm is governed by its adaptivity, which measures the number of sequential rounds needed if the algorithm can execute polynomially-many independent oracle queries in parallel. While low adaptivity is ideal, it is not sufficient for an algorithm to be efficient in practice—there are many applications of distributed submodular optimization where the number of function evaluations becomes prohibitively expensive. Motivated by these applications, we study the adaptivity and query complexity of submodular maximization. In this paper, we give the first constant-factor approximation algorithm for maximizing a non-monotone submodular function subject to a cardinality constraint $k$ that runs in $O(\log(n))$ adaptive rounds and makes $O(n \log(k))$ oracle queries in expectation. In our empirical study, we use three real-world applications to compare our algorithm with several benchmarks for non-monotone submodular maximization. The results demonstrate that our algorithm finds competitive solutions using significantly fewer rounds and queries.

paragraphs: Subset-selection algorithms can be expensive in two distinct ways: they may require many sequential rounds, or they may evaluate the objective too often. This paper studies both costs for non-monotone submodular maximization with a cardinality constraint. Non-monotonicity means adding an item need not improve the objective, making selection more delicate.

Adaptivity counts rounds that must occur sequentially when independent objective queries within a round can run in parallel. Reducing this count alone may still leave too many expensive function evaluations. The proposed algorithm achieves a constant-factor approximation using O(log(n)) adaptive rounds and O(n log(k)) oracle queries in expectation, with k specifying the cardinality constraint.

The authors identify this as the first algorithm to achieve that combination of guarantees for the stated problem. They also compare it with several benchmarks across three real-world applications. The experiments find competitive solutions with substantially fewer rounds and queries. The contribution therefore addresses both parallel progress and total evaluation cost, connecting theoretical efficiency measures with the observed computational demands of subset selection.
summary.tldr: A constant-factor subset-selection algorithm combines logarithmic adaptivity with low expected query complexity and competitive empirical solutions.

title: Non-monotone Submodular Maximization with Nearly Optimal Adaptivity and Query Complexity

abstract: Non-concave maximization has been the subject of much recent study in the optimization and machine learning communities, specifically in deep learning. Recent papers ([Ge et al. 2015, Lee et al 2017] and references therein) indicate that first order methods work well and avoid saddles points. Results as in [Lee \etal 2017], however, are limited to the unconstrained case or for cases where the critical points are in the interior of the feasibility set, which fail to capture some of the most interesting applications. In this paper we focus on constrained non-concave maximization. We analyze a variant of a well-established algorithm in machine learning called Multiplicative Weights Update (MWU) for the maximization problem $\max_{\mathbf{x} \in D} P(\mathbf{x})$, where $P$ is non-concave, twice continuously differentiable and $D$ is a product of simplices. We show that MWU converges almost always for small enough stepsizes to critical points that satisfy the second order KKT conditions, by combining techniques from dynamical systems as well as taking advantage of a recent connection between Baum Eagon inequality and MWU [Palaiopanos et al 2017].

paragraphs: First-order optimization methods can avoid saddles in many unconstrained problems, but those results do not automatically handle constraints or critical points on a boundary. This paper studies nonconcave maximization over a product of simplices, a domain that appears when variables represent distributions or normalized allocations.

The authors analyze a variant of Multiplicative Weights Update for a twice continuously differentiable objective. Their proof combines dynamical-systems techniques with a connection between the Baum–Eagon inequality and multiplicative updates. This allows the analysis to address the geometry of the constrained feasible set instead of requiring all relevant critical points to lie in its interior.

For sufficiently small step sizes, the method converges almost always to critical points satisfying second-order Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions. The result strengthens the theoretical understanding of a familiar distributed optimization procedure. Second-order KKT conditions are the relevant constrained optimality criterion here; the abstract does not claim that all such points are global maximizers of the nonconcave objective.
summary.tldr: Multiplicative weights almost always reaches second-order constrained stationary points for the analyzed nonconcave problems.

title: Multiplicative Weights Updates as a distributed constrained optimization algorithm: Convergence to second-order stationary points almost always

abstract: We propose an accelerated version of stochastic variance reduced coordinate descent – ASVRCD. As other variance reduced coordinate descent methods such as SEGA or SVRCD, our method can deal with problems that include a non-separable and non-smooth regularizer, while accessing a random block of partial derivatives in each iteration only. However, ASVRCD incorporates Nesterov’s momentum, which offers favorable iteration complexity guarantees over both SEGA and SVRCD. As a by-product of our theory, we show that a variant of Katyusha (Allen-Zhu, 2017) is a specific case of ASVRCD, recovering the optimal oracle complexity for the finite sum objective.

As a by-product of our theory, we show that a variant of Katyusha (Allen-Zhu, 2017) is a specific case of ASVRCD, recovering the optimal oracle complexity for the finite sum objective.

paragraphs: ASVRCD is an accelerated form of stochastic variance-reduced coordinate descent. At each iteration it accesses only a random block of partial derivatives, making partial derivative access a defining feature of the method. It can handle objectives with a regularizer that is both nonsmooth and nonseparable, meaning the regularization need not split into independent terms for individual coordinates.

The method adds Nesterov’s momentum to the variance-reduced coordinate framework. The authors establish iteration-complexity guarantees that improve on those for SEGA and SVRCD, two related methods. This is a theoretical improvement in the number of iterations required, while retaining support for the stated broad class of regularizers.

The analysis also connects coordinate methods to finite-sum optimization, where an objective consists of many component terms. A variant of Katyusha appears as a special case of ASVRCD, recovering the optimal oracle complexity for that objective setting. This connection shows that the proposed framework encompasses an established accelerated finite-sum method as well as providing a new coordinate-descent algorithm.
summary.tldr: ASVRCD adds momentum to variance-reduced coordinate descent, improves iteration guarantees, and recovers optimal finite-sum oracle complexity through a Katyusha special case.

title: Variance Reduced Coordinate Descent with Acceleration: New Method With a Surprising Application to Finite-Sum Problems

abstract: Recently there have been several attempts to extend Nesterov’s accelerated algorithm to smooth stochastic and variance-reduced optimization. In this paper, we show that there is a simpler approach to acceleration: applying optimistic online learning algorithms and querying the gradient oracle at the online average of the intermediate optimization iterates. In particular, we tighten a recent result of Cutkosky (2019) to demonstrate theoretically that online iterate averaging results in a reduced optimization gap, independently of the algorithm involved. We show that carefully combining this technique with existing generic optimistic online learning algorithms yields the optimal accelerated rates for optimizing strongly-convex and non-strongly-convex, possibly composite objectives, with deterministic as well as stochastic first-order oracles. We further extend this idea to variance-reduced optimization. Finally, we also provide “universal” algorithms that achieve the optimal rate for smooth and non-smooth composite objectives simultaneously without further tuning, generalizing the results of Kavis et al. (2019) and solving a number of their open problems.

paragraphs: Accelerated optimization aims to reduce an objective faster by making better use of successive gradient evaluations. This paper develops a simpler route to acceleration through optimistic online learning and iterative averaging. Its key choice is where to request a gradient: at the running average of intermediate optimization points.

The authors strengthen a theoretical result showing that online averaging reduces the optimization gap independently of the particular underlying algorithm. They then carefully combine averaging with existing optimistic online learning methods. That combination achieves optimal accelerated rates for both strongly convex and non-strongly-convex objectives, including composite objectives, using either deterministic gradients or stochastic first-order information.

In addition, the paper provides universal algorithms that attain optimal rates for smooth and nonsmooth composite objectives without additional tuning. The significance is a common construction behind several acceleration results: averaging supplies a broadly applicable improvement, while its combination with optimism yields the stated optimal guarantees.
summary.tldr: Combining online iterate averaging with optimistic learning yields a unified route to optimal accelerated optimization rates.

title: A simpler approach to accelerated optimization: iterative averaging meets optimism

abstract: Most algorithms for solving optimization problems or finding saddle points of convex-concave functions are fixed-point algorithms. In this work we consider the generic problem of finding a fixed point of an average of operators, or an approximation thereof, in a distributed setting. Our work is motivated by the needs of federated learning. In this context, each local operator models the computations done locally on a mobile device. We investigate two strategies to achieve such a consensus: one based on a fixed number of local steps, and the other based on randomized computations. In both cases, the goal is to limit communication of the locally-computed variables, which is often the bottleneck in distributed frameworks. We perform convergence analysis of both methods and conduct a number of experiments highlighting the benefits of our approach.

paragraphs: Federated learning distributes computation across devices, where communicating locally computed variables can become a bottleneck. This paper studies that issue through fixed-point methods. A fixed point is a value that an update operator leaves unchanged, and many optimization and convex-concave saddle-point algorithms can be described in this form.

The target is a fixed point of an average of local operators, or an approximation to it. Each operator represents computation carried out on a device. This formulation broadens the discussion beyond local stochastic gradient descent to a more general class of distributed update procedures that seek agreement through an averaged operator.

The authors investigate two ways to limit communication: one uses a fixed number of local steps, and the other uses randomized computations. They analyze convergence for both strategies and conduct experiments illustrating their benefits. The contribution places communication-saving local computation within a general fixed-point framework, allowing the same research question to encompass more than one particular optimization algorithm.
summary.tldr: Two distributed fixed-point strategies reduce communication through local computation and come with convergence analyses.

title: From Local SGD to Local Fixed-Point Methods for Federated Learning

abstract: We consider a high-dimensional mixture of two Gaussians in the noisy regime where even an oracle knowing the centers of the clusters misclassifies a small but finite fraction of the points. We provide a rigorous analysis of the generalization error of regularized convex classifiers, including ridge, hinge and logistic regression, in the high-dimensional limit where the number $n$ of samples and their dimension $d$ go to infinity while their ratio is fixed to $\alpha=n/d$. We discuss surprising effects of the regularization that in some cases allows to reach the Bayes-optimal performances. We also illustrate the interpolation peak at low regularization, and analyze the role of the respective sizes of the two clusters.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification when data come from two high-dimensional Gaussian clusters that overlap enough to create unavoidable errors. Even an oracle that knows the cluster centers misclassifies a small but nonzero fraction of points. This provides a noisy setting in which to examine how regularization affects generalization.

The authors rigorously analyze regularized convex classifiers, including ridge, hinge, and logistic regression. Their analysis takes a high-dimensional limit: both sample count and dimension grow without bound while their ratio remains fixed. This scaling keeps the amount of data relative to the number of dimensions central to the characterization of prediction error.

The results reveal that regularization can, in some cases, bring these classifiers to Bayes-optimal performance, the best achievable for the underlying prediction problem. The paper also illustrates an interpolation peak under weak regularization and examines the effect of unequal cluster sizes. These findings clarify how regularization, dimensionality, and class proportions interact within this specific noisy Gaussian model.
summary.tldr: A rigorous high-dimensional analysis shows how regularization affects Gaussian-mixture classification and can sometimes achieve Bayes-optimal performance.

title: The Role of Regularization in Classification of High-dimensional Noisy Gaussian Mixture

abstract: Games are an increasingly useful tool for training and testing learning algorithms. Recent examples include GANs, AlphaZero and the AlphaStar league. However, multi-agent learning can be extremely difficult to predict and control. Learning dynamics even in simple games can yield chaotic behavior. In this paper, we present basic \emph{mechanism design} tools for constructing games with predictable and controllable dynamics. We show that arbitrarily large and complex network games, encoding both cooperation (team play) and competition (zero-sum interaction), exhibit conservation laws when agents use the standard regret-minimizing dynamics known as Follow-the-Regularized-Leader. These laws persist when different agents use different dynamics and encode long-range correlations between agents’ behavior, even though the agents may not interact directly. Moreover, we provide sufficient conditions under which the dynamics have multiple, linearly independent, conservation laws. Increasing the number of conservation laws results in more predictable dynamics, eventually making chaotic behavior formally impossible in some cases.

paragraphs: Learning agents can behave unpredictably when their decisions continually affect one another. Even simple games can produce chaotic learning dynamics. This paper approaches that problem through game design, seeking structures that make the evolution of interacting agents more predictable and controllable.

The authors study network games that combine cooperation within teams and zero-sum competition. They show that games of arbitrarily large size and complexity can exhibit conservation laws when agents follow Follow-the-Regularized-Leader dynamics. These laws describe quantities preserved as learning proceeds. They also persist when different agents use different dynamics and reveal correlations between agents that need not interact directly.

The paper gives sufficient conditions for multiple independent conservation laws. Each additional law constrains how the system can evolve, increasing predictability. In some cases, enough such constraints make chaotic behavior formally impossible. The result provides a route to controlling learning through the structure of the game, with the exclusion of chaos applying to the cases covered by the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies conservation laws in learning games and conditions under which they can rule out chaotic dynamics.

title: From Chaos to Order: Symmetry and Conservation Laws in Game Dynamics

abstract: We consider distributions arising from a mixture of causal models, where each model is represented by a directed acyclic graph (DAG). We provide a graphical representation of such mixture distributions and prove that this representation encodes the conditional independence relations of the mixture distribution. We then consider the problem of structure learning based on samples from such distributions. Since the mixing variable is latent, we consider causal structure discovery algorithms such as FCI that can deal with latent variables. We show that such algorithms recover a “union” of the component DAGs and can identify variables whose conditional distribution across the component DAGs vary. We demonstrate our results on synthetic and real data showing that the inferred graph identifies nodes that vary between the different mixture components. As an immediate application, we demonstrate how retrieval of this causal information can be used to cluster samples according to each mixture component.

paragraphs: A dataset can combine observations generated by several different causal models. This paper studies mixtures in which each component model is represented by a directed acyclic graph. The component responsible for an observation is hidden, making structure discovery a problem involving an unobserved mixing variable.

The authors construct a graphical representation for the mixture distribution and prove that it encodes the distribution’s conditional independence relationships. They then examine structure-learning algorithms that accommodate latent variables, including FCI. Their analysis shows that these algorithms recover a union of the component graphs and can identify variables whose conditional distributions differ across components.

The authors also show how this causal information can help cluster observations by their generating component. The contribution connects a description of dependencies in mixed data with information about where the underlying mechanisms change. The recovered union provides a combined structural view rather than simply presenting a separate complete graph for every hidden component.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes causal mixtures graphically and shows how latent-variable discovery methods can recover combined structure and identify changing mechanisms.

title: Causal Structure Discovery from Distributions Arising from Mixtures of DAGs

abstract: Attribution methods aim to explain a neural network’s prediction by highlighting the most relevant image areas. A popular approach is to backpropagate (BP) a custom relevance score using modified rules, rather than the gradient. We analyze an extensive set of modified BP methods: Deep Taylor Decomposition, Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), Excitation BP, PatternAttribution, DeepLIFT, Deconv, RectGrad, and Guided BP. We find empirically that the explanations of all mentioned methods, except for DeepLIFT, are independent of the parameters of later layers. We provide theoretical insights for this surprising behavior and also analyze why DeepLIFT does not suffer from this limitation. Empirically, we measure how information of later layers is ignored by using our new metric, cosine similarity convergence (CSC). The paper provides a framework to assess the faithfulness of new and existing modified BP methods theoretically and empirically.

Empirically, we measure how information of later layers is ignored by using our new metric, cosine similarity convergence (CSC). The paper provides a framework to assess the faithfulness of new and existing modified BP methods theoretically and empirically.

paragraphs: Attribution methods highlight image regions intended to explain a neural network's prediction. This paper examines methods that propagate custom relevance scores backward through the network using modified backpropagation rules. The central question is whether those explanations remain sensitive to the learned model, especially the parameters in its later layers.

The authors study Deep Taylor Decomposition, Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, Excitation Backpropagation, PatternAttribution, DeepLIFT, Deconv, RectGrad, and Guided Backpropagation. Empirically, they find that all examined methods except DeepLIFT produce explanations independent of later-layer parameters. They provide theoretical insights into this behavior and analyze why DeepLIFT avoids the particular limitation they identify.

To measure how later-layer information is ignored, the paper introduces cosine similarity convergence, or CSC. The metric complements the theoretical analysis with an empirical assessment of information loss in the explanation process. The contribution is a framework for evaluating the faithfulness of modified backpropagation methods. DeepLIFT's exception concerns the identified failure mode; the abstract does not present it as proof that every explanation it produces is fully faithful.
summary.tldr: Many examined modified-backpropagation explanations empirically ignore later-layer parameters, with DeepLIFT avoiding this identified failure mode.

title: When Explanations Lie: Why Many Modified BP Attributions Fail

abstract: The reproducibility debate has caused a renewed interest in changing how one reports uncertainty, from $p$-value for testing a null hypothesis to a confidence interval (CI) for the corresponding parameter. When CIs for multiple selected parameters are being reported, the analog of the false discovery rate (FDR) is the false coverage rate (FCR), which is the expected ratio of number of reported CIs failing to cover their respective parameters to the total number of reported CIs. Here, we consider the general problem of FCR control in the online setting, where one encounters an infinite sequence of fixed unknown parameters ordered by time. We propose a novel solution to the problem which only requires the scientist to be able to construct marginal CIs. As special cases, our framework yields algorithms for online FDR control and online sign-classification procedures that control the false sign rate (FSR). All of our methodology applies equally well to prediction intervals, having particular implications for selective conformal inference.

When CIs for multiple selected parameters are being reported, the analog of the false discovery rate (FDR) is the false coverage rate (FCR), which is the expected ratio of number of reported CIs failing to cover their respective parameters to the total number of reported CIs. Here, we consider the general problem of FCR control in the online setting, where one encounters an infinite sequence of fixed unknown parameters ordered by time. We propose a novel solution to the problem which only requires the scientist to be able to construct marginal CIs. As special cases, our framework yields algorithms for online FDR control and online sign-classification procedures that control the false sign rate (FSR). All of our methodology applies equally well to prediction intervals, having particular implications for selective conformal inference.

paragraphs: Reporting confidence intervals for selected results creates a collective uncertainty problem. The relevant error measure is the false coverage rate: the expected fraction of reported intervals that fail to contain their corresponding parameters. This paper studies control of that rate when parameters arrive sequentially over time.

The setting allows an infinite sequence of fixed, unknown parameters. The authors propose a framework that requires the scientist to be able to construct marginal confidence intervals. Its purpose is to manage error across the selected intervals reported throughout the sequence, making the reporting process itself part of the statistical problem.

The framework also yields online false discovery rate procedures and methods for classifying parameter signs while controlling the false sign rate. The same methodology applies to prediction intervals, with implications for selective conformal inference. These connections matter because selection affects more than hypothesis testing: it also affects which intervals and directional conclusions become visible. The paper provides a shared approach to controlling these related reporting errors as results accumulate.
summary.tldr: An online framework controls errors among selected confidence intervals and also yields false discovery and false sign rate procedures.

title: Online Control of the False Coverage Rate and False Sign Rate

abstract: We consider risk minimization problems where the (source) distribution $P_S$ of the training observations $Z_1, \ldots, Z_n$ differs from the (target) distribution $P_T$ involved in the risk that one seeks to minimize. Under the natural assumption that $P_S$ dominates $P_T$, \textit{i.e.} $P_T< \! \!<P_S$, we develop a semi-parametric framework in the situation where we \textit{do not} observe any sample from $P_T$, but rather have access to some auxiliary information at the target population scale. More precisely, assuming that the Radon-Nikodym derivative $dP_T/dP_S(z)$ belongs to a parametric class $\{g(z,\alpha), \alpha\in \mathcal{A}\}$ and that some (generalized) moments of $P_T$ are available to the learner, we propose a two-step learning procedure to perform the risk minimization task. We first select $\hat{\alpha}$ so as to match the moment constraints as closely as possible and then reweight each (biased) training observation $Z_i$ by $g(Z_i,\hat{\alpha})$ in the final Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) algorithm. We establish a $O_{\mathbb{P}}(1/\sqrt{n})$ generalization bound proving that, remarkably, the solution to the weighted ERM problem thus constructed achieves a learning rate of the same order as that attained in absence of any sampling bias. Beyond these theoretical guarantees, numerical results providing strong empirical evidence of the relevance of the approach promoted in this article are displayed.

The approach assumes that the source distribution covers the target distribution and that their density ratio belongs to a specified parametric family. Learning then proceeds in two steps. First, the method selects ratio parameters that match the target moment constraints as closely as possible. It then uses the estimated ratio to reweight training observations before minimizing empirical risk.

This matches the order of the learning rate available without sampling bias. Numerical results also support the approach. The significance is that aggregate target information can support effective bias correction without requiring a target-population sample.
summary.tldr: Target-population moment information can support reweighted learning with an unbiased-order learning rate under density-ratio assumptions.

title: Learning from Biased Data: A Semi-Parametric Approach

abstract: Based on the Delaunay triangulation, we propose the crystallization learning to estimate the conditional expectation function in the framework of nonparametric regression. By conducting the crystallization search for the Delaunay simplices closest to the target point in a hierarchical way, the crystallization learning estimates the conditional expectation of the response by fitting a local linear model to the data points of the constructed Delaunay simplices. Instead of conducting the Delaunay triangulation for the entire feature space which would encounter enormous computational difficulty, our approach focuses only on the neighborhood of the target point and thus greatly expedites the estimation for high-dimensional cases. Because the volumes of Delaunay simplices are adaptive to the density of feature data points, our method selects neighbor data points uniformly in all directions and thus is more robust to the local geometric structure of the data than existing nonparametric regression methods. We develop the asymptotic properties of the crystallization learning and conduct numerical experiments on both synthetic and real data to demonstrate the advantages of our method in estimation of the conditional expectation function and prediction of the response.

paragraphs: Crystallization learning estimates the expected response at a target input without specifying one global regression formula. It uses the geometry of nearby data points to decide where to fit a local linear model. The geometric structure comes from Delaunay simplices, which organize groups of points around the target.

Constructing a Delaunay triangulation across the entire feature space can be computationally difficult, especially in high dimensions. The proposed method instead searches hierarchically for nearby simplices and constructs only the neighborhood needed for the target prediction. This local focus greatly accelerates estimation in the high-dimensional cases considered by the authors.

The simplices’ volumes adapt to the density of the feature data, allowing neighbors to be selected uniformly across directions. The authors argue that this makes the method more robust to local data geometry than existing nonparametric regression methods. They develop asymptotic properties and use synthetic and real-data experiments to demonstrate advantages in estimating conditional expectations and predicting responses.
summary.tldr: Crystallization learning builds local Delaunay neighborhoods to make geometrically adaptive regression more computationally practical in high dimensions.

title: Crystallization Learning with the Delaunay Triangulation

abstract: For the past century, the anatomy of a neuron has been considered one of its defining features: The shape of a neuron’s dendrites and axon fundamentally determines what other neurons it can connect to. These neurites have been described using mathematical tools e.g. in the context of cell type classification, but generative models of these structures have only rarely been proposed and are often computationally inefficient. Here we propose MorphVAE, a sequence-to-sequence variational autoencoder with spherical latent space as a generative model for neural morphologies. The model operates on walks within the tree structure of a neuron and can incorporate expert annotations on a subset of the data using semi-supervised learning. We develop our model on artificially generated toy data and evaluate its performance on dendrites of excitatory cells and axons of inhibitory cells of mouse motor cortex (M1) and dendrites of retinal ganglion cells. We show that the learned latent feature space allows for better cell type discrimination than other commonly used features. By sampling new walks from the latent space we can easily construct new morphologies with a specified degree of similarity to their reference neuron, providing an efficient generative model for neural morphologies.

paragraphs: A neuron's branching shape helps determine which other neurons it can connect to, making morphology useful for understanding and distinguishing cell types. MorphVAE models these shapes through walks along a neuron's tree structure. It uses a sequence-to-sequence variational autoencoder with a spherical latent space to learn representations and generate new structures.

The model can incorporate expert annotations available for only part of the dataset through semi-supervised learning. The authors develop it on artificial toy data and evaluate it on excitatory-cell dendrites and inhibitory-cell axons from mouse motor cortex, as well as retinal ganglion cell dendrites. These evaluations cover several kinds of neuronal branching structures.

The learned latent features distinguish cell types better than other commonly used features in the reported evaluation. Sampling new walks from the latent space also enables efficient construction of new morphologies with a specified degree of similarity to a reference neuron. The same representation therefore supports both discrimination between cell types and controlled generation of related neuronal shapes.
summary.tldr: MorphVAE learns from walks through neuronal trees to distinguish cell types and efficiently generate morphologies with controlled similarity to reference neurons.

title: MorphVAE: Generating Neural Morphologies from 3D-Walks using a Variational Autoencoder with Spherical Latent Space

abstract: Knowledge transferability, or transfer learning, has been widely adopted to allow a pre-trained model in the source domain to be effectively adapted to downstream tasks in the target domain. It is thus important to explore and understand the factors affecting knowledge transferability. In this paper, as the first work, we analyze and demonstrate the connections between knowledge transferability and another important phenomenon–adversarial transferability, \emph{i.e.}, adversarial examples generated against one model can be transferred to attack other models. Our theoretical studies show that adversarial transferability indicates knowledge transferability, and vice versa. Moreover, based on the theoretical insights, we propose two practical adversarial transferability metrics to characterize this process, serving as bidirectional indicators between adversarial and knowledge transferability. We conduct extensive experiments for different scenarios on diverse datasets, showing a positive correlation between adversarial transferability and knowledge transferability. Our findings will shed light on future research about effective knowledge transfer learning and adversarial transferability analyses.

paragraphs: Knowledge transferability concerns how effectively a pretrained model can be adapted to a downstream task. Adversarial transferability concerns whether examples designed to attack one model can also attack another. This paper studies the relationship between these two phenomena to better understand what makes learned knowledge transferable.

The authors' theoretical analysis shows that adversarial transferability indicates knowledge transferability, and that the relationship also works in the reverse direction. Guided by these results, they propose two practical adversarial-transferability metrics. The metrics are intended to characterize the connection and act as indicators between successful knowledge transfer and successful attack transfer.

Experiments across diverse datasets and scenarios find a positive correlation between the two forms of transferability. This empirical association supports the theoretical connection and suggests that examining transferred attacks can provide information relevant to transfer learning. The result is about linked behavior and useful indicators; a positive correlation does not mean that every transferable attack guarantees a successful downstream adaptation. The work offers a shared perspective for studying model reuse and adversarial behavior.
summary.tldr: Theoretical analysis and experiments connect the transferability of adversarial attacks with the transferability of pretrained knowledge.

title: Uncovering the Connections Between Adversarial Transferability and Knowledge Transferability

abstract: In many statistical problems, incorporating priors can significantly improve performance. However, the use of prior knowledge in differentially private query release has remained underexplored, despite such priors commonly being available in the form of public datasets, such as previous US Census releases. With the goal of releasing statistics about a private dataset, we present PMW^Pub, which—unlike existing baselines—leverages public data drawn from a related distribution as prior information. We provide a theoretical analysis and an empirical evaluation on the American Community Survey (ACS) and ADULT datasets, which shows that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, PMW^Pub scales well to high-dimensional data domains, where running many existing methods would be computationally infeasible.

paragraphs: Private query release aims to publish statistics about a private dataset while maintaining differential privacy. The paper asks how public data can help this process. Related public datasets, such as earlier census releases, can provide prior information, yet the abstract identifies their use in private query release as underexplored.

The authors introduce PMW^Pub, which incorporates public data drawn from a related distribution. That relationship is central to the setup: the public dataset serves as information about the statistical problem involving the private data. The method brings this source of prior knowledge into the query-release procedure and is accompanied by a theoretical analysis.

Empirical evaluations on the American Community Survey and ADULT datasets show better performance than the state-of-the-art methods compared. The authors also report that PMW^Pub scales to high-dimensional domains where many existing approaches would be computationally infeasible. Its significance therefore involves both statistical performance and computational practicality: available public information can help make private statistical release more effective in settings whose dimensionality poses difficulties for existing methods.
summary.tldr: PMW^Pub uses related public data as prior information to improve the performance and scalability of private query release.

title: Leveraging Public Data for Practical Private Query Release

abstract: In many classification tasks there is a requirement of monotonicity. Concretely, if all else remains constant, increasing (resp. decreasing) the value of one or more features must not decrease (resp. increase) the value of the prediction. Despite comprehensive efforts on learning monotonic classifiers, dedicated approaches for explaining monotonic classifiers are scarce and classifier-specific. This paper describes novel algorithms for the computation of one formal explanation of a (black-box) monotonic classifier. These novel algorithms are polynomial (indeed linear) in the run time complexity of the classifier. Furthermore, the paper presents a practically efficient model-agnostic algorithm for enumerating formal explanations.

paragraphs: Some classification tasks require predictions to respect a known ordering: increasing an input feature, while holding other features fixed, must not decrease the prediction. Such monotonicity requirements constrain how a classifier behaves. This paper studies how that structure can support formal explanations of predictions, an area the authors describe as having few dedicated, broadly applicable methods.

The authors introduce algorithms for computing one formal explanation of a monotonic classifier treated as a black box. Because the algorithms work through the classifier’s behavior, the contribution is not tied to one particular model architecture. Their computational complexity is polynomial, and specifically linear in the classifier’s runtime complexity, giving a concrete efficiency result for obtaining an explanation.

The paper also presents a practically efficient, model-agnostic algorithm for enumerating formal explanations. This addresses the separate task of finding multiple explanations rather than stopping after one. Together, the results make monotonicity useful not only as a constraint on predictions but also as structure that enables efficient explanation procedures.
summary.tldr: Monotonicity enables efficient black-box algorithms for computing and enumerating formal classifier explanations.

title: Explanations for Monotonic Classifiers.

abstract: Discrepancy measures between probability distributions, often termed statistical distances, are ubiquitous in probability theory, statistics and machine learning. To combat the curse of dimensionality when estimating these distances from data, recent work has proposed smoothing out local irregularities in the measured distributions via convolution with a Gaussian kernel. Motivated by the scalability of this framework to high dimensions, we investigate the structural and statistical behavior of the Gaussian-smoothed $p$-Wasserstein distance $\mathsf{W}_p^{(\sigma)}$, for arbitrary $p\geq 1$. After establishing basic metric and topological properties of $\mathsf{W}_p^{(\sigma)}$, we explore the asymptotic statistical properties of $\mathsf{W}_p^{(\sigma)}(\hat{\mu}_n,\mu)$, where $\hat{\mu}_n$ is the empirical distribution of $n$ independent observations from $\mu$. We prove that $\mathsf{W}_p^{(\sigma)}$ enjoys a parametric empirical convergence rate of $n^{-1/2}$, which contrasts the $n^{-1/d}$ rate for unsmoothed $\Wp$ when $d \geq 3$. Our proof relies on controlling $\mathsf{W}_p^{(\sigma)}$ by a $p$th-order smooth Sobolev distance $\mathsf{d}_p^{(\sigma)}$ and deriving the limit distribution of $\sqrt{n}\,\mathsf{d}_p^{(\sigma)}(\hat{\mu}_n,\mu)$ for all dimensions $d$. As applications, we provide asymptotic guarantees for two-sample testing and minimum distance estimation using $\mathsf{W}_p^{(\sigma)}$, with experiments for $p=2$ using a maximum mean discrepancy formulation of $\mathsf{d}_2^{(\sigma)}$.

The analysis covers every order p of at least one and establishes basic metric and topological properties.

The central statistical result is an empirical convergence rate of n to the power minus one-half for the smoothed distance. The abstract contrasts this with the n to the power minus one-over-d rate for unsmoothed Wasserstein distance in dimensions of at least three. Thus, the reported smoothed rate avoids deterioration of its exponent as dimension increases.

The proof controls the smoothed Wasserstein distance through a smooth Sobolev distance and derives a limiting distribution for the latter. Applications provide asymptotic guarantees for two-sample testing and minimum-distance estimation. Experiments for p equal to two use a maximum mean discrepancy formulation, connecting the theoretical analysis to a concrete statistical implementation.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-smoothed Wasserstein distances achieve a parametric empirical convergence rate and support asymptotic guarantees for statistical testing and estimation.

title: Smooth $p$-Wasserstein Distance: Structure, Empirical Approximation, and Statistical Applications

abstract: Selective labels are a common feature of high-stakes decision-making applications, referring to the lack of observed outcomes under one of the possible decisions. This paper studies the learning of decision policies in the face of selective labels, in an online setting that balances learning costs against future utility. In the homogeneous case in which individuals’ features are disregarded, the optimal decision policy is shown to be a threshold policy. The threshold becomes more stringent as more labels are collected; the rate at which this occurs is characterized. In the case of features drawn from a finite domain, the optimal policy consists of multiple homogeneous policies in parallel. For the general infinite-domain case, the homogeneous policy is extended by using a probabilistic classifier and bootstrapping to provide its inputs. In experiments on synthetic and real data, the proposed policies achieve consistently superior utility with no parameter tuning in the finite-domain case and lower parameter sensitivity in the general case.

paragraphs: Selective labels arise when an outcome is observed after one decision but remains unavailable after another. A decision policy consequently affects both immediate utility and the evidence available for future learning. This paper studies that interaction online, explicitly balancing the cost of acquiring information against its potential value for later decisions.

When individual features are ignored, the authors prove that the optimal policy uses a threshold. That threshold becomes stricter as more labels accumulate, and the analysis characterizes how quickly this happens. When features take values in a finite domain, the optimal policy consists of several such homogeneous policies operating in parallel, extending the simpler result to feature-dependent decisions.

For an infinite feature domain, the authors extend the homogeneous policy using inputs supplied by a probabilistic classifier and bootstrapping. Experiments on synthetic and real data show consistently higher utility for the proposed policies. The finite-domain method needs no parameter tuning, while the general extension has lower parameter sensitivity. Optimality is established for the homogeneous and finite-domain settings; the broader extension is supported by empirical results.
summary.tldr: The paper derives optimal finite-domain policies for selective labels and extends them to general feature spaces using classification and bootstrapping.

title: Decision-Making Under Selective Labels: Optimal Finite-Domain Policies and Beyond

abstract: We consider the problem of reinforcement learning when provided with (1) a baseline control policy and (2) a set of constraints that the learner must satisfy. The baseline policy can arise from demonstration data or a teacher agent and may provide useful cues for learning, but it might also be sub-optimal for the task at hand, and is not guaranteed to satisfy the specified constraints, which might encode safety, fairness or other application-specific requirements. In order to safely learn from baseline policies, we propose an iterative policy optimization algorithm that alternates between maximizing expected return on the task, minimizing distance to the baseline policy, and projecting the policy onto the constraint-satisfying set. We analyze our algorithm theoretically and provide a finite-time convergence guarantee. In our experiments on five different control tasks, our algorithm consistently outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines, achieving 10 times fewer constraint violations and 40% higher reward on average.

paragraphs: A baseline controller can give a reinforcement learning agent useful guidance, but following it may conflict with the learner’s requirements. A teacher or demonstration policy might earn poor rewards or violate constraints concerning safety, fairness, or other application needs. This paper studies how to benefit from that guidance without assuming the baseline already satisfies those constraints.

The proposed algorithm alternates among three operations: improving expected reward, moving closer to the baseline, and projecting the policy onto the set of policies that satisfy the constraints. These operations give the baseline a specific role as a learning aid, while constraint satisfaction remains a separate part of optimization. The learner therefore has a way to use an imperfect teacher without simply copying its behavior.

The authors establish a finite-time convergence guarantee. Across five control tasks, they report consistently better performance than several leading baselines, with ten times fewer constraint violations and 40% higher reward on average. These experimental results support the approach’s ability to improve both learning performance and constraint handling; they do not amount to a claim of zero violations.
summary.tldr: Alternating reward improvement, baseline imitation, and constraint projection helps reinforcement learning use imperfect teachers with fewer constraint violations.

title: Accelerating Safe Reinforcement Learning with Constraint-mismatched Baseline Policies

abstract: We present a conceptual framework, datamodeling , for analyzing the behavior of a model class in terms of the training data. For any fixed “target” example $x$, training set $S$, and learning algorithm, a datamodel is a parameterized function $2^S \to \mathbb{R}$ that for any subset of $S’ \subset S$—using only information about which examples of $S$ are contained in $S’$—predicts the outcome of training a model on $S’$ and evaluating on $x$. Despite the complexity of the underlying process being approximated (e.g. end-to-end training and evaluation of deep neural networks), we show that even simple linear datamodels successfully predict model outputs. We then demonstrate that datamodels give rise to a variety of applications, such as: accurately predicting the effect of dataset counterfactuals; identifying brittle predictions; finding semantically similar examples; quantifying train-test leakage; and embedding data into a well-behaved and feature-rich representation space.

paragraphs: Datamodeling asks how the choice of training examples shapes a model's prediction on one fixed target example. For a fixed dataset and learning algorithm, a datamodel takes the membership of a training subset as input. It predicts the outcome of training on that subset and evaluating the resulting model on the target.

This replaces a complicated training-and-evaluation process with a function of which examples were included. The authors show that even linear datamodels can successfully predict model outputs despite the complexity of the underlying neural-network training. The finding concerns the usefulness of this approximation; it does not require the trained neural network itself to be linear.

The paper demonstrates several uses of this perspective: predicting the consequences of changing a dataset, detecting brittle predictions, finding semantically related examples, and quantifying train-test leakage. Datamodels also produce rich representations of data. These applications share a common idea: examples can be understood through the effects their inclusion has on predictions, linking model behavior directly to training-set composition.
summary.tldr: Datamodels predict how training-set membership affects model outputs, enabling analysis of dataset changes, brittle predictions, and relationships between examples.

title: Datamodels: Understanding Predictions with Data and Data with Predictions

abstract: In this paper, we consider online decision problems with submodular loss functions. For such problems, existing studies have only dealt with worst-case analysis. This study goes beyond worst-case analysis to show instance-dependent regret bounds. More precisely, for each of the full-information and bandit-feedback settings, we propose an algorithm that achieves a gap-dependent O(log T)-regret bound in the stochastic environment and is comparable to the best existing algorithm in the adversarial environment. The proposed algorithms also work well in the stochastic environment with adversarial corruptions, which is an intermediate setting between the stochastic and adversarial environments.

paragraphs: Online submodular minimization chooses decisions repeatedly while incurring losses with submodular structure. Existing analyses had emphasized worst-case environments, potentially obscuring better behavior when losses are generated stochastically. This paper seeks algorithms whose guarantees adapt to the difficulty of the environment.

For both full-information and bandit feedback, the authors propose algorithms with gap-dependent O(log T) regret in stochastic settings. The dependence on the gap makes the guarantee sensitive to the particular problem instance. At the same time, their adversarial-environment performance is comparable to the best existing algorithm, so the stronger stochastic result does not require abandoning worst-case protection.

The algorithms also handle stochastic environments containing adversarial corruptions, which fall between the two extremes. The contribution is a best-of-both-worlds analysis for submodular losses across feedback models. The abstract does not provide the full dependence on gap sizes or corruption levels, which determines how these guarantees translate to a specific finite-horizon problem.
summary.tldr: Online submodular-minimization algorithms gain logarithmic stochastic regret while retaining adversarial and corruption robustness.

title: Revisiting Online Submodular Minimization: Gap-Dependent Regret Bounds, Best of Both Worlds and Adversarial Robustness

abstract: We present Translatotron 2, a neural direct speech-to-speech translation model that can be trained end-to-end. Translatotron 2 consists of a speech encoder, a linguistic decoder, an acoustic synthesizer, and a single attention module that connects them together. Experimental results on three datasets consistently show that Translatotron 2 outperforms the original Translatotron by a large margin on both translation quality (up to +15.5 BLEU) and speech generation quality, and approaches the same of cascade systems. In addition, we propose a simple method for preserving speakers’ voices from the source speech to the translation speech in a different language. Unlike existing approaches, the proposed method is able to preserve each speaker’s voice on speaker turns without requiring for speaker segmentation. Furthermore, compared to existing approaches, it better preserves speaker’s privacy and mitigates potential misuse of voice cloning for creating spoofing audio artifacts.

Translation gains reach up to 15.5 BLEU, and the system approaches the quality of cascade systems. These findings show substantial progress for the proposed direct speech-to-speech architecture across the evaluated datasets.

The paper also introduces a method for carrying speakers' voices from the source recording into translated speech. It preserves individual voices across speaker turns without requiring speaker segmentation. Compared with existing approaches, the authors report better preservation of speaker privacy and reduced potential misuse for voice-cloning spoofing. This is a qualified mitigation claim, alongside the method's ability to preserve voice identity during translation.
summary.tldr: Translatotron 2 improves direct speech translation quality and preserves speakers' voices across turns without speaker segmentation.

title: Translatotron 2: High-quality direct speech-to-speech translation with voice preservation

abstract: Probabilistic solvers for ordinary differential equations (ODEs) have emerged as an efficient framework for uncertainty quantification and inference on dynamical systems. In this work, we explain the mathematical assumptions and detailed implementation schemes behind solving high-dimensional ODEs with a probabilistic numerical algorithm. This has not been possible before due to matrix-matrix operations in each solver step, but is crucial for scientifically relevant problems—most importantly, the solution of discretised partial differential equations. In a nutshell, efficient high-dimensional probabilistic ODE solutions build either on independence assumptions or on Kronecker structure in the prior model. We evaluate the resulting efficiency on a range of problems, including the probabilistic numerical simulation of a differential equation with millions of dimensions.

paragraphs: Probabilistic solvers for ordinary differential equations support uncertainty quantification and inference about dynamical systems. Scaling these methods to high-dimensional equations has been obstructed by matrix-matrix computations within every solver step. This paper explains the mathematical assumptions and implementation schemes that make much larger probabilistic numerical solutions possible.

The efficient formulations rely on one of two kinds of structure in the prior model: independence assumptions or Kronecker structure. These are substantive modeling ingredients behind the computational improvement. Organizing the prior in these ways enables the method to address the expensive operations that previously prevented high-dimensional use.

The authors evaluate efficiency on a range of problems, including a probabilistic simulation with millions of dimensions. Such scale matters particularly for partial differential equations that become large systems of ordinary differential equations after discretization. The paper’s contribution is therefore both a practical demonstration and an explanation of the structure supporting it, connecting high-dimensional computation with the assumptions used to represent numerical uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Independence assumptions or Kronecker-structured priors enable probabilistic ODE solvers to scale to demonstrated problems with millions of dimensions.

title: Probabilistic ODE Solutions in Millions of Dimensions

abstract: Neural Processes (NPs) are a popular class of approaches for meta-learning. Similar to Gaussian Processes (GPs), NPs define distributions over functions and can estimate uncertainty in their predictions. However, unlike GPs, NPs and their variants suffer from underfitting and often have intractable likelihoods, which limit their applications in sequential decision making. We propose Transformer Neural Processes (TNPs), a new member of the NP family that casts uncertainty-aware meta learning as a sequence modeling problem. We learn TNPs via an autoregressive likelihood-based objective and instantiate it with a novel transformer-based architecture that respects the inductive biases inherent to the problem structure, such as invariance to the observed data points and equivariance to the unobserved points. We further design knobs within the TNP architecture to tradeoff the increase in expressivity of the decoding distribution with extra computation. Empirically, we show that TNPs achieve state-of-the-art performance on various benchmark problems, outperforming all previous NP variants on meta regression, image completion, contextual multi-armed bandits, and Bayesian optimization.

paragraphs: Neural Processes learn distributions over functions, allowing them to make predictions with uncertainty across tasks. However, underfitting and frequently intractable likelihoods limit existing variants, particularly for sequential decisions. This paper introduces Transformer Neural Processes, which formulate uncertainty-aware meta-learning as sequence modeling and use an autoregressive likelihood objective for training.

The transformer architecture preserves structural requirements of the problem. Reordering observed data points should not change the inference, while reordering unobserved points should correspondingly reorder their predictions. The authors also provide architectural controls that trade a more expressive decoding distribution against additional computation, making that cost-versus-expressivity choice explicit.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on meta-regression, image completion, contextual multi-armed bandits, and Bayesian optimization, outperforming previous Neural Process variants on the evaluated benchmarks. These tasks connect prediction and uncertainty estimation with downstream decision-making. The contribution is a sequence-based formulation that combines an explicit likelihood objective with the ordering properties the problem requires, supported by results across several types of meta-learning and sequential-decision applications.
summary.tldr: Transformer Neural Processes use structured sequence modeling for uncertainty-aware meta-learning and outperform earlier variants across the reported benchmarks.

title: Transformer Neural Processes: Uncertainty-Aware Meta Learning Via Sequence Modeling

abstract: Anomaly detection aims at identifying data points that show systematic deviations from the majority of data in an unlabeled dataset. A common assumption is that clean training data (free of anomalies) is available, which is often violated in practice. We propose a strategy for training an anomaly detector in the presence of unlabeled anomalies that is compatible with a broad class of models. The idea is to jointly infer binary labels to each datum (normal vs. anomalous) while updating the model parameters. Inspired by outlier exposure (Hendrycks et al., 2018) that considers synthetically created, labeled anomalies, we thereby use a combination of two losses that share parameters: one for the normal and one for the anomalous data. We then iteratively proceed with block coordinate updates on the parameters and the most likely (latent) labels. Our experiments with several backbone models on three image datasets, 30 tabular data sets, and a video anomaly detection benchmark showed consistent and significant improvements over the baselines.

paragraphs: Anomaly detectors often assume their training data contains only normal examples. In practice, an unlabeled dataset may already contain the anomalies the model is supposed to detect. This paper develops a training strategy for that contaminated setting, so learning can account for possible outliers instead of treating every training example as normal.

The method jointly estimates a binary normal-or-anomalous label for each example and updates the detector’s parameters. It uses two losses with shared parameters, one for normal data and one for anomalous data. Training alternates between parameter updates and updates to the most likely hidden labels. This adapts the idea of outlier exposure to anomalies whose labels are unknown within the training data.

The strategy is compatible with a broad class of models. Experiments use several backbone models across three image datasets, 30 tabular datasets, and a video anomaly detection benchmark, reporting consistent and significant improvements over baselines. These findings support explicitly modeling contamination during training and show that the approach can benefit multiple model and data types in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Latent Outlier Exposure alternates between estimating anomaly labels and training a detector, improving anomaly detection with contaminated, unlabeled training data.

title: Latent Outlier Exposure for Anomaly Detection with Contaminated Data

abstract: Max-value entropy search (MES) is one of the state-of-the-art approaches in Bayesian optimization (BO). In this paper, we propose a novel variant of MES for constrained problems, called Constrained MES via Information lower BOund (CMES-IBO), that is based on a Monte Carlo (MC) estimator of a lower bound of a mutual information (MI). Unlike existing studies, our MI is defined so that uncertainty with respect to feasibility can be incorporated. We derive a lower bound of the MI that guarantees non-negativity, while a constrained counterpart of conventional MES can be negative. We further provide theoretical analysis that assures the low-variability of our estimator which has never been investigated for any existing information-theoretic BO. Moreover, using the conditional MI, we extend CMES-IBO to the parallel setting while maintaining the desirable properties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CMES-IBO by several benchmark functions and real-world problems.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization must sometimes search for a high-performing choice while also satisfying constraints. In that setting, uncertainty concerns both the objective and whether candidate choices are feasible. This paper develops CMES-IBO, a constrained form of max-value entropy search that explicitly incorporates uncertainty about feasibility into its information measure.

The method uses a Monte Carlo estimate of a lower bound on mutual information. The derived bound is guaranteed to be nonnegative, whereas a constrained counterpart of conventional max-value entropy search can produce negative values. The authors also provide theoretical analysis supporting low variability of the estimator, addressing how reliably this information quantity can be estimated.

Using conditional mutual information, they extend the method to select evaluations in parallel while retaining its desirable properties. Experiments on benchmark functions and real-world problems demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution combines a feasibility-aware information objective with an estimator whose sign and variability receive theoretical attention, supporting both sequential and parallel constrained optimization.
summary.tldr: CMES-IBO handles feasibility uncertainty using a nonnegative information lower bound with a low-variability estimator for sequential and parallel optimization.

title: Sequential and Parallel Constrained Max-value Entropy Search via Information Lower Bound

abstract: Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown prominent performance in graph representation learning by leveraging knowledge from both graph structure and node features. However, most of them have two major limitations. First, GNNs can learn higher-order structural information by stacking more layers but can not deal with large depth due to the over-smoothing issue. Second, it is not easy to apply these methods on large graphs due to the expensive computation cost and high memory usage. In this paper, we present node-adaptive feature smoothing (NAFS), a simple non-parametric method that constructs node representations without parameter learning. NAFS first extracts the features of each node with its neighbors of different hops by feature smoothing, and then adaptively combines the smoothed features. Besides, the constructed node representation can further be enhanced by the ensemble of smoothed features extracted via different smoothing strategies. We conduct experiments on four benchmark datasets on two different application scenarios: node clustering and link prediction. Remarkably, NAFS with feature ensemble outperforms the state-of-the-art GNNs on these tasks and mitigates the aforementioned two limitations of most learning-based GNN counterparts.

paragraphs: Graph representations often combine a node's own features with information from its neighbors. Deep graph neural networks can gather information from farther away, but may make node representations overly similar and require substantial computation and memory. This paper introduces node-adaptive feature smoothing, or NAFS, as a method that constructs representations without learning parameters.

NAFS smooths features using neighborhoods at different hop distances and then adaptively combines those results for each node. This allows the final representation to draw on several neighborhood ranges. The authors also enhance the representation by combining smoothed features obtained through different smoothing strategies, creating an ensemble of complementary feature constructions.

Experiments cover node clustering and link prediction on four benchmark datasets. NAFS with feature ensembling outperforms the compared state-of-the-art graph neural networks and mitigates the depth and resource problems discussed in the paper. The results establish a strong non-parametric baseline for these tasks and show that useful graph representations can emerge from carefully combining neighborhood information without parameter training.
summary.tldr: NAFS builds strong graph representations without parameter learning by adaptively combining smoothed features from multiple neighborhoods.

title: NAFS: A Simple yet Tough-to-beat Baseline for Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Heterogeneous federated learning (HFL) enables clients with different computation and communication capabilities to collaboratively train their own customized models via a query-response paradigm on auxiliary datasets. However, such a paradigm raises serious privacy concerns due to the leakage of highly sensitive query samples and response predictions. We put forth GuardHFL, the first-of-its-kind efficient and privacy-preserving HFL framework. GuardHFL is equipped with a novel HFL-friendly secure querying scheme built on lightweight secret sharing and symmetric-key techniques. The core of GuardHFL is two customized multiplication and comparison protocols, which substantially boost the execution efficiency. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that GuardHFL significantly outperforms the alternative instantiations based on existing state-of-the-art techniques in both runtime and communication cost.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous federated learning lets clients with different computing and communication resources collaboratively train customized models. In the setting studied here, collaboration uses queries and prediction responses on auxiliary datasets. Those exchanges introduce a privacy problem because both the queried samples and the returned predictions may contain sensitive information.

GuardHFL provides a secure querying scheme designed for this form of collaboration. It combines lightweight secret sharing with symmetric-key techniques. At its core are customized protocols for multiplication and comparison, operations whose efficient implementation is central to the framework. The design targets the privacy-sensitive exchange itself while seeking to keep the cost of collaborative learning manageable.

The authors evaluate GuardHFL against alternative implementations built from existing state-of-the-art techniques. They report substantial improvements in both runtime and communication cost. These findings support the benefit of designing secure computation around the particular query-response workflow of heterogeneous federated learning. The contribution addresses both the protection of exchanged information and the execution costs that accompany that protection.
summary.tldr: GuardHFL protects query-response exchanges in heterogeneous federated learning while reducing runtime and communication costs in evaluations.

title: GuardHFL: Privacy Guardian for Heterogeneous Federated Learning

abstract: Causal effect estimation has been studied by many researchers when only observational data is available. Sound and complete algorithms have been developed for pointwise estimation of identifiable causal queries. For non-identifiable causal queries, researchers developed polynomial programs to estimate tight bounds on causal effect. However, these are computationally difficult to optimize for variables with large support sizes. In this paper, we analyze the effect of "weak confounding’" on causal estimands. More specifically, under the assumption that the unobserved confounders that render a query non-identifiable have small entropy, we propose an efficient linear program to derive the upper and lower bounds of the causal effect. We show that our bounds are consistent in the sense that as the entropy of unobserved confounders goes to zero, the gap between the upper and lower bound vanishes. Finally, we conduct synthetic and real data simulations to compare our bounds with the bounds obtained by the existing work that cannot incorporate such entropy constraints and show that our bounds are tighter for the setting with weak confounders.
