paragraphs: Observational data do not always determine a unique causal effect. When hidden variables leave several causal explanations compatible with the observations, researchers can instead calculate upper and lower bounds. Existing approaches can produce tight bounds, but their polynomial optimization problems become difficult when variables have many possible values.

This paper makes a specific assumption about the hidden variables responsible for that ambiguity: they have small entropy, meaning limited uncertainty in their values. Under this definition of weak confounding, the authors formulate an efficient linear program for bounding the causal effect. The approach incorporates information about the confounders that the comparison methods cannot use.

The authors show that the bounds close together as the confounders’ entropy approaches zero. This gives a precise connection between weakening hidden uncertainty and narrowing causal ambiguity. Simulations using synthetic and real data also produce tighter bounds than existing approaches in settings with weak confounders. The contribution is therefore a computationally practical way to obtain more informative causal ranges under an explicit entropy assumption.
summary.tldr: An efficient linear program bounds otherwise unidentified causal effects more tightly when the relevant hidden confounders have small entropy.

title: Approximate Causal Effect Identification under Weak Confounding

abstract: While reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved great success in acquiring complex skills solely from environmental interactions, it assumes that resets to the initial state are readily available at the end of each episode. Such an assumption hinders the autonomous learning of embodied agents due to the time-consuming and cumbersome workarounds for resetting in the physical world. Hence, there has been a growing interest in autonomous RL (ARL) methods that are capable of learning from non-episodic interactions. However, existing works on ARL are limited by their reliance on prior data and are unable to learn in environments where task-relevant interactions are sparse. In contrast, we propose a demonstration-free ARL algorithm via Implicit and Bi-directional Curriculum (IBC). With an auxiliary agent that is conditionally activated upon learning progress and a bidirectional goal curriculum based on optimal transport, our method outperforms previous methods, even the ones that leverage demonstrations.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly assumes that an environment can return to its initial state after each episode. For an embodied agent, arranging those resets can require cumbersome physical intervention. Autonomous reinforcement learning instead seeks to learn through continuing interactions, making the organization of experience especially important when useful task-related encounters are sparse.

The paper proposes Implicit and Bidirectional Curriculum, or IBC, as an autonomous learning method that does not require demonstrations. It combines an auxiliary agent, activated conditionally according to learning progress, with a bidirectional curriculum over goals. The goal curriculum is based on optimal transport, providing a structured mechanism for organizing the learning process.

The reported comparison finds that IBC outperforms previous methods, including methods that use demonstrations. This supports the value of coordinating assistance and goal selection when learning must proceed without routine episodic resets. The contribution is a way to structure autonomous experience without demonstration data, addressing both the practical reset burden and the difficulty of obtaining task-relevant interactions.
summary.tldr: IBC combines progress-dependent assistance with a bidirectional goal curriculum to improve autonomous reinforcement learning without demonstrations.

title: Demonstration-free Autonomous Reinforcement Learning via Implicit and Bidirectional Curriculum

abstract: In the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem, a randomized probability matching policy called Thompson sampling (TS) has shown excellent performance in various reward models. In addition to the empirical performance, TS has been shown to achieve asymptotic problem-dependent lower bounds in several models. However, its optimality has been mainly addressed under light-tailed or one-parameter models that belong to exponential families. In this paper, we consider the optimality of TS for the Pareto model that has a heavy tail and is parameterized by two unknown parameters. Specifically, we discuss the optimality of TS with probability matching priors that include the Jeffreys prior and the reference priors. We first prove that TS with certain probability matching priors can achieve the optimal regret bound. Then, we show the suboptimality of TS with other priors, including the Jeffreys and the reference priors. Nevertheless, we find that TS with the Jeffreys and reference priors can achieve the asymptotic lower bound if one uses a truncation procedure. These results suggest carefully choosing noninformative priors to avoid suboptimality and show the effectiveness of truncation procedures in TS-based policies.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling chooses among uncertain options through randomized probability matching. Although it has strong performance and optimality results in several reward models, much of that theory concerns light-tailed distributions or one-parameter exponential families. This paper studies a different setting: Pareto rewards, which are heavy-tailed and have two unknown parameters.

The authors examine how the choice of probability-matching prior affects regret, the accumulated performance shortfall from learning which option is best. They prove that certain priors allow Thompson sampling to achieve an optimal regret bound. Other priors yield suboptimal behavior, including the Jeffreys and reference priors. A prior's noninformative status therefore does not by itself ensure the desired performance in this model.

A truncation procedure changes that outcome for Thompson sampling with Jeffreys and reference priors: the authors show that it can then attain the asymptotic lower bound. The results establish both successful and unsuccessful prior choices and a procedure that restores asymptotic optimality for the identified cases. Their practical message is that prior selection and truncation can materially affect Thompson sampling in two-parameter, heavy-tailed reward settings.
summary.tldr: For two-parameter Pareto bandits, Thompson sampling's optimality depends on the prior, and truncation restores asymptotic optimality for Jeffreys and reference priors.

title: Optimality of Thompson Sampling with Noninformative Priors for Pareto Bandits

abstract: Current protein language models (PLMs) learn protein representations mainly based on their sequences, thereby well capturing co-evolutionary information, but they are unable to explicitly acquire protein functions, which is the end goal of protein representation learning. Fortunately, for many proteins, their textual property descriptions are available, where their various functions are also described. Motivated by this fact, we first build the ProtDescribe dataset to augment protein sequences with text descriptions of their functions and other important properties. Based on this dataset, we propose the ProtST framework to enhance Protein Sequence pre-training and understanding by biomedical Texts. During pre-training, we design three types of tasks, i.e., unimodal mask prediction, multimodal representation alignment and multimodal mask prediction, to enhance a PLM with protein property information with different granularities and, at the same time, preserve the PLM’s original representation power. On downstream tasks, ProtST enables both supervised learning and zero-shot prediction. We verify the superiority of ProtST-induced PLMs over previous ones on diverse representation learning benchmarks. Under the zero-shot setting, we show the effectiveness of ProtST on zero-shot protein classification, and ProtST also enables functional protein retrieval from a large-scale database without any function annotation.

paragraphs: Protein language models learn useful sequence representations, including co-evolutionary information, but sequence-based training does not explicitly provide protein functions. This paper uses biomedical descriptions as an additional source of information. It first builds ProtDescribe, a dataset pairing protein sequences with text describing their functions and other properties.

The ProtST framework trains with three kinds of tasks: mask prediction within one modality, alignment between sequence and text representations, and mask prediction across modalities. Together, these tasks introduce property information at different levels of detail while aiming to preserve the original representational strength of the protein model. Text becomes part of pretraining rather than merely a description consulted afterward.

The resulting models support both supervised downstream learning and zero-shot prediction. Evaluations report improvements over previous protein language models on diverse representation benchmarks and demonstrate zero-shot protein classification. ProtST also enables functional retrieval from a large protein database without function annotations. These findings support using textual descriptions to connect sequence representations more directly to the functional information sought in downstream applications.
summary.tldr: ProtST combines protein sequences with biomedical descriptions to improve representations and support zero-shot classification and functional retrieval.

title: ProtST: Multi-Modality Learning of Protein Sequences and Biomedical Texts

abstract: Generating molecules with high binding affinities to target proteins (a.k.a. structure-based drug design) is a fundamental and challenging task in drug discovery. Recently, deep generative models have achieved remarkable success in generating 3D molecules conditioned on the protein pocket. However, most existing methods consider molecular generation for protein pockets independently while neglecting the underlying connections such as subpocket-level similarities. Subpockets are the local protein environments of ligand fragments and pockets with similar subpockets may bind the same molecular fragment (motif) even though their overall structures are different. Therefore, the trained models can hardly generalize to unseen protein pockets in real-world applications. In this paper, we propose a novel method DrugGPS for generalizable structure-based drug design. With the biochemical priors, we propose to learn subpocket prototypes and construct a global interaction graph to model the interactions between subpocket prototypes and molecular motifs. Moreover, a hierarchical graph transformer encoder and motif-based 3D molecule generation scheme are used to improve the model’s performance. The experimental results show that our model consistently outperforms baselines in generating realistic drug candidates with high affinities in challenging out-of-distribution settings.

summary.tldr: DrugGPS shares information through subpocket prototypes and molecular motifs to improve molecule generation for unseen protein pockets.

title: Learning Subpocket Prototypes for Generalizable Structure-based Drug Design

abstract: Touch is an important sensing modality for humans, but it has not yet been incorporated into a multimodal generative language model. This is partially due to the difficulty of obtaining natural language labels for tactile data and the complexity of aligning tactile readings with both visual observations and language descriptions. As a step towards bridging that gap, this work introduces a new dataset of 44K in-the-wild visiontouch pairs, with English language labels annotated by humans (10%) and textual pseudo-labels from GPT-4V (90%). We use this dataset to train a vision-language-aligned tactile encoder for open-vocabulary classification and a touch-visionlanguage (TVL) model for text generation using the trained encoder. Results suggest that by incorporating touch, the TVL model improves (+29% classification accuracy) tactile-vision-language alignment over existing models trained on any pair of those modalities. Although only a small fraction of the dataset is human labeled, the TVL model demonstrates improved visual-tactile understanding over GPT-4V (+12%) and open-source vision-language models (+32%) on a new touch-vision understanding benchmark. Code, checkpoints and data are available on https: //tactile-vlm.github.io.

The dataset contains 44,000 vision–touch pairs collected in the wild, with human annotations for 10% and GPT-4V-generated textual labels for the remaining 90%.

The authors use these examples to train a tactile encoder aligned with vision and language. This encoder supports open-vocabulary classification and becomes part of a touch–vision–language model that generates text. The approach gives tactile measurements a representation that can participate in tasks involving the other two modalities.

On a new touch–vision understanding benchmark, the model also reports improvements of 12% over GPT-4V and 32% over open-source vision-language models. These findings support the usefulness of adding touch even when most language labels are generated automatically.
summary.tldr: A dataset of 44,000 vision–touch pairs supports models that connect tactile sensing with images and language, improving reported multimodal understanding.

title: A Touch, Vision, and Language Dataset for Multimodal Alignment

abstract: This study investigates how weight decay affects the update behavior of individual neurons in deep neural networks through a combination of applied analysis and experimentation. Weight decay can cause the expected magnitude and angular updates of a neuron’s weight vector to converge to a steady state we call rotational equilibrium. These states can be highly homogeneous, effectively balancing the average rotation—a proxy for the effective learning rate—across different layers and neurons. Our work analyzes these dynamics across optimizers like Adam, Lion, and SGD with momentum, offering a new simple perspective on training that elucidates the efficacy of widely used but poorly understood methods in deep learning. We demonstrate how balanced rotation plays a key role in the effectiveness of normalization like Weight Standardization, as well as that of AdamW over Adam with L2-regularization. Finally, we show that explicitly controlling the rotation provides the benefits of weight decay while substantially reducing the need for learning rate warmup.

paragraphs: Weight decay changes more than the size of neural-network weights: it also affects how their directions evolve during training. This paper studies those dynamics at the level of individual neurons. It introduces rotational equilibrium, a steady state in the expected magnitude and angular size of weight updates.

Through analysis and experiments with Adam, Lion, and momentum SGD, the authors show that these equilibria can balance average rotation across layers and neurons. Rotation serves as a proxy for effective learning rate. This perspective helps explain the benefits of Weight Standardization and differences between AdamW and Adam with an L2 penalty.

The paper also finds that explicitly controlling rotation can retain benefits associated with weight decay while substantially reducing the need for learning-rate warmup. The contribution is a mechanism connecting familiar optimization choices to balanced update behavior. It does not imply that weight decay has only one effect or that the same equilibrium holds identically for every training configuration.
summary.tldr: Weight decay can balance neuron-wise angular updates, explaining optimization benefits and motivating explicit rotation control.

title: Rotational Equilibrium: How Weight Decay Balances Learning Across Neural Networks

abstract: Statistical model discovery is a challenging search over a vast space of models subject to domain-specific constraints. Efficiently searching over this space requires expertise in modeling and the problem domain. Motivated by the domain knowledge and programming capabilities of large language models (LMs), we introduce a method for language model driven automated statistical model discovery. We cast our automated procedure within the principled framework of Box’s Loop: the LM iterates between proposing statistical models represented as probabilistic programs, acting as a modeler, and critiquing those models, acting as a domain expert. By leveraging LMs, we do not have to define a domain-specific language of models or design a handcrafted search procedure, which are key restrictions of previous systems. We evaluate our method in three settings in probabilistic modeling: searching within a restricted space of models, searching over an open-ended space, and improving expert models under natural language constraints (e.g., this model should be interpretable to an ecologist). Our method identifies models on par with human expert designed models and extends classic models in interpretable ways. Our results highlight the promise of LM-driven model discovery.

paragraphs: Choosing a statistical model involves searching through many possible explanations while respecting constraints from the application domain. This paper uses a language model's programming ability and domain knowledge to help conduct that search. Candidate models are expressed as probabilistic programs, giving the language model a concrete representation to propose and revise.

The procedure follows Box's Loop: the language model alternates between creating models and criticizing them. These roles combine model construction with domain-oriented assessment. In these settings, the method finds models comparable to human expert designs and produces interpretable extensions of classic models. The findings support language models as tools for iterative statistical discovery, including tasks where the desired qualities of a model are expressed in ordinary language.
summary.tldr: A language model alternates between proposing and critiquing probabilistic programs to discover statistical models under domain-specific constraints.

title: Automated Statistical Model Discovery with Language Models

abstract: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) have achieved impressive success in visual reasoning, particularly in visual mathematics. However, problem-solving capabilities in graph theory remain less explored for LMMs, despite being a crucial aspect of mathematical reasoning that requires an accurate understanding of graphical structures and multi-step reasoning on visual graphs. To step forward in this direction, we are the first to design a benchmark named VisionGraph, used to explore the capabilities of advanced LMMs in solving multimodal graph theory problems. It encompasses eight complex graph problem tasks, from connectivity to shortest path problems. Subsequently, we present a Description-Program-Reasoning (DPR) chain to enhance the logical accuracy of reasoning processes through graphical structure description generation and algorithm-aware multi-step reasoning. Our extensive study shows that 1) GPT-4V outperforms Gemini Pro in multi-step graph reasoning; 2) All LMMs exhibit inferior perception accuracy for graphical structures, whether in zero/few-shot settings or with supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which further affects problem-solving performance; 3) DPR significantly improves the multi-step graph reasoning capabilities of LMMs and the GPT-4V (DPR) agent achieves SOTA performance.

paragraphs: VisionGraph evaluates multimodal models on graph theory problems presented visually. Solving these tasks requires both accurately reading a graph's structure and reasoning through multiple steps. The benchmark contains eight task types, including connectivity and shortest-path problems, making these abilities explicit objects of evaluation.

The paper also introduces a Description-Program-Reasoning chain. It combines generation of a description of the graphical structure with algorithm-aware, multi-step reasoning to improve logical accuracy. This organizes the solution process around the graph being interpreted and the computational reasoning required by the question.

In the reported study, GPT-4V performs better than Gemini Pro on multi-step graph reasoning. All evaluated models show weak graphical-structure perception across zero-shot, few-shot, and supervised fine-tuning settings, which affects their problem-solving performance. The proposed reasoning chain significantly improves results, with the GPT-4V DPR agent reaching state-of-the-art performance. Together, the findings identify visual structure perception as a persistent difficulty while showing benefits from explicitly organizing the reasoning process.
summary.tldr: VisionGraph benchmarks visual graph reasoning and shows that a structured Description-Program-Reasoning chain improves performance despite persistent graph-perception errors.

title: VisionGraph: Leveraging Large Multimodal Models for Graph Theory Problems in Visual Context

abstract: Many scientific and industrial applications require the joint optimization of multiple, potentially competing objectives. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) is a sample-efficient framework for identifying Pareto-optimal solutions. At the heart of MOBO is the acquisition function, which determines the next candidate to evaluate by navigating the best compromises among the objectives. Acquisition functions that rely on integrating over the objective space scale poorly to a large number of objectives. In this paper, we show a natural connection between the non-dominated solutions and the highest multivariate rank, which coincides with the extreme level line of the joint cumulative distribution function (CDF). Motivated by this link, we propose the CDF indicator, a Pareto-compliant metric for evaluating the quality of approximate Pareto sets, that can complement the popular hypervolume indicator. We then introduce an acquisition function based on the CDF indicator, called BOtied. BOtied can be implemented efficiently with copulas, a statistical tool for modeling complex, high-dimensional distributions. Our experiments on a variety of synthetic and real-world experiments demonstrate that BOtied outperforms state-of-the-art MOBO algorithms while being computationally efficient for many objectives.

paragraphs: Optimizing several competing objectives means searching for useful tradeoffs. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization chooses which candidate to evaluate next through an acquisition function. Some existing acquisition functions become computationally expensive as the number of objectives grows because they integrate over the space of possible objective values.

The paper connects non-dominated solutions, which cannot be improved in one objective without sacrificing another, to the highest multivariate rank. This rank corresponds to an extreme level line of the joint cumulative distribution function. Using that connection, the authors introduce a CDF indicator for assessing approximate Pareto sets. Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems report better performance than state-of-the-art multi-objective Bayesian optimization methods while remaining computationally efficient. The contribution therefore links a new way to assess tradeoff sets with a practical rule for directing the search.
summary.tldr: BOtied uses multivariate ranks and a CDF-based quality indicator to guide efficient Bayesian optimization across many competing objectives.

title: BOtied: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization with tied multivariate ranks

abstract: Often times in imitation learning (IL), the environment we collect expert demonstrations in and the environment we want to deploy our learned policy in aren’t exactly the same (e.g. demonstrations collected in simulation but deployment in the real world). Compared to policy-centric approaches to IL like behavioural cloning, reward-centric approaches like inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) often better replicate expert behaviour in new environments. This transfer is usually performed by optimising the recovered reward under the dynamics of the target environment. However, (a) we find that modern deep IL algorithms frequently recover rewards which induce policies far weaker than the expert, even in the same environment the demonstrations were collected in. Furthermore, (b) these rewards are often quite poorly shaped, necessitating extensive environment interaction to optimise effectively. We provide simple and scalable fixes to both of these concerns. For (a), we find that reward model ensembles combined with a slightly different training objective significantly improves re-training and transfer performance. For (b), we propose a novel evolution-strategies based method (EvIL) to optimise for a reward-shaping term that speeds up re-training in the target environment, closing a gap left open by the classical theory of IRL. On a suite of continuous control tasks, we are able to re-train policies in target (and source) environments more interaction-efficiently than prior work.

paragraphs: Imitation learning often needs to transfer behavior from the environment where demonstrations were collected to a different deployment environment. The paper identifies two problems with rewards recovered by modern deep imitation-learning methods.

First, optimizing a recovered reward can produce policies much weaker than the expert, even in the original environment. The authors find that reward-model ensembles combined with a modified training objective substantially improve retraining and transfer. Second, recovered rewards can provide poor learning guidance, requiring extensive environment interaction before an effective policy emerges.

EvIL addresses this second problem using evolution strategies to optimize a reward-shaping term that accelerates retraining in the target environment. Across continuous-control tasks, the combined approach retrains policies more efficiently in terms of environment interactions than prior work, in both source and target environments. The contribution improves both the usefulness of learned rewards and the ease of optimizing them.
summary.tldr: Reward ensembles and evolution-based reward shaping make imitation-learned rewards more effective and more efficient to optimize across environments.

title: EvIL: Evolution Strategies for Generalisable Imitation Learning

abstract: Continual learning requires learning incremental tasks with dynamic data distributions. So far, it has been observed that employing a combination of contrastive loss and distillation loss for training in continual learning yields strong performance. To the best of our knowledge, however, this contrastive continual learning framework lacks convincing theoretical explanations. In this work, we fill this gap by establishing theoretical performance guarantees, which reveal how the performance of the model is bounded by training losses of previous tasks in the contrastive continual learning framework. Our theoretical explanations further support the idea that pre-training can benefit continual learning. Inspired by our theoretical analysis of these guarantees, we propose a novel contrastive continual learning algorithm called CILA, which uses adaptive distillation coefficients for different tasks. These distillation coefficients are easily computed by the ratio between average distillation losses and average contrastive losses from previous tasks. Our method shows great improvement on standard benchmarks and achieves new state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to absorb successive tasks as data distributions change. Combining contrastive learning with distillation has worked well empirically, but the paper identifies a gap in the theoretical explanation. It develops performance guarantees to explain how training on earlier tasks constrains performance within this learning framework.

The resulting bounds relate model performance to previous tasks’ training losses. They also support the idea that pretraining can help continual learning. Building on the analysis, the authors propose CILA, an algorithm that assigns adaptive distillation coefficients to different tasks. These coefficients are computed using ratios of average distillation losses to average contrastive losses from previous tasks.

This makes the balance between the two training objectives responsive to information from the learning history. The authors report substantial improvements and state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks. The contribution connects theory and algorithm design: the analysis explains a successful combination of losses, while the proposed method uses quantities appearing in that perspective to guide task-dependent training.
summary.tldr: Performance bounds for contrastive continual learning motivate CILA, which adapts distillation strength using previous tasks’ losses.

title: Provable Contrastive Continual Learning

abstract: This paper aims to provide differential privacy (DP) guarantees for Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms. In a first part, we establish DP guarantees on samples output by MCMC algorithms as well as Monte Carlo estimators associated with these methods under assumptions on the convergence properties of the underlying Markov chain. In particular, our results highlight the critical condition of ensuring the target distribution is differentially private itself. In a second part, we specialise our analysis to the unadjusted Langevin algorithm and stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics and establish guarantees on their (Rényi) DP. To this end, we develop a novel methodology based on Girsanov’s theorem combined with a perturbation trick to obtain bounds for an unbounded domain and in a non-convex setting. We establish: (i) uniform in $n$ privacy guarantees when the state of the chain after $n$ iterations is released, (ii) bounds on the privacy of the entire chain trajectory. These findings provide concrete guidelines for privacy-preserving MCMC.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms generate samples through a sequence of dependent random states. This paper studies when releasing their outputs provides differential privacy. It considers both individual samples and Monte Carlo estimators constructed using the method, connecting their privacy guarantees to assumptions about how the underlying chain converges.

A central condition in the analysis is that the target distribution itself must satisfy differential privacy. The authors then specialize their results to the unadjusted Langevin algorithm and stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. They combine Girsanov’s theorem with a perturbation technique to establish Rényi differential privacy bounds in settings with unbounded domains and non-convex structure.

The results distinguish releasing the state after n iterations from releasing the entire trajectory. For the single released state, the authors obtain privacy guarantees uniform in n; they separately bound privacy for the full sequence. This distinction matters because a final sample and a record of the sampling process are different disclosures. The analysis supplies concrete guidance for designing privacy-preserving MCMC under the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional privacy guarantees for MCMC outputs and trajectories, including Langevin methods in non-convex, unbounded settings.

title: Differential Privacy Guarantees of Markov Chain Monte Carlo Algorithms

abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) models represent a significant advancement in large language model (LLM) development through their efficient parameter utilization. These models achieve substantial performance improvements at reduced inference costs. However, the deployment of SMoE models faces constraints from extensive memory requirements of expert components in resource-limited environments. To address these limitations, this paper introduces Hierarchical Clustering for Sparsely activated Mixture of Experts (HC-SMoE), a task-agnostic expert merging framework for parameter reduction without retraining. HC-SMoE introduces a novel hierarchical clustering approach based on expert outputs to ensure merging robustness independent of routing decisions. The proposed output-based clustering method enables effective capture of functional relationships between experts for largescale architectures. We provide theoretical analysis and comprehensive evaluations across multiple zero-shot language tasks to demonstrate HC-SMoE’s effectiveness in state-of-the-art models including Qwen and Mixtral. The experimental results validate HC-SMoE’s superior performance and practical applicability for real-world deployments. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/wazenmai/HC-SMoE.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models reduce inference computation by activating only selected experts, but all their expert components still create a large memory burden. This can constrain deployment in environments with limited resources. HC-SMoE addresses that burden by merging experts to reduce parameters without retraining the model.

The framework uses hierarchical clustering based on expert outputs. This organizes experts according to their functional relationships, providing a basis for deciding which components to merge. The authors design the clustering to make merging robust independently of routing decisions. The framework is also task-agnostic, so its merging formulation is not tied to a particular downstream task.

The paper provides theoretical analysis and evaluates the method across multiple zero-shot language tasks using models including Qwen and Mixtral. The reported results show superior performance and support practical deployment. Its central contribution is to use what experts produce as the basis for compression, connecting functional similarity with a retraining-free way to reduce the memory requirements of sparse expert architectures.
summary.tldr: HC-SMoE reduces sparse MoE parameters without retraining by hierarchically clustering and merging experts according to their outputs.

title: Retraining-free Merging of Sparse MoE via Hierarchical Clustering

abstract: Diffusion models approximate the denoising distribution as a Gaussian and predict its mean, whereas flow matching models reparameterize the Gaussian mean as flow velocity. However, they underperform in few-step sampling due to discretization error and tend to produce over-saturated colors under classifier-free guidance (CFG). To address these limitations, we propose a novel Gaussian mixture flow matching (GMFlow) model: instead of predicting the mean, GMFlow predicts dynamic Gaussian mixture (GM) parameters to capture a multi-modal flow velocity distribution, which can be learned with a KL divergence loss. We demonstrate that GMFlow generalizes previous diffusion and flow matching models where a single Gaussian is learned with an $L_2$ denoising loss. For inference, we derive GM-SDE/ODE solvers that leverage analytic denoising distributions and velocity fields for precise few-step sampling. Furthermore, we introduce a novel probabilistic guidance scheme that mitigates the over-saturation issues of CFG and improves image generation quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GMFlow consistently outperforms flow matching baselines in generation quality, achieving a Precision of 0.942 with only 6 sampling steps on ImageNet 256$\times$256.
originalAbstract: Diffusion models approximate the denoising distribution as a Gaussian and predict its mean, whereas flow matching models reparameterize the Gaussian mean as flow velocity. However, they underperform in few-step sampling due to discretization error and tend to produce over-saturated colors under classifier-free guidance (CFG). To address these limitations, we propose a novel Gaussian mixture flow matching (GMFlow) model: instead of predicting the mean, GMFlow predicts dynamic Gaussian mixture (GM) parameters to capture a multi-modal flow velocity distribution, which can be learned with a KL divergence loss. We demonstrate that GMFlow generalizes previous diffusion and flow matching models where a single Gaussian is learned with an $L_2$ denoising loss. For inference, we derive GM-SDE/ODE solvers that leverage analytic denoising distributions and velocity fields for precise few-step sampling. Furthermore, we introduce a novel probabilistic guidance scheme that mitigates the over-saturation issues of CFG and improves image generation quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GMFlow consistently outperforms flow matching baselines in generation quality, achieving a Precision of 0.942 with only 6 sampling steps on ImageNet 256$\times$256.

paragraphs: Standard diffusion and flow-matching formulations use a single Gaussian description, predicting either its mean or a corresponding flow velocity. The paper identifies two difficulties: errors when generation uses few sampling steps and oversaturated colors under classifier-free guidance. GMFlow addresses these through a richer probabilistic description of the generation process.

Instead of predicting one mean, GMFlow predicts changing Gaussian-mixture parameters to represent a flow-velocity distribution with multiple modes. Training uses a KL-divergence loss. The authors show that this formulation generalizes previous single-Gaussian models trained with a squared-error denoising loss, placing those models within the broader framework.

For generation, the paper derives stochastic and deterministic solvers that use analytic denoising distributions and velocity fields. A probabilistic guidance scheme also reduces the oversaturation associated with classifier-free guidance. Experiments consistently favor GMFlow over flow-matching baselines, including a reported Precision of 0.942 with six sampling steps on ImageNet at 256 by 256 resolution. The results support combining richer distributions with solvers and guidance designed to use them.
summary.tldr: GMFlow predicts Gaussian-mixture flow distributions and uses tailored solvers and guidance to improve few-step image generation.

title: Gaussian Mixture Flow Matching Models

abstract: Kronecker-sparse (KS) matrices—whose supports are Kronecker products of identity and all-ones blocks—underpin the structure of Butterfly and Monarch matrices and offer the promise of more efficient models. However, existing GPU kernels for KS matrix multiplication suffer from high data movement costs, with up to 50% of time spent on memory-bound tensor permutations. We propose a fused, output-stationary GPU kernel that eliminates these overheads, reducing global memory traffic threefold. Across 600 KS patterns, our kernel achieves in FP32 a median speedup of x1.4 and lowers energy consumption by 15%. A simple heuristic based on KS pattern parameters predicts when our method outperforms existing ones. We release all code at github.com/PascalCarrivain/ksmm, including a PyTorch-compatible KSLinear layer, and demonstrate in FP32 end-to-end latency reductions of up to 22% in ViT-S/16 and 16% in GPT-2 medium.

paragraphs: Kronecker-sparse matrices have structured nonzero patterns that support efficient model designs, including Butterfly and Monarch matrices. Their theoretical structure does not automatically translate into fast GPU execution. Existing kernels can spend up to half their time on memory-bound tensor permutations, making data rearrangement a major obstacle to realizing the promised efficiency.

The paper introduces a fused, output-stationary GPU kernel that eliminates these permutation overheads and reduces global memory traffic threefold. The design targets the movement of data during matrix multiplication. A simple heuristic based on the parameters of the sparsity pattern predicts when the new kernel will outperform existing alternatives.

Across 600 Kronecker-sparse patterns in FP32, the kernel achieves a median speedup of 1.4 times and reduces energy consumption by 15%. The authors also provide a PyTorch-compatible KSLinear layer and demonstrate end-to-end FP32 latency reductions of up to 22% in ViT-S/16 and 16% in GPT-2 medium. These results connect lower-level memory savings to practical model inference improvements.
summary.tldr: A fused GPU kernel reduces data movement in Kronecker-sparse multiplication and improves measured model inference latency.

title: Fast Inference with Kronecker-Sparse Matrices

abstract: The Spiking Neural Network (SNN), a biologically inspired neural network infrastructure, has garnered significant attention recently. SNNs utilize binary spike activations for efficient information transmission, replacing multiplications with additions, thereby enhancing energy efficiency. However, binary spike activation maps often fail to capture sufficient data information, resulting in reduced accuracy. To address this challenge, we advocate reversing the bit of the weight and activation, called ReverB, inspired by recent findings that highlight greater accuracy degradation from quantizing activations compared to weights. Specifically, our method employs real-valued spike activations alongside binary weights in SNNs. This preserves the event-driven and multiplication-free advantages of standard SNNs while enhancing the information capacity of activations. Additionally, we introduce a trainable factor within binary weights to adaptively learn suitable weight amplitudes during training, thereby increasing network capacity. To maintain efficiency akin to vanilla ReverB, our trainable binary weight SNNs are converted back to standard form using a re-parameterization technique during inference. Extensive experiments across various network architectures and datasets, both static and dynamic, demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks use binary spike activations to transmit information efficiently, replacing multiplications with additions. The paper argues that these binary activations can carry too little information, reducing accuracy. Motivated by findings that activation quantization damages accuracy more than weight quantization, it changes where the network uses binary values.

ReverB uses real-valued spike activations with binary weights. According to the paper, this increases activation information capacity while preserving event-driven operation and multiplication-free computation. A trainable factor further allows the binary weights’ amplitudes to adapt during training, increasing the capacity of the network.

At inference, re-parameterization converts the trainable-weight version back into the standard ReverB form to maintain comparable efficiency. Experiments across multiple architectures and both static and dynamic datasets report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a change in how numerical precision is allocated between activations and weights, together with a way to gain training flexibility without retaining that extra parameterization during inference.
summary.tldr: ReverB improves spiking-network information capacity by pairing real-valued spike activations with binary weights while preserving stated efficiency advantages.

title: ReverB-SNN: Reversing Bit of the Weight and Activation for Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Federated learning faces severe communication bottlenecks due to the high dimensionality of model updates. Communication compression with contractive compressors (e.g., Top-$K$) is often preferable in practice but can degrade performance without proper handling. Error feedback (EF) mitigates such issues but has been largely restricted for smooth, unconstrained problems, limiting its real-world applicability where non-smooth objectives and safety constraints are critical. We advance our understanding of EF in the canonical non-smooth convex setting by establishing new lower complexity bounds for first-order algorithms with contractive compression. Next, we propose Safe-EF, a novel algorithm that matches our lower bound (up to a constant) while enforcing safety constraints essential for practical applications. Extending our approach to the stochastic setting, we bridge the gap between theory and practical implementation. Extensive experiments in a reinforcement learning setup, simulating distributed humanoid robot training, validate the effectiveness of Safe-EF in ensuring safety and reducing communication complexity.

paragraphs: Federated learning can spend substantial communication on high-dimensional model updates. Compressors such as Top-K reduce what is transmitted, but compression can damage optimization performance. Error feedback addresses this problem, yet much of its existing theory concerns smooth objectives without constraints. The paper extends the analysis to non-smooth convex optimization with safety constraints.

The authors first establish lower complexity bounds for first-order algorithms that use contractive compression. These bounds set a theoretical benchmark for the resources such algorithms require. They then introduce Safe-EF, which matches their lower bound up to a constant while enforcing safety constraints. An extension covers stochastic optimization, bringing the method closer to settings with uncertain update information.

Experiments use a reinforcement-learning setup simulating distributed training of humanoid robots. The reported results support both safety enforcement and reduced communication complexity. The paper's contribution combines a lower-bound analysis with an algorithm designed to attain it, expanding error feedback to a setting where non-smoothness and constraints are central parts of the optimization problem.
summary.tldr: Safe-EF extends error feedback to non-smooth constrained optimization, matching a compression-related lower bound up to a constant while enforcing safety constraints.

title: Safe-EF: Error Feedback for Non-smooth Constrained Optimization

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have demonstrated remarkable ability to generate diverse and high-quality images by efficiently modeling complex data distributions. They have also been explored as powerful generative priors for signal recovery, resulting in a substantial improvement in the quality of reconstructed signals. However, existing research on signal recovery with diffusion models either focuses on specific reconstruction problems or is unable to handle nonlinear measurement models with discontinuous or unknown link functions. In this work, we focus on using DMs to achieve accurate recovery from semi-parametric single index models, which encompass a variety of popular nonlinear models that may have discontinuous and unknown link functions. We propose an efficient reconstruction method that only requires one round of unconditional sampling and (partial) inversion of DMs. Theoretical analysis on the effectiveness of the proposed methods has been established under appropriate conditions. We perform numerical experiments on image datasets for different nonlinear measurement models. We observe that compared to competing methods, our approach can yield more accurate reconstructions while utilizing significantly fewer neural function evaluations.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can supply prior information about plausible signals when recovering them from measurements. This paper targets nonlinear measurement settings that are difficult for existing diffusion-based recovery methods, particularly when the link function relating a signal to its measurements is unknown or discontinuous. It focuses on semi-parametric single index models, a family encompassing several such nonlinear problems.

The proposed reconstruction method requires one round of unconditional diffusion-model sampling and partial inversion. This design keeps the use of the diffusion model compact while applying its learned signal distribution to recovery. The paper establishes theoretical effectiveness under appropriate conditions, so its analytical guarantees are conditional rather than a claim that arbitrary nonlinear measurements can always be inverted accurately.

Experiments use image datasets with different nonlinear measurement models. Compared with competing methods, the approach can produce more accurate reconstructions while requiring significantly fewer neural function evaluations. The result connects reconstruction quality with computational economy: the reported improvements arise in a method designed to use the diffusion model sparingly, including in settings with challenging link functions.
summary.tldr: A diffusion-prior recovery method handles single index models with unknown or discontinuous links using one sampling round and partial inversion.

title: Learning Single Index Models with Diffusion Priors

abstract: In a fixed-confidence pure exploration problem in stochastic multi-armed bandits, an algorithm iteratively samples arms and should stop as early as possible and return the correct answer to a query about the arms distributions. We are interested in batched methods, which change their sampling behaviour only a few times, between batches of observations. We give an instance-dependent lower bound on the number of batches used by any sample efficient algorithm for any pure exploration task. We then give a general batched algorithm and prove upper bounds on its expected sample complexity and batch complexity. We illustrate both lower and upper bounds on best-arm identification and thresholding bandits.

paragraphs: In bandit pure exploration, an algorithm samples uncertain options to answer a question about their distributions with a prescribed level of confidence. It should reach the correct answer using as few observations as possible. This paper studies batched algorithms, whose sampling choices can change only between groups of observations.

Batching introduces a second resource to analyze: how often the algorithm must revise its sampling behavior. The authors establish an instance-dependent lower bound on the number of batches required by any sample-efficient algorithm for any pure exploration task. The qualification matters because the bound concerns algorithms that also use observations efficiently.

They then propose a general batched algorithm and prove upper bounds on its expected sample complexity and batch complexity. Best-arm identification and thresholding bandits illustrate both sides of the analysis. Together, the results characterize limits and achievable guarantees for balancing the number of observations with opportunities to adapt sampling decisions, making the cost of restricted adaptivity explicit.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds how many batches sample-efficient bandit exploration requires and provides a general algorithm with sample and batch complexity guarantees.

title: The Batch Complexity of Bandit Pure Exploration

abstract: Multi-View Reinforcement Learning (MVRL) seeks to provide agents with multi-view observations, enabling them to perceive environment with greater effectiveness and precision. Recent advancements in MVRL focus on extracting latent representations from multiview observations and leveraging them in control tasks. However, it is not straightforward to learn compact and task-relevant representations, particularly in the presence of redundancy, distracting information, or missing views. In this paper, we propose Multi-view Fusion State for Control (MFSC), firstly incorporating bisimulation metric learning into MVRL to learn task-relevant representations. Furthermore, we propose a multiview-based mask and latent reconstruction auxiliary task that exploits shared information across views and improves MFSC’s robustness in missing views by introducing a mask token. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in MVRL tasks. Even in more realistic scenarios with interference or missing views, MFSC consistently maintains high performance. The project code is available at https://github.com/zpwdev/MFSC.

paragraphs: Multiple views can help a reinforcement-learning agent perceive its environment, but they also introduce redundant or distracting information. Some views may be missing altogether. Multi-view Fusion State for Control, or MFSC, seeks a compact representation that combines useful information across observations while retaining what matters for control.

MFSC incorporates bisimulation metric learning into multi-view reinforcement learning to guide task-relevant representations. It also adds an auxiliary task that masks information across views and reconstructs latent representations. A mask token explicitly represents missing views. This training design uses information shared across observations to improve the representation’s robustness when not every view is available.

The reported experiments show better performance than existing approaches on multi-view reinforcement-learning tasks. MFSC also maintains high performance in evaluated scenarios involving interference or absent views. These findings support the value of jointly learning which information matters for control and how views can compensate for one another. The contribution concerns useful fusion under imperfect observation conditions, as well as ordinary multi-view performance.
summary.tldr: MFSC learns control-relevant representations from multiple views and uses masked reconstruction to improve robustness to distractions and missing observations.

title: Learning Fused State Representations for Control from Multi-View Observations

abstract: Recent Diffusion models (DMs) advancements have explored incorporating the second-order diffusion Fisher information (DF), defined as the negative Hessian of log density, into various downstream tasks and theoretical analysis. However, current practices typically approximate the diffusion Fisher by applying auto-differentiation to the learned score network. This black-box method, though straightforward, lacks any accuracy guarantee and is time-consuming. In this paper, we show that the diffusion Fisher actually resides within a space spanned by the outer products of score and initial data. Based on the outer-product structure, we develop two efficient approximation algorithms to access the trace and matrix-vector multiplication of DF, respectively. These algorithms bypass the auto-differentiation operations with time-efficient vector-product calculations. Furthermore, we establish the approximation error bounds for the proposed algorithms. Experiments in likelihood evaluation and adjoint optimization demonstrate the superior accuracy and reduced computational cost of our proposed algorithms. Additionally, based on the novel outer-product formulation of DF, we design the first numerical verification experiment for the optimal transport property of the general PF-ODE deduced map.

paragraphs: The diffusion Fisher studied here is the negative Hessian of log density, a second-order quantity describing its local curvature. It is useful in diffusion-model analysis and downstream tasks. Existing practice often approximates it by automatically differentiating a learned score network, which the authors describe as expensive and lacking accuracy guarantees.

The paper establishes that this quantity lies in a space spanned by outer products involving the score and initial data. That structure enables two approximation algorithms: one for its trace and another for multiplying it by a vector. Both replace the relevant automatic-differentiation operations with vector-product calculations, and the authors derive bounds on their approximation errors.

Experiments in likelihood evaluation and adjoint optimization report better accuracy and lower computational cost. The outer-product formulation also enables what the authors describe as the first numerical verification experiment for the optimal-transport property of a general probability-flow ODE map. The practical advance is access to useful second-order operations with explicit error analysis, accompanied by an additional tool for investigating diffusion theory.
summary.tldr: An outer-product characterization enables faster diffusion Fisher approximations with error bounds and improved reported accuracy.

title: Efficiently Access Diffusion Fisher: Within the Outer Product Span Space

abstract: Node classification is a fundamental task in graph analysis, with broad applications across various fields. Recent breakthroughs in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled LLM-based approaches for this task. Although many studies demonstrate the impressive performance of LLM-based methods, the lack of clear design guidelines may hinder their practical application. In this work, we aim to establish such guidelines through a fair and systematic comparison of these algorithms. As a first step, we developed LLMNodeBed, a comprehensive codebase and testbed for node classification using LLMs. It includes 10 homophilic datasets, 4 heterophilic datasets, 8 LLM-based algorithms, 8 classic baselines, and 3 learning paradigms. Subsequently, we conducted extensive experiments, training and evaluating over 2,700 models, to determine the key settings (e.g., learning paradigms and homophily) and components (e.g., model size and prompt) that affect performance. Our findings uncover 8 insights, e.g., (1) LLM-based methods can significantly outperform traditional methods in a semi-supervised setting, while the advantage is marginal in a supervised setting; (2) Graph Foundation Models can beat open-source LLMs but still fall short of strong LLMs like GPT-4o in a zero-shot setting. We hope that the release of LLMNodeBed, along with our insights, will facilitate reproducible research and inspire future studies in this field. Codes and datasets are released at https://llmnodebed.github.io/.

Its goal is to turn scattered performance results into practical design guidance through a systematic comparison. The researchers build LLMNodeBed, a shared codebase and testbed covering different graph structures, algorithms, and learning settings.

The testbed includes 10 homophilic datasets, four heterophilic datasets, eight LLM-based algorithms, eight classical baselines, and three learning paradigms. Across more than 2,700 trained and evaluated models, the study examines factors such as homophily, learning paradigm, model size, and prompting. In zero-shot evaluation, graph foundation models can outperform open-source LLMs but remain behind strong LLMs such as GPT-4o. These findings make the benefit conditional on the setting and model choice, providing more specific guidance than an overall claim that LLMs improve graph prediction.
summary.tldr: A large node-classification comparison shows that LLM benefits depend strongly on the learning setting and model choice.

title: When Do LLMs Help With Node Classification? A Comprehensive Analysis

abstract: Model-free reinforcement learning algorithms have seen remarkable progress, but key challenges remain. Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) is known for ensuring monotonic policy improvement through conservative updates within a trust region, backed by strong theoretical guarantees. However, its reliance on complex second-order optimization limits its practical efficiency. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) addresses this by simplifying TRPO’s approach using ratio clipping, improving efficiency but sacrificing some theoretical robustness. This raises a natural question: Can we combine the strengths of both methods? In this paper, we introduce Simple Policy Optimization (SPO), a novel unconstrained first-order algorithm. By slightly modifying the policy loss used in PPO, SPO can achieve the best of both worlds. Our new objective improves upon ratio clipping, offering stronger theoretical properties and better constraining the probability ratio within the trust region. Empirical results demonstrate that SPO outperforms PPO with a simple implementation, particularly for training large, complex network architectures end-to-end.

paragraphs: Simple Policy Optimization addresses a tradeoff between cautious policy updates and efficient training. TRPO offers strong theoretical guarantees through trust-region updates, but relies on complex second-order optimization. PPO simplifies the process with probability-ratio clipping, gaining practical efficiency while giving up some theoretical robustness. SPO aims to combine advantages of these approaches.

The proposed algorithm makes a small change to PPO’s policy loss and remains an unconstrained first-order method. Its objective provides stronger theoretical properties than ratio clipping and better constrains the probability ratio within the trust region. This ratio captures how the new policy’s action probabilities compare with those of the previous policy, making it central to controlling update size.

The authors report that SPO outperforms PPO empirically while retaining a simple implementation. Gains are particularly apparent when training large, complex networks end-to-end. The contribution shows how a modest objective change can improve both the theoretical treatment of policy updates and observed learning performance without requiring TRPO’s second-order optimization machinery.
summary.tldr: SPO modifies PPO’s loss to better control policy updates, offering stronger theoretical properties and improved reported performance with first-order optimization.

title: Simple Policy Optimization

abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) enhance interpretability by explaining predictions through human-understandable concepts but typically assume that training and test data share the same distribution. This assumption often fails under domain shifts, leading to degraded performance and poor generalization. To address these limitations and improve the robustness of CBMs, we propose the Concept-based Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (CUDA) framework. CUDA is designed to: (1) align concept representations across domains using adversarial training, (2) introduce a relaxation threshold to allow minor domain-specific differences in concept distributions, thereby preventing performance drop due to over-constraints of these distributions, (3) infer concepts directly in the target domain without requiring labeled concept data, enabling CBMs to adapt to diverse domains, and (4) integrate concept learning into conventional domain adaptation (DA) with theoretical guarantees, improving interpretability and establishing new benchmarks for DA. Experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art CBM and DA methods on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Concept Bottleneck Models explain predictions through concepts that people can understand. Their performance can deteriorate when the data encountered after training differs from the training distribution. CUDA addresses this problem by adapting concept-based models across domains, aiming to preserve the usefulness of concept explanations while improving performance under distribution changes.

The framework uses adversarial training to align concept representations between domains. It also introduces a relaxation threshold that permits small domain-specific differences. This matters because requiring concept distributions to match too strictly can itself hurt prediction. CUDA further infers concepts in the target domain without requiring labeled concept data there, supporting adaptation when those annotations are unavailable.

The paper connects concept learning with conventional domain adaptation and provides theoretical guarantees for that integration. Experiments on real-world datasets show significant improvements over the compared concept bottleneck and domain adaptation methods. The stated findings support treating interpretable concepts as part of the adaptation process, with room for meaningful differences between domains.
summary.tldr: CUDA adapts interpretable concept models across domains by aligning representations while allowing small domain-specific differences.

title: Concept-Based Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: We propose a framework for adaptive data collection aimed at robust learning in multi-distribution scenarios under a fixed data collection budget. In each round, the algorithm selects a distribution source to sample from for data collection and updates the model parameters accordingly. The objective is to find the model parameters that minimize the expected loss across all the data sources. Our approach integrates upper-confidence-bound (UCB) sampling with online gradient descent (OGD) to dynamically collect and annotate data from multiple sources. By bridging online optimization and multi-armed bandits, we provide theoretical guarantees for our UCB-OGD approach, demonstrating that it achieves a minimax regret of $O(T^{\frac{1}{2}}(K\ln T)^{\frac{1}{2}})$ over $K$ data sources after $T$ rounds. We further provide a lower bound showing that the result is optimal up to a $\ln T$ factor. Extensive evaluations on standard datasets and a real-world testbed for object detection in smart-city intersections validate the consistent performance improvements of our method compared to baselines such as random sampling and various active learning methods.
originalAbstract: We propose a framework for adaptive data collection aimed at robust learning in multi-distribution scenarios under a fixed data collection budget. In each round, the algorithm selects a distribution source to sample from for data collection and updates the model parameters accordingly. The objective is to find the model parameters that minimize the expected loss across all the data sources. Our approach integrates upper-confidence-bound (UCB) sampling with online gradient descent (OGD) to dynamically collect and annotate data from multiple sources. By bridging online optimization and multi-armed bandits, we provide theoretical guarantees for our UCB-OGD approach, demonstrating that it achieves a minimax regret of $O(T^{\frac{1}{2}}(K\ln T)^{\frac{1}{2}})$ over $K$ data sources after $T$ rounds. We further provide a lower bound showing that the result is optimal up to a $\ln T$ factor. Extensive evaluations on standard datasets and a real-world testbed for object detection in smart-city intersections validate the consistent performance improvements of our method compared to baselines such as random sampling and various active learning methods.

paragraphs: When training data comes from several sources, a fixed collection budget creates a practical choice: which source should supply the next example? This paper makes that choice part of learning itself. At each round, its algorithm selects a source, collects and annotates data, and updates the model, aiming to minimize expected loss across the sources.

The method, UCB-OGD, combines upper-confidence-bound sampling with online gradient descent. The sampling component uses uncertainty to guide source selection, while the optimization component updates the model from the collected evidence. Connecting these decisions lets data collection adapt as training proceeds, rather than committing the entire budget to a fixed allocation beforehand.

The authors prove a minimax regret bound of O(sqrt(T K ln T)) for K sources over T rounds, with a lower bound establishing optimality up to a logarithmic factor. Evaluations on standard datasets and smart-city intersection object detection report consistent improvements over random sampling and several active learning methods. Together, these results support adaptive source selection both theoretically and empirically.
summary.tldr: UCB-OGD adaptively chooses data sources during training, improving reported performance under a fixed collection budget with near-optimal regret guarantees.

title: Adaptive Data Collection for Robust Learning Across Multiple Distributions

abstract: Despite growing interest in incorporating feedback to improve language models, most efforts focus only on sequence-level annotations. In this work, we explore the potential of utilizing fine-grained span-level annotations from offline datasets to improve model quality. We develop a simple finetuning algorithm, called Training with Annotations (TWA), to directly train machine translation models on such annotated data. TWA utilizes targeted span-level error information while also flexibly learning what to penalize within a span. Moreover, TWA considers the overall trajectory of a sequence when deciding which non-error spans to utilize as positive signals. Experiments on English-German and Chinese-English machine translation show that TWA outperforms baselines such as supervised finetuning on sequences filtered for quality and Direct Preference Optimization on pairs constructed from the same data.

paragraphs: Feedback about an entire translation gives a broad quality signal, but annotations marking specific error spans provide more localized information. This paper investigates how machine translation models can learn from that finer-grained feedback in existing offline datasets. The aim is to make use of the locations of mistakes while also extracting useful supervision from the rest of a sequence.

The proposed algorithm, Training with Annotations, or TWA, directly fine-tunes models on annotated translations. It uses the identified error spans while retaining flexibility over what to penalize within each span. It also considers the trajectory of the whole sequence when selecting non-error spans as positive learning signals, making their use sensitive to the surrounding translation.

Experiments on English-German and Chinese-English translation show improvements over supervised fine-tuning on quality-filtered sequences and Direct Preference Optimization using pairs built from the same data. These comparisons support the usefulness of preserving span-level feedback during training. The findings show that localized error annotations can offer training value beyond sequence filtering or pairwise preference construction.
summary.tldr: TWA improves machine translation by learning selectively from annotated error spans and contextually useful non-error spans.

title: Learning from others’ mistakes: Finetuning machine translation models with span-level error annotations

abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) extract features from LLM internal activations, meant to correspond to interpretable concepts. A core SAE training hyperparameter is L0: how many SAE features should fire per token on average. Existing work compares SAE algorithms using sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff plots, implying L0 is a free parameter with no inherently correct value aside from its effect on reconstruction. In this work we study the effect of L0 on SAEs, and show that if L0 is not set correctly, the SAE fails to disentangle the underlying features of the LLM. If L0 is too low, the SAE will mix correlated features to improve reconstruction. If L0 is too high, the SAE finds degenerate solutions that also mix features. Further, we present a proxy metric that can help guide the search for the correct L0 for an SAE on a given training distribution. We show that our method finds the correct L0 in toy models and coincides with peak sparse probing performance in LLM SAEs. We find that most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low. Our work shows that practitioners must set L0 correctly to train SAEs with monosemantic features.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders try to break a language model’s internal activations into features corresponding to interpretable concepts. Their L0 setting controls how many features activate per token on average. This paper challenges the practice of treating that number mainly as a trade-off between sparsity and reconstruction, arguing that it also determines whether underlying features are separated correctly.

The authors identify problems at both extremes. When L0 is too low, the autoencoder mixes correlated features to improve reconstruction. When it is too high, degenerate solutions can also mix features. Good reconstruction and a chosen sparsity level therefore do not by themselves establish that the learned features each represent a single concept.

It finds the correct value in toy models and aligns with peak sparse-probing performance in language-model autoencoders. The authors also find that most commonly used autoencoders set L0 too low. Their results make selecting L0 correctly a requirement for the monosemantic features these methods seek.
summary.tldr: Sparse autoencoders can mix underlying concepts when their activation count is too low or too high, and a proposed proxy helps select that count.

title: Sparse but Wrong: Incorrect L0 Leads to Incorrect Features in Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) internalizes reasoning within continuous hidden states, offering a promising alternative to verbose discrete reasoning traces. However, robust latent reasoning remains difficult because outcome supervision provides weak learning signals and leaves latent trajectories prone to semantic drift. In this work, we analyze Latent CoT from an information-theoretic perspective and identify this failure as a dual collapse: gradient attenuation along the optimization path and representational drift in the latent space. We further decompose process supervision into two complementary dimensions: Trajectory Supervision, which injects dense stepwise reasoning signals, and Space Supervision, which preserves the semantic structure of the latent manifold. Our analysis shows that rigid geometric compression can collapse the reasoning space, whereas generative reconstruction provides a more flexible semantic anchor that better preserves information capacity. To measure these effects, we introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP), which quantifies the mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps. Experiments reveal a clear Information–Performance Binding: reasoning accuracy depends on the information fidelity preserved in the latent chain. These findings provide a principled framework for latent reasoning supervision and suggest shifting from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization. Our code will be released at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Supervision-in-Latent-CoT.

paragraphs: Latent chain-of-thought carries reasoning through continuous hidden states instead of explicit text steps. Training only on the final outcome can leave those states poorly supervised. This paper analyzes two connected failure modes: learning signals weaken along the optimization path, and hidden representations drift away from their intended reasoning meaning.

The authors separate process supervision into two roles. Trajectory supervision supplies dense signals at individual reasoning steps, while space supervision preserves semantic structure within the latent representation. Their analysis finds that rigid geometric compression can collapse the reasoning space. Generative reconstruction offers a more flexible anchor that better preserves its capacity to retain information.

To assess that retention, the Unified Latent Probe measures mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps. Experiments reveal a binding between information fidelity in the latent chain and reasoning accuracy. These findings motivate supervision that preserves reasoning information, and suggest emphasizing mutual information maximization over geometric imitation when designing training signals for latent reasoning.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic analysis links latent reasoning accuracy to preserved reasoning information and motivates complementary trajectory and semantic supervision.

title: What Makes Effective Supervision in Latent Chain-of-Thought: An Information-Theoretic Analysis

abstract: We present a constructive lower bound of $\Omega(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ for Frank-Wolfe (FW) when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex, showing that the known uniform $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ guarantees in this regime are tight. It is known that under additional assumptions on the position of the optimizer, FW can converge linearly. However, it remained unclear whether strong convexity of the set can yield rates uniformly faster than $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$, i.e., irrespective of the position of the optimizer. To investigate this question, we focus on a simple yet representative problem class: minimizing a strongly convex quadratic over the Euclidean unit ball, with the optimizer on the boundary. We analyze the dynamics of FW for this problem in detail and develop a novel computational approach to construct worst-case FW trajectories, which is of independent interest. Guided by these constructions, we develop an analytical proof establishing the lower bound.
