paragraphs: Frank–Wolfe has a known iteration guarantee proportional to 1/√ε when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex. This paper asks whether the curvature of the constraint set could support a uniformly faster guarantee. Uniformity matters here: the guarantee must hold regardless of where the optimizer lies.

The authors study a concrete problem family consisting of strongly convex quadratic objectives minimized over the Euclidean unit ball, with the optimizer on its boundary. They analyze the algorithm's dynamics and develop a computational method for constructing worst-case trajectories. Those constructions guide an analytical proof of a matching lower bound proportional to 1/√ε.

The result establishes that the existing uniform rate is tight in this regime: smoothness and strong convexity alone do not justify a faster worst-case guarantee. It remains compatible with known linear convergence under additional assumptions about the optimizer's position. The contribution therefore clarifies the distinction between favorable individual problem geometry and a rate that must cover every permitted optimizer location.
summary.tldr: A constructive lower bound proves that Frank–Wolfe's uniform 1/√ε iteration guarantee is tight even with smooth, strongly convex objectives and constraint sets.

title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

abstract: Modern conversational agents condition on an ever-growing dialogue history at each turn, incurring redundant attention and encoding costs that grow with conversation length. Naive truncation or summarization degrades fidelity, while existing context compressors lack cross-turn memory sharing or revision, causing information loss and compounding errors in long dialogues. We revisit the context compression under conversational dynamics and empirically present its fragility. To improve both efficiency and robustness, we introduce Context-Driven Incremental Compression (C-DIC), which treats a conversation as interleaved contextual threads and stores revisable per-thread compression states in a single, compact dialogue memory. At each turn, a lightweight retrieve $\rightarrow$ revise $\rightarrow$ write-back loop shares information across turns and updates stale memories, stabilizing long-horizon behavior. In addition, we adapt truncated backpropagation-through-time (TBPTT) to our multi-turn setting, learning cross-turn dependencies without full-history backpropagation. Extensive experiments on long-form dialogue benchmarks demonstrate superior performance and efficiency of C-DIC; notably, C-DIC maintains near-constant inference time and stable perplexity even over hundreds of dialogue turns, supporting a scalable path to high-quality dialogue modeling.

paragraphs: Long conversations repeatedly expose a model to an expanding history, increasing attention and encoding costs. Compressing that history can lose details, especially when earlier summaries cannot be shared or revised across turns. The paper examines this fragility and proposes a dialogue memory that changes as the conversation develops.

Context-Driven Incremental Compression treats a conversation as several interleaved contextual threads. Each thread has a revisable compressed state within one compact memory. At each turn, the system retrieves relevant memory, revises it using the current context, and writes it back. This allows later information to update stale memories instead of letting outdated compressed descriptions persist.

The training method adapts truncated backpropagation through time so the model learns dependencies across turns without backpropagating through the entire history. On long-form dialogue benchmarks, the authors report better performance and efficiency, including near-constant inference time and stable perplexity over hundreds of turns. The findings support treating compression as ongoing memory maintenance, where preserving conversational continuity requires both reuse and revision.
summary.tldr: C-DIC maintains revisable memories for conversational threads, supporting efficient and stable dialogue generation over hundreds of turns.

title: Context-Driven Incremental Compression for Multi-Turn Dialogue Generation

abstract: Disentanglement learning aims to separate the underlying factors of variation (FoV) to improve generalization. However, most FoV-based latent-vector-centric methods impose objective-driven constraints at a bottleneck, and it is difficult to translate disentanglement into consistent gains on downstream tasks without inductive bias. Motivated by architectural approaches complementary to vector-centric objectives for downstream tasks, we propose the Orthogonal Subspaces Projection (OSP) layer, a plug-and-play module that integrates into intermediate layers and promotes FoV separation by projecting latent features into mutually orthogonal subspaces. Across diverse domains and tasks, models equipped with the OSP layer improve disentanglement quality and generalization in downstream tasks, including computer vision (classification, detection, and segmentation), natural language processing (word analogy, and text classification), and fine-tuning settings on large backbones.

paragraphs: Disentanglement aims to separate the underlying factors that vary in data so models can generalize more effectively. Many approaches constrain a latent vector at a bottleneck through a training objective. The paper points out that these constraints do not easily translate into consistent downstream improvements without a suitable inductive bias.

The proposed Orthogonal Subspaces Projection layer supplies an architectural mechanism for encouraging separation. It can be inserted into intermediate layers and projects latent features into mutually orthogonal subspaces. This builds a preference for separated representations into the model’s structure. The approach is presented as complementary to objectives that operate on latent vectors, broadening where disentanglement can be encouraged.

Across the reported experiments, adding OSP improves both disentanglement quality and downstream generalization. The evaluations span image classification, detection, segmentation, word analogy, text classification, and fine-tuning of large backbones. This breadth matters because the intended benefit is useful task performance as well as cleaner internal representations. The reported findings support the module across several domains and model settings without establishing that every possible model or task will benefit.
summary.tldr: The OSP layer encourages disentangled features through orthogonal projections, improving downstream generalization across the evaluated vision and language tasks.

title: Layer-Centric Factors of Variation Disentanglement for Task- and Model-Agnostic Generalization

abstract: Real-world domains often contain heterogeneous tables whose headers vary while their underlying attribute semantics are shared, making it difficult to induce domain-specialized semantics from table-local evidence alone. Existing encoders model parts of this problem, but often underuse column-level value distributions and apply uniform objectives across attributes with different semantic roles. We propose NAVI, a segment-centric pretraining framework that treats each header–value pair as the unit for aggregating schema-level structural evidence and column-level distributional evidence. We realize this design through Masked Segment Modeling and Entropy-driven Segment Alignment, which jointly enforce structured header–value coupling and semantic alignment across stable and instance-specific attributes. Experiments on heterogeneous in-domain tables show improved reconstruction, semantic consistency, and downstream utility across evaluation settings overall.

paragraphs: Tables from the same domain can describe shared attributes using different headers. A representation learned from one table alone may therefore miss common meanings across tables. The paper also identifies two underused signals: the distribution of values in a column and differences in the semantic roles that attributes play.

NAVI organizes pretraining around segments, with each segment consisting of a header and value pair. This unit brings together evidence from the table’s schema and the column’s value distribution. Its Masked Segment Modeling and Entropy-driven Segment Alignment objectives jointly encourage structured header–value relationships and semantic alignment across stable and instance-specific attributes.

The approach matters because it connects the naming and organization of an attribute with evidence from the values it contains. It also avoids treating every attribute’s semantic role as interchangeable within the learning objectives. Experiments on heterogeneous tables within a domain report overall improvements in reconstruction, semantic consistency, and downstream usefulness across the evaluation settings. Those findings support the segment-centered design for learning shared domain semantics from varied tables.
summary.tldr: NAVI learns heterogeneous table representations from header–value segments, combining schema structure with column distributions to improve semantic consistency and downstream utility.

title: Segment-driven Structural Induction and Semantic Alignment for Heterogeneous Tabular Representation

abstract: Active feature acquisition (AFA) is a sequential decision-making problem where the goal is to improve model performance for test instances by adaptively selecting which features to acquire. In practice, AFA methods often learn from retrospective data with systematic missingness in the features and limited task-specific labels. To address this limitation, we introduce Learning-to-Measure (L2M), which consists of i) reliable uncertainty quantification over unseen tasks, and ii) an uncertainty-guided feature acquisition agent that maximizes conditional mutual information. We demonstrate an autoregressive pre-training approach that underpins reliable uncertainty quantification and acquisition for tasks with arbitrary missingness. L2M operates directly on datasets with retrospective missingness and performs the task in-context, eliminating per-task retraining. Across synthetic and real-world tabular benchmarks, L2M matches or surpasses task-specific baselines, particularly under scarce labels and high missingness.

paragraphs: Active feature acquisition asks which additional measurement would most improve a prediction for a particular test instance. The decision must be made sequentially, using what is already known. In practice, training data may themselves contain systematic gaps, and only a small number of labels may be available for the task of interest.

Learning-to-Measure combines uncertainty estimation across unseen tasks with an acquisition agent guided by that uncertainty. The agent maximizes conditional mutual information, selecting features for the information they are expected to provide given the current observations. An autoregressive pre-training approach supports uncertainty estimation and acquisition for tasks with arbitrary missingness.

L2M works directly with retrospectively incomplete datasets and performs new tasks in context, without retraining separately for each one. Across synthetic and real-world tabular benchmarks, it matches or exceeds task-specific baselines, with particular strengths when labels are scarce and missingness is high. The findings support using a shared pre-trained system to guide measurement decisions across different tasks.
summary.tldr: L2M uses in-context uncertainty estimates to choose informative measurements, performing well on tabular tasks with scarce labels and substantial missing data.

title: Learning-To-Measure: In-Context Active Feature Acquisition

abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become a predominant approach for aligning large language models with human preferences. Recent work has used perplexity differentials to identify unreliable preference labels, but these methods apply uniform calibration strategies across all samples. We observe that the reliability of perplexity signals varies substantially across task types: perplexity differentials strongly correlate with preference quality for factual tasks but provide weak signals for creative tasks where novelty is valued. Based on this observation, we propose Task-Aware Preference Calibration (TAPC), which learns task-conditioned calibration functions that adapt to the characteristics of different prompt types. TAPC employs a task encoder to extract prompt representations and learns task-specific slope and bias parameters for mapping perplexity signals to confidence targets. Through meta-learning on a small reference dataset, TAPC discovers how to weight perplexity signals appropriately for each task category. Experiments on Llama-3-8B and Qwen2-7B demonstrate that TAPC outperforms existing methods across multiple benchmarks, with particularly large improvements on creative and open-ended tasks where uniform calibration strategies fail.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization trains language models using preferred and dispreferred responses, making unreliable preference labels a problem. Some methods use differences in perplexity to judge label reliability. This paper finds that the signal depends strongly on the task: it correlates well with preference quality for factual prompts but weakly for creative prompts, where novelty matters.

Task-Aware Preference Calibration, or TAPC, learns how to interpret that signal for different prompt types. A task encoder represents the prompt, and task-specific slope and bias parameters map perplexity differences into confidence targets. Meta-learning on a small reference dataset teaches the system how much weight to give the signal for each task category.

Experiments with Llama-3-8B and Qwen2-7B show improvements over existing methods across multiple benchmarks. Gains are particularly large on creative and open-ended tasks, where uniform calibration performs poorly. The contribution is a way to account for the changing meaning of a reliability indicator: a useful clue for factual quality should receive a different interpretation when the task rewards novel responses.
summary.tldr: TAPC calibrates preference-label confidence by task type, improving DPO especially on creative and open-ended tasks.

title: Task-Aware Preference Calibration for Direct Preference Optimization

abstract: Despite their dominance in vision and language, deep neural networks often underperform relative to tree-based models on tabular data. To bridge this gap, we incorporate five key inductive biases into deep tabular learning: robustness to irrelevant features, axis alignment, localized irregularities, feature heterogeneity, and training stability. We propose LassoFlexNet, an architecture that evaluates the linear and nonlinear marginal contribution of each input via Per-Feature Embeddings, and sparsely selects relevant variables using a Tied Group Lasso mechanism. Because these components introduce optimization challenges that destabilize standard proximal methods, we analyze stochastic hierarchical proximal dynamics and develop a Sequential Hierarchical Proximal Adaptive Gradient optimizer with exponential moving averages (EMA) designed to stabilize training in practice. Across 52 datasets from three benchmarks, LassoFlexNet matches or outperforms leading tree-based models, achieving up to a $10$% relative gain, while maintaining Lasso-like interpretability. We substantiate these empirical results with ablation studies and theoretical proofs confirming the architecture’s enhanced expressivity and structural breaking of undesired rotational invariance.

paragraphs: Neural networks often trail tree-based models on tabular data. LassoFlexNet addresses this by building in properties suited to tables: resistance to irrelevant inputs, respect for individual feature axes, localized irregular behavior, differences among feature types, and stable training. These design choices make the architecture sensitive to how tabular variables are organized.

Per-feature embeddings assess each input’s linear and nonlinear contribution, while a tied group-lasso mechanism selects relevant variables sparsely. These components create optimization difficulties for standard proximal methods. The authors therefore analyze hierarchical proximal dynamics and develop a sequential adaptive-gradient optimizer with exponential moving averages to stabilize training in practice.

Across 52 datasets from three benchmarks, LassoFlexNet matches or exceeds leading tree-based models, with relative gains reaching 10%, while retaining lasso-like interpretability. Ablations support the design choices, and theoretical results establish enhanced expressivity and the structural removal of unwanted rotational invariance. Together, the results connect competitive tabular performance to an architecture that treats individual variables as meaningful and can explicitly suppress irrelevant ones.
summary.tldr: LassoFlexNet combines per-feature modeling, sparse variable selection, and specialized optimization to achieve competitive tabular prediction with interpretable feature selection.

title: LassoFlexNet: a Flexible Neural Architecture for Tabular Data

abstract: Continuous-time, event-native spiking neural networks (SNNs) operate strictly on spike events, treating spike timing and ordering as the representation rather than an artifact of time discretization. This viewpoint aligns with biological computation and with the native resolution of event sensors and neuromorphic processors, while enabling compute and memory that scale with the number of events. However, two challenges hinder practical, end-to-end trainable event-based SNN systems: 1) exact charge–fire–reset dynamics impose inherently sequential processing of input spikes, and 2) precise spike times must be solved without time bins. We address both. First, we use parallel associative scans to consume multiple input spikes at once, yielding up to 44x speedups over sequential simulation while retaining exact hard-reset dynamics. Second, we implement differentiable spike time solvers that compute spike times to machine-precision without discrete-time approximations or restrictive analytic assumptions. We demonstrate the viability of training SNNs using our solutions on four event-based datasets on GPUs.

title: Bullet Trains: Parallelizing Training of Temporally Precise Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Generating high-fidelity 3D indoor scenes remains a significant challenge due to data scarcity and the complexity of modeling intricate spatial relations. Current methods often struggle to scale beyond training distribution to dense scenes or rely on LLMs/VLMs that lack the ability for precise spatial reasoning. Building on top of the observation that object placement relies mainly on local dependencies instead of information-redundant global distributions, in this paper, we propose Pair2Scene, a novel procedural generation framework that integrates learned local rules with scene hierarchies and physics-based algorithms. These rules mainly capture two types of inter-object relations, namely support relations that follow physical hierarchies, and functional relations that reflect semantic links. We model these rules through a network, which estimates spatial position distributions of dependent objects conditioned on position and geometry of the anchor ones. Accordingly, we curate a dataset 3D-Pairs from existing scene data to train the model. During inference, our framework can generate scenes by recursively applying our model within a hierarchical structure, leveraging collision-aware rejection sampling to align local rules into coherent global layouts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing methods in generating complex environments that go beyond training data while maintaining physical and semantic plausibility.

paragraphs: Creating detailed indoor scenes requires placing objects in arrangements that are both physically possible and semantically sensible. Pair2Scene builds on the observation that placement depends mainly on nearby object relationships. It learns these local rules and combines them with scene hierarchies and physics-based procedures to construct larger environments.

The learned rules cover support relationships, which follow physical hierarchies, and functional relationships, which capture semantic connections. A network predicts where a dependent object might be placed from an anchor object’s position and geometry. The authors curate 3D-Pairs from existing scene data to provide training examples of these relationships.

Experiments show that Pair2Scene outperforms existing methods on complex environments extending beyond the training data while preserving physical and semantic plausibility. The result supports composing learned local relationships as a way to scale scene generation beyond the complete layouts seen during training.
summary.tldr: Pair2Scene assembles complex indoor scenes from learned object-pair relationships, hierarchies, and collision-aware sampling.

title: Pair2Scene: Learning Local Object Relations for Procedural Scene Generation

abstract: We derive algorithms for smooth nonconvex nonconcave minimax optimization and establish linear convergence rates for problems that satisfy the two-sided Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) inequality. At the core of our approach is the observation that Lyapunov functions can be used not only to certify convergence a posteriori, but also to design algorithms. By replacing an idealized, intractable Lyapunov function with a computable surrogate based on gradient information, we derive TALDA (Tri-Action Lyapunov Descent Ascent), a single-loop algorithm that enforces Lyapunov descent by construction. TALDA guarantees linear convergence under the two-sided PL condition, with a rate that depends explicitly on the cross-smoothness constant. This recovers existing worst-case guarantees while yielding sharper convergence rates in weakly coupled min–max problems.

paragraphs: Minimax optimization involves variables pulling an objective in opposing directions: one side minimizes while the other maximizes. This paper studies smooth problems that may be neither convex on the minimizing side nor concave on the maximizing side. Its convergence results apply to problems satisfying the two-sided Polyak–Lojasiewicz condition, a specific structural assumption on both sides.

The central idea is to use a Lyapunov function to construct the optimization algorithm itself. Such functions usually serve as measures of progress when analyzing an existing method. Here, the authors replace an idealized but intractable Lyapunov function with a computable surrogate based on gradients, then design updates that enforce descent in that surrogate.

The resulting single-loop algorithm, TALDA, has a linear convergence guarantee under the stated condition. Its rate explicitly reflects cross-smoothness, which captures coupling between the minimizing and maximizing variables. This recovers existing worst-case guarantees while giving sharper rates when the two sides interact weakly. The contribution connects a proof tool directly to algorithm design and makes the convergence analysis sensitive to problem structure.
summary.tldr: TALDA turns Lyapunov analysis into an algorithm-design principle, with linear convergence under the two-sided PL condition and sharper rates for weakly coupled problems.

title: From Lyapunov Analysis to Algorithm Design in two-sided PL Minimax Optimization

abstract: This paper develops a general transfer learning framework for nonparametric regression with data consisting of multiple groups. Under the assumption that groups share a common structure along with group-specific deviations in additive form, the proposed method employs a two-stage offset learning procedure: the first stage pools data from all groups to estimate an overall mean function, and the second stage estimates offsets for each group, yielding final group-level estimators through additive combination. Upper bounds on the $\mathcal L_2$ error are established for the proposed framework, covering a broad class of nonparametric estimators under mild complexity and noise conditions. When instantiated with deep ReLU networks, explicit convergence rates are derived under hierarchical composition models, demonstrating the ability to overcome the curse of dimensionality. Conditions that enable positive transfer with faster rates are considered, including learning with simpler functions and data augmentation through pooling samples across groups. Various simulations and real-data experiments further validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression across multiple groups that share an underlying structure but also have group-specific differences. Its key assumption is additive: each group’s function can be represented through shared structure plus a deviation. That setup creates an opportunity to borrow information across groups while retaining the features that make each group distinct.

The proposed procedure has two stages. First, it pools observations from all groups to estimate an overall mean function. Second, it learns an offset for each group and adds that offset to the pooled estimate. For deep ReLU networks, they derive explicit convergence rates under hierarchical composition models, showing how the method can overcome the curse of dimensionality in that setting. They also examine conditions for faster rates through positive transfer, including simpler functions and pooling-based sample augmentation. Simulations and real-data experiments support the approach’s effectiveness alongside these conditional theoretical results.
summary.tldr: A pooled regression estimate plus group-specific offsets enables transfer learning, with favorable error rates under shared additive structure and stated model conditions.

title: Transfer Learning in Nonparametric Regression with Deep ReLU Networks

abstract: Principal component analysis classically requires full $d$-dimensional samples, yet in various applications hardware limits acquisition to a few scalar measurements per sample. We analyze a compressed variant of Oja’s algorithm for estimating the principal eigenvector of the data covariance matrix using only two adaptive measurements per sample. At each iteration, we observe one measurement along the current estimate and one in a random orthogonal direction. We prove that after $t$ iterations, the expected sine-squared error to the true eigenvector is $\mathcal{O}(\lambda_1\lambda_2 d^2 / (\Delta^2 t))$, where $d$ is the ambient dimension, $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ are the leading eigenvalues, and $\Delta = \lambda_1 - \lambda_2$ is the eigengap. We complement this with a matching information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(\lambda_1\lambda_2 d^2 / (\Delta^2 t))$ — the first for compressed eigenvector estimation — proving that the $d^2$ factor, an additional factor of $d$ compared to the fully-observed minimax rate $\Theta(\lambda_1\lambda_2 d / (\Delta^2 t))$, is the fundamental cost of compression and cannot be improved. In contrast, any non-adaptive scheme with two measurements per iteration suffers $\Omega(\lambda_2^2 d^3 / (\Delta^2 t))$, an additional power of $d$. This separates fully-observed, adaptive-compressed, and non-adaptive-compressed PCA across three powers of $d$. Our analysis handles the noisy setting where the covariance has nonzero trailing eigenvalues, providing the first convergence guarantee for adaptive compressed subspace tracking beyond the noiseless case.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis usually assumes access to every coordinate of each data sample. This paper considers hardware that permits only two scalar measurements per sample. It analyzes a compressed version of Oja’s algorithm that measures along the current principal-direction estimate and along a randomly chosen orthogonal direction.

The authors prove that expected squared angular error decreases at a rate proportional to λ₁λ₂d²/(Δ²t), where t is the number of iterations, d is dimension, and Δ separates the two leading eigenvalues. Fully observed estimation instead has linear dependence on dimension.

This distinguishes the costs of full observation, adaptive compression, and non-adaptive compression. The analysis includes noise represented by nonzero trailing covariance eigenvalues, extending convergence guarantees beyond the noiseless case. Adaptively choosing measurements therefore has a provable role in limiting the statistical price of restricted sensing.
summary.tldr: Two adaptive measurements per sample achieve a provably optimal compressed principal-eigenvector estimation rate in the analyzed setting.

title: Global Convergence of Adaptive Sensing for Principal Eigenvector Estimation

abstract: We introduce Distribution Contractive Reinforcement Learning (DICE-RL), a framework that uses reinforcement learning (RL) as a "distribution contraction" operator to refine pretrained generative robot policies. DICE-RL turns a pretrained behavior prior into a high-performing "pro" policy by amplifying high-success behaviors from online feedback. We pretrain a diffusion- or flow-based policy for broad behavioral coverage, then finetune it with a stable, sample-efficient residual off-policy RL framework that combines selective behavior regularization with value-guided action selection. Extensive experiments and analyses show that DICE-RL reliably improves performance with strong stability and sample efficiency. It enables mastery of complex long-horizon manipulation skills directly from high-dimensional pixel inputs, both in simulation and on a real robot. Project website: dice.rl.2026.

paragraphs: DICE-RL studies how to turn a broadly capable pretrained robot policy into a more consistently successful one. Its central idea is to use reinforcement learning to concentrate the policy’s behavior distribution around actions that work well. Online feedback identifies successful behaviors that the refinement process can amplify.

The starting policy uses diffusion or flow modeling to provide broad behavioral coverage. A residual off-policy reinforcement-learning framework then refines it, combining selective behavior regularization with value-guided action selection. These components connect the existing behavior prior to feedback about action quality, supporting improvement while maintaining stable learning.

The reported experiments show reliable performance gains with strong stability and sample efficiency. DICE-RL also supports complex manipulation skills that unfold over long sequences, using high-dimensional pixel inputs in both simulation and a real robot. The findings suggest that broad generative pretraining and focused reinforcement-learning refinement can play complementary roles: the prior supplies behavioral possibilities, and feedback concentrates execution on more successful ones.
summary.tldr: DICE-RL refines pretrained generative robot policies by concentrating their behavior on actions that succeed under online feedback.

title: From Prior to Pro: Efficient Skill Mastery via Distribution Contractive RL Finetuning

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale large language models efficiently by sparsely activating experts, but once an expert is selected, it is executed fully. Hence, the trade-off between accuracy and computation in an MoE model typically exhibits large discontinuities. We propose Mixture of Slimmable Experts (MoSE), an MoE architecture in which each expert has a nested, slimmable structure that can be executed at variable widths. This enables conditional computation not only over which experts are activated but also over how much of each expert is utilized. Consequently, a single pretrained MoSE model can support a more continuous spectrum of accuracy-compute trade-offs at inference time. We present a simple and stable training recipe for slimmable experts under sparse routing, combining multi-width training with standard MoE objectives. During inference, we explore strategies for runtime width determination, including a lightweight test-time training mechanism that learns how to map router confidence/probabilities to expert widths under a fixed budget. Experiments on GPT-style models, various routing regimes, zero-shot downstream reasoning benchmarks, and continual pre-training adaptation of DeepSeek model show that MoSE matches or improves standard MoE at full width and consistently shifts the compute-quality frontier toward lower inference FLOPs. The code can be found at: https://github.com/tnurbek/mose.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts language models save computation by activating only selected experts, but typically execute each chosen expert in full. This makes changes in computational cost relatively coarse. MoSE adds another decision: how much of each selected expert to run, allowing one pretrained model to operate across a more continuous range of compute budgets.

Each expert has a nested structure that supports execution at different widths. Training combines multiple widths with standard mixture-of-experts objectives so that sparse routing and variable expert size work together. The findings support controlling both expert selection and expert width as complementary ways to allocate computation.
summary.tldr: MoSE lets selected experts run at variable widths, giving a single language model finer control over inference cost and quality.

title: MoSE: Mixture of Slimmable Experts for Efficient and Adaptive Language Models

abstract: Process rewards have been widely used in deep reinforcement learning to improve training efficiency, reduce variance, and prevent reward hacking. In LLM reasoning, existing works also explore various solutions for learning effective process reward models (PRM) with or without the help of an expert policy. However, existing methods either rely on strong assumptions about the expert policies (e.g., requiring their reward functions) or suffer intrinsic limitations (e.g., entropy collapse), resulting in weak PRMs or limited generalizability. In this paper, we introduce rePIRL, an inverse RL-inspired framework that learns effective PRMs with minimal assumptions about expert policies. Specifically, we design a dual learning process that updates the policy and the PRM interchangeably. Our learning algorithm has customized techniques to address the challenges of scaling traditional inverse RL to LLMs. We theoretically show that our proposed learning framework can unify both online and offline PRM learning methods, justifying that rePIRL can learn PRMs with minimal assumptions. Empirical evaluations on standardized math and coding reasoning datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of rePIRL over existing methods. We further show the application of our trained PRM in test-time training, test-time scaling, and providing an early signal for training hard problems. Finally, we validate our training recipe and key design choices via a detailed ablation study.

title: rePIRL: Learn PRM with Inverse RL for LLM Reasoning

abstract: In automated machine learning, scientific discovery, and other applications of Bayesian optimization, deciding when to stop evaluating expensive black-box functions in a cost-aware manner is an important but underexplored practical consideration. A natural performance metric for this purpose is the cost-adjusted simple regret, which explicitly captures the trade-off between solution quality and cumulative evaluation cost. Existing stopping rules for Bayesian optimization are either heuristic, or are theoretically grounded but designed to optimize simple regret without accounting for evaluation costs; as a result, they provide no guarantees against unnecessary evaluations when costs are high. We propose a principled cost-aware stopping rule for Bayesian optimization that adapts to varying evaluation costs without heuristic tuning. Our rule is grounded in a theoretical connection to state-of-the-art cost-aware acquisition functions, namely the Pandora’s Box Gittins Index (PBGI) and log expected improvement per cost (LogEIPC). When paired with either acquisition function, we prove that the resulting policy satisfies a theoretical guarantee bounding the expected cost-adjusted simple regret. Across synthetic tasks and empirical benchmarks including hyperparameter optimization and neural architecture size search, pairing our stopping rule with PBGI or LogEIPC usually matches or outperforms other acquisition-function–stopping-rule pairs in terms of cost-adjusted simple regret.

It also needs a stopping decision: another evaluation may improve the answer, but incur more cost than the improvement justifies. This paper studies that trade-off through cost-adjusted simple regret, a measure that combines solution quality with accumulated evaluation cost.

The qualification matters: the empirical result is generally favorable, while the theoretical guarantee applies to the specified pairings. Together, these results make stopping part of the optimization objective itself.
summary.tldr: A theoretically grounded stopping rule helps Bayesian optimization balance further solution improvements against evaluation costs.

title: Cost-aware Stopping for Bayesian Optimization

abstract: We study grokking — the onset of generalization long after overfitting — in a classical ridge regression setting. We prove end-to-end grokking results for learning over-parameterized linear regression models using gradient descent with weight decay. Specifically, we prove that the following stages occur: (i) the model overfits the training data early during training; (ii) poor generalization persists long after overfitting has manifested; and (iii) the generalization error eventually becomes arbitrarily small. Moreover, we show, both theoretically and empirically, that grokking can be amplified or eliminated in a principled manner through proper hyperparameter tuning. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first rigorous quantitative bounds on the generalization delay (which we refer to as the "grokking time") in terms of training hyperparameters. Lastly, going beyond the linear setting, we empirically demonstrate that our quantitative bounds also capture the behavior of grokking on non-linear neural networks. Our results suggest that grokking is not an inherent failure mode of deep learning, but rather a consequence of specific training conditions, and thus does not require fundamental changes to the model architecture or learning algorithm to avoid.

paragraphs: Grokking describes a training pattern in which a model fits its training data well long before it begins to generalize. This paper proves that the phenomenon can occur in classical ridge regression, using overparameterized linear models trained with gradient descent and weight decay. That setting makes the delay mathematically analyzable.

The results establish the full sequence: early overfitting, an extended period of poor generalization, and eventual arbitrarily small generalization error. The authors also derive quantitative bounds on the delay in terms of training hyperparameters. Theory and experiments show that suitable hyperparameter choices can amplify or eliminate grokking, connecting its timing to controllable aspects of training.

That extension is empirical, while the end-to-end proof concerns the linear setting. Together, the results suggest that grokking can arise from particular training conditions and may be avoidable through tuning, without requiring fundamental changes to the architecture or learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: The paper proves grokking in ridge regression and quantifies how training hyperparameters can prolong or eliminate delayed generalization.

title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

abstract: Existing LLM test-time scaling laws emphasize the emergence of self-reflective behaviors through extended reasoning length. Nevertheless, this vertical scaling strategy often encounters plateaus in exploration as the model becomes locked into specific thinking pattern. By shifting from depth to parallelism, parallel thinking mitigates the narrowing of exploration. However, the extension of this paradigm to visual domain remains an open research question. In this paper, we first examine the role of visual partitioning in parallelized reasoning and subsequently propose two distinct strategies. Based on the above, we introduce Visual Para-Thinker, representing the inaugural parallel reasoning framework for MLLMs. To maintain path independence and promote diversity in reasoning, our approach integrates Pa-Attention alongside LPRoPE. Leveraging the vLLM framework, we have developed a native multimodal implementation that facilitates high-efficiency parallel processing. Empirical results on benchmark datasets such as V*, CountBench, RefCOCO, and HallusionBench confirm that Visual Para-Thinker successfully extends the benefits of parallel reasoning to the visual domain.
originalAbstract: Existing LLM test-time scaling laws emphasize the emergence of self-reflective behaviors through extended reasoning length. Nevertheless, this vertical scaling strategy often encounters plateaus in exploration as the model becomes locked into specific thinking pattern. By shifting from depth to parallelism, parallel thinking mitigates the narrowing of exploration. However, the extension of this paradigm to visual domain remains an open research question. In this paper, we first examine the role of visual partitioning in parallelized reasoning and subsequently propose two distinct strategies. Based on the above, we introduce Visual Para-Thinker, representing the inaugural parallel reasoning framework for MLLMs. To maintain path independence and promote diversity in reasoning, our approach integrates Pa-Attention alongside LPRoPE. Leveraging the vLLM framework, we have developed a native multimodal implementation that facilitates high-efficiency parallel processing. Empirical results on benchmark datasets such as V*, CountBench, RefCOCO, and HallusionBench confirm that Visual Para-Thinker successfully extends the benefits of parallel reasoning to the visual domain.

paragraphs: Giving a model more time to reason does not always broaden its exploration: a longer reasoning sequence can remain trapped in one pattern. Parallel thinking instead pursues multiple reasoning paths. This paper investigates how that strategy can be extended to visual comprehension, where the organization of visual information becomes part of the reasoning design.

The authors first study visual partitioning and propose two strategies, then introduce Visual Para-Thinker for multimodal large language models. The framework combines Pa-Attention with LPRoPE to maintain independence among paths and encourage diverse reasoning. Those components support the goal of obtaining distinct explorations rather than allowing parallel paths to collapse into the same line of thought.

A native multimodal implementation built on vLLM supports efficient parallel processing. Experiments on V*, CountBench, RefCOCO, and HallusionBench report that the benefits of parallel reasoning extend to visual tasks. The contribution connects visual partitioning, path independence, and execution efficiency within one framework, providing empirical support for parallelism as an additional way to scale visual reasoning.
summary.tldr: Visual Para-Thinker combines visual partitioning and independent parallel reasoning paths to improve multimodal visual comprehension.

title: Visual Para-Thinker: Divide-and-Conquer Reasoning for Visual Comprehension

abstract: Recent advances in group-based reinforcement learning (RL) greatly improve LLMs’ ability in text reasoning. Yet, these methods lack sufficient modeling of multimodal information, leading to significant reasoning hallucination. In this work, we propose POLIA, a novel group-based RL method with visual-object-level intrinsic advantage for multimodal reasoning. POLIA introduces two advantage computation stages over candidate answers and visual objects, respectively. The answer-level extrinsic advantages are computed based on the extrinsic rewards of a group of candidate answers. Moreover, we compute an intrinsic advantage for each visual object based on its confidence score and reference relations with final answers. Intuitively, the intrinsic advantage of an object reflects its potential contribution to the correct answer. This two-stage advantage computation ensures an accurate credit assignment mechanism over multimodal reasoning sequences with multiple visual objects. Experimental results on diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that POLIA significantly outperforms open MLLMs and strong baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/dudu115/POLIAcode.

paragraphs: Group-based reinforcement learning can improve text reasoning, but multimodal reasoning also requires identifying which visual evidence supports an answer. The paper argues that insufficient modeling of this information contributes to reasoning hallucinations. POLIA adds learning signals at the level of individual visual objects alongside rewards for complete candidate answers.

The method computes advantages in two stages. First, it compares candidate answers using their external rewards. Second, it assigns each visual object an intrinsic advantage based on its confidence score and its reference relationships with final answers. This object-level quantity reflects the object's potential contribution to reaching a correct answer.

The combined signal supports credit assignment across reasoning sequences involving multiple objects. It helps training account for the visual elements involved in an answer as well as the answer's overall success. Experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report significant improvements over open multimodal language models and strong baselines. The contribution is a training method that explicitly connects answer-level evaluation with object-level evidence, giving multimodal reasoning a more detailed basis for learning.
summary.tldr: POLIA improves multimodal reinforcement learning by assigning credit to individual visual objects as well as complete answers.

title: POLIA: Policy Optimization with Visual-Object-Level Intrinsic Advantage for Multimodal Reasoning

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables decentralized clients to collaboratively train a global model without sharing raw data. However, most existing FL frameworks assume that clients train on static local datasets collected in advance or that the data follows a fixed underlying distribution, which limits their applicability in dynamic environments where data evolves over time. A parallel line of research, online FL, removes all assumptions and adopts an adversarial perspective, but this approach is often overly pessimistic and neglects the structured, partially predictable nature of real-world data dynamics. To bridge this gap, we propose SFedPO, a streaming federated learning framework that incorporates a prediction oracle to capture the temporal evolution of client-side data distributions. We theoretically analyze the convergence bounds of SFedPO and develop two practical sampling strategies: a Distribution-guided Data Sampling (DDS) strategy that dynamically selects training data under limited storage by balancing historical reuse and distribution adaptation, and a Shift-aware Aggregation Weights (SAW) mechanism that modulates global aggregation based on client-specific sampling behaviors. We further establish robustness guarantees under prediction errors. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SFedPO effectively adapts to streaming scenarios with distribution shifts and significantly outperforms existing methods.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines training across clients without sharing their raw data, but many approaches assume local data distributions stay fixed. Streaming applications violate that assumption. SFedPO instead treats temporal change as partly predictable, occupying a middle ground between static-data methods and fully adversarial online formulations that can be overly pessimistic.

The framework uses a prediction oracle to anticipate how client-side distributions evolve. Distribution-guided Data Sampling selects training examples under limited storage, balancing reuse of historical data with adaptation to the current distribution. Shift-aware Aggregation Weights adjust how client contributions enter the global model according to their sampling behavior, connecting local data selection to global learning.

The paper analyzes convergence and establishes robustness guarantees when the predictions contain errors. Extensive experiments show effective adaptation to streaming distribution shifts and significant improvements over existing methods. The findings support using forecasts of data evolution to guide both what clients retain for training and how their updates are combined, while the theory explicitly accounts for imperfect predictions.
summary.tldr: SFedPO uses predicted distribution changes to guide client sampling and aggregation in streaming federated learning.

title: SFedPO: Streaming Federated Learning with a Prediction Oracle under Temporal Shifts

abstract: Image-to-3D generation faces inherent semantic ambiguity under occlusion, where partial observation alone is often insufficient to determine object category. In this work, we formalize text-driven amodal 3D generation, where text prompts steer the completion of unseen regions while strictly preserving input observation. Crucially, we identify that these objectives demand distinct control granularities: rigid control for the observation versus relaxed structural control for the prompt. To this end, we propose RelaxFlow, a training-free dual-branch framework that decouples control granularity via a Multi-Prior Consensus Module and a Relaxation Mechanism. Theoretically, we prove that our relaxation is equivalent to applying a low-pass filter on the generative vector field, which suppresses high-frequency instance details to isolate geometric structure that accommodates the observation. To facilitate evaluation, we introduce two diagnostic benchmarks, ExtremeOcc-3D and AmbiSem-3D. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RelaxFlow successfully steers the generation of unseen regions to match the prompt intent without compromising visual fidelity. Code and datasets will be released.

paragraphs: A partially hidden object can admit several plausible 3D interpretations, so an image alone may not reveal its category or unseen shape. This paper formalizes a task in which text directs completion of the hidden regions while the visible observation must remain strictly preserved. The challenge is to make these two forms of guidance cooperate.

RelaxFlow assigns them different levels of control. Its training-free dual-branch framework combines a Multi-Prior Consensus Module with a Relaxation Mechanism, keeping observation constraints rigid while allowing the prompt to guide broader structure. The authors prove that the relaxation is equivalent to low-pass filtering the generative vector field, suppressing fine instance details to isolate geometry that can accommodate the observation.

The paper introduces ExtremeOcc-3D and AmbiSem-3D as diagnostic benchmarks. Experiments show that RelaxFlow can steer unseen regions toward the prompt's intended meaning without compromising visual fidelity. The central contribution is a principled separation of precise visual constraints from more flexible semantic guidance, addressing the ambiguity inherent in reconstructing objects from incomplete views.
summary.tldr: RelaxFlow separates rigid observation constraints from flexible text guidance to complete hidden 3D geometry without compromising visible fidelity.

title: RelaxFlow: Text-Driven Amodal 3D Generation

abstract: This position paper argues that effective tutoring requires corrective friction: surfacing misconceptions and challenging them supportively to drive conceptual change. Yet preference-aligned LLMs can trade epistemic rigor for agreeableness. We identify a Reasoning-Sycophancy Paradox: models that resist context-switch frame attacks can still capitulate under social-epistemic pressure, especially authority ("my notes say I’m right") and social-affective face-saving ("please don’t tell me I’m wrong”). We introduce EduFrameTrap, a tutoring benchmark across math, physics, economics, chemistry, biology, and computer science that varies student confidence and pressure (context-switch, authority, social-affective). Across two frontier LLMs, context-switch failures are comparatively lower for GPT-5.2, while authority and social pressure more often trigger epistemic retreat. In contrast, Claude shows substantial context-switch fragility in this run. Because these failures are hard to judge automatically, we report two-judge disagreement as a reliability signal. We argue benchmarks should measure social-epistemic courage, i.e., supportive but corrective tutoring, and treat kind-but-correct behavior as a safety requirement.

paragraphs: Good tutoring requires supportive correction of misconceptions. This paper argues that language models aligned with user preferences can sacrifice correctness to maintain agreement. It identifies a paradox: a model may withstand attempts to change the conversational frame yet still abandon a sound position when a student invokes authority or asks to avoid embarrassment.

The authors introduce EduFrameTrap, covering mathematics, physics, economics, chemistry, biology, and computer science. It varies student confidence and three forms of pressure: context switching, appeals to authority, and social or emotional pressure. This design examines whether a tutor preserves its corrective role under different interaction conditions.

Across two frontier models, GPT-5.2 has comparatively fewer context-switch failures, while authority and social pressure more often prompt retreat from correctness. Claude exhibits substantial context-switch fragility in this run. Because judging these failures automatically is difficult, the authors report disagreement between two judges as a reliability signal. They advocate evaluating supportive correction directly and treating behavior that remains both kind and correct as an educational safety requirement.
summary.tldr: EduFrameTrap tests whether LLM tutors maintain supportive correction when students apply conversational, authority, or social pressure.

title: Position: Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks

abstract: Benchmark datasets are critical for reproducible, reliable, and discriminative evaluation of LLMs. However, recent studies reveal that many benchmark datasets are included in pretraining corpora, i.e., contaminated, which diminishes their value as reliable measures of model generalization. In this paper, we argue that benchmark datasets should be contamination-resistant, i.e., unlearnable, but support inference. To accomplish this, we first highlight the wide prevalence of benchmark dataset contamination and outline the properties of contamination-resistant datasets. Second, we highlight how the asymmetry between the inference and training pipelines in the Transformer architecture can be leveraged to support contamination-resistance. Third, we outline mathematical advancements to make these datasets interoperable across various LLM architectures. Based on the above, we call on the community to ensure the reliability of LLM benchmarking by: (i) advancing novel contamination-resistant methodologies, (ii) developing supporting methods and platforms, and (iii) adopting contamination-resistant benchmarks into existing evaluation pipelines.

paragraphs: A benchmark becomes a weaker test of generalization when its examples enter a model’s training data. This paper argues that the response should include redesigning benchmark datasets themselves. The proposed target is contamination resistance: data that supports evaluation during inference while resisting learning through the training process.

The authors first describe the prevalence of contamination and outline the properties such datasets should have. They then identify differences between Transformer training and inference pipelines as a possible technical basis for this resistance. The central idea is to exploit an asymmetry between how a model learns from data and how it uses inputs when producing answers.

The paper also outlines mathematical developments intended to make contamination-resistant datasets work across different LLM architectures. Its contribution is a direction for benchmark design and an agenda for supporting research and infrastructure. The authors call for new methods, platforms, and adoption within existing evaluation workflows so that benchmarks can retain their ability to distinguish model performance and provide reliable evidence of generalization.
summary.tldr: The paper advocates benchmarks that remain usable during inference while resisting learning if they enter training data.

abstract: Regularized Kernel Discriminant Analysis (RKDA) performs linear discriminant analysis in the feature space via the kernel trick. The performance of RKDA depends on the selection of kernels. In this paper, we consider the problem of learning an optimal kernel over a convex set of kernels. We show that the kernel learning problem can be formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP) in the binary-class case. We further extend the SDP formulation to the multi-class case. It is based on a key result established in this paper, that is, the multi-class kernel learning problem can be decomposed into a set of binary-class kernel learning problems. In addition, we propose an approximation scheme to reduce the computational complexity of the multi-class SDP formulation. The performance of RKDA also depends on the value of the regularization parameter. We show that this value can be learned automatically in the framework. Experimental results on benchmark data sets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed SDP formulations.

paragraphs: Regularized kernel discriminant analysis performs linear discriminant analysis in a feature space defined through a kernel. Its performance depends on both the kernel and the regularization parameter. This paper brings these choices into an optimization framework, seeking an optimal kernel within a specified convex set of candidate kernels.

For two classes, the authors show that kernel learning can be written as a semidefinite program. They then establish that the multiclass kernel learning problem can be decomposed into a collection of binary problems. This result supports a multiclass extension of the optimization formulation, connecting the more complex setting to the two-class construction.

The paper also proposes an approximation scheme to reduce the computational cost of the multiclass formulation. In addition, the regularization parameter can be learned automatically within the same framework. Experiments on benchmark datasets support the effectiveness of the formulations. The contribution is thus a shared optimization approach for two consequential modeling choices, together with a computational approximation for the multiclass case.
summary.tldr: Semidefinite programming learns kernels and regularization for discriminant analysis, with a binary decomposition and approximation supporting multiclass problems.

title: Discriminant kernel and regularization parameter learning via semidefinite programming

abstract: Nearest neighbor ($k$-NN) graphs are widely used in machine learning and data mining applications, and our aim is to better understand what they reveal about the cluster structure of the unknown underlying distribution of points. Moreover, is it possible to identify spurious structures that might arise due to sampling variability? Our first contribution is a statistical analysis that reveals how certain subgraphs of a $k$-NN graph form a consistent estimator of the cluster tree of the underlying distribution of points. Our second and perhaps most important contribution is the following finite sample guarantee. We carefully work out the tradeoff between aggressive and conservative pruning and are able to guarantee the removal of all spurious cluster structures while at the same time guaranteeing the recovery of salient clusters. This is the first such finite sample result in the context of clustering.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor graphs are often used to reveal clusters, but a finite sample can also produce apparent structure that does not reflect the underlying distribution. This paper asks what these graphs reliably reveal and how to remove spurious branches from a cluster hierarchy without discarding meaningful clusters.

The first contribution analyzes particular subgraphs of a k-nearest-neighbor graph as estimators of the distribution's cluster tree. The authors establish statistical consistency, connecting the graph-based hierarchy to the underlying distribution as more data become available. This gives a theoretical basis for using those subgraphs to estimate hierarchical cluster structure.

The second contribution addresses finite samples, where pruning requires balancing aggressive removal against preservation of real structure. The paper derives a guarantee that removes all spurious cluster structures while recovering salient clusters within its analysis. This matters because an asymptotic consistency result alone does not resolve the pruning decision for a finite dataset. The authors identify their result as the first such finite-sample guarantee in clustering.
summary.tldr: A statistical analysis of nearest-neighbor cluster trees gives finite-sample pruning guarantees that remove spurious structure while preserving salient clusters.

title: Pruning nearest neighbor cluster trees
